# AutoDev Console Migration Tracker

> **Scope:** Current implementation state, gaps, cutover dependencies, and acceptance evidence for the AutoDev Console/OpenLIT migration.
>
> **Authority:** [autodev-console-target-state.md](autodev-console-target-state.md) is authoritative for product, architecture, UI, ownership, and correctness requirements. This file records only observed implementation state and remaining migration work.
>
> **Last reviewed:** 2026-10-19 (OpenLIT patch 58 Memory UI retirement and live GitHub Actions/Console verification; external/live evidence retains its observation dates).

## Current baseline

The repository is on the four-workspace TypeScript layout (Console, Runtime, Core, Data) and the obsolete root implementation tree is gone. OpenLIT plus the AutoDev Control API are the target observability/control foundation, but the migration is not complete: the unified Console still lacks full feature parity, the OpenLIT product shell still contains unwanted generic product code, RuleSync role/permission parity is incomplete, and router-owned direct OTLP/history paths remain.

The active local OpenLIT baseline is:

- upstream OpenLIT openlit-2.1.0 at commit 9938c66638666ca5d3bcb850350faa82e510924b;
- published baseline image ghcr.io/openlit/openlit@sha256:94552ccd09379b5e2fec3c51c4fec1b41d88d6b56b0a5ccc895c116673884fa8;
- active OpenLIT container runs `autodev-openlit:openlit-9938c6663866-p28c7add35b2db7ba`, image ID `sha256:a7a2477d9bb02eef6c12e2353612674630f6c2b6914ed97846d68ae2e391dcad` (healthy; started 2026-10-19 21:20 UTC), matching `$CODEX_HOME/openlit-patched.lock` and the current source patch-set hash `28c7add35b2db7ba`;
- `scripts/openlit/up.sh` rebuilt/reconciled this exact 58-patch set, restarted OpenLIT, and passed the live Usage v5 contract verifier;
- telemetry retention 730 hours (about 30 days), with durable local volumes and no automated backup.

The source patch series has since moved to 64 patches: 59 adds the `requests-by-workspace` Usage widget the Workspaces surface reads, 60 removes the fork's dead client modules together with the dependency and the unresolvable import that came with them, 61 removes the fork's write half of the provider and model catalog, 62 corrects two stale assertions in the fork's own test suite that patches 56 and the counter-deltas work had left behind, 63 carries the collector's memory budget and its Codex-internal span filter into the fork, and 64 carries the ClickHouse merge pool and memory budget with it. All six are verified to apply cleanly to the pinned revision, with the removal assertions and the client's dependency contract checked against the patched tree. Patches 63 and 64 exist because the mounted Collector and ClickHouse configs were edited in the mounted copy only: the fork's own copies still carried the upstream budgets, so the file the product ran and the file the image was built from were two owners of one config. The deployed image is still the 58-patch p28c7 build, so patches 59 to 64 are source-only: the live Usage API does not yet answer the `requests-by-workspace` widget, and the live client still carries the dead modules and the second provider and model authority. The current p28c7 image passed the pinned OpenLIT Next production build and is deployed from the matching patch hash. `scripts/openlit/up.sh` verified the v5 Usage contract live; it left the existing 65 prompts, 10 agent roles, 6 providers/40 models unchanged and synchronized five workspace records. Three warm `/usage` HTTP requests to the local Console dev server on :3300 returned 200 in 0.94–1.32s. At 390/768/1280, headless Chromium verified all six compaction labels, the explicit empty-source state, `data-usage-observed=true`, no Usage error codes, no page/console errors, and no document overflow. This is local-dev browser evidence; broader production route/navigation/mutation browser acceptance remains open. The isolated synthetic Playwright suite passes all 13 browser tests; its staging build and dynamic ports avoid overwriting a live `.next`.

An Oct 14 repeat reproduced the reported invalid-response state only on three pre-existing unmanaged `next start` processes running an older Console bundle (9/9 requests); the live OpenLIT endpoint returned v4/19-widget payloads and the current Data client validated 15 sequential plus 4 concurrent reads. The current Console dev server rendered `/usage` successfully on 3/3 refreshes. This isolates the failure to a stale Console bundle held by long-lived `next start` processes, not malformed OpenLIT query data. The normal installer now builds into a unique staging directory, promotes only a completed `BUILD_ID`, then reloads and verifies the managed Console after Runtime; direct `next start` remains unsupported. A read-only probe isolated the live Usage banner to the detached Playwright `next start` still on port 3377 (its synthetic Control API fixture remains on 4311): `/usage` there returns `autodev_openlit_usage_invalid_response`, while `/usage` on the dev Console at 3300 is clean against the same OpenLIT v4 endpoint. This stale test server was left untouched; the new E2E runner avoids its ports and output directory. The shared services were not restarted during this task.

A read-only 2026-10-14 port sweep found `/usage` clean on the current dev Console at 3300 and `autodev_openlit_usage_invalid_response` on all three detached Playwright `next start` servers at 3377–3379. The 3377 process is paired with the synthetic Control API fixture on 4311; process ancestry identifies these as long-lived `nohup pnpm start` E2E servers, not managed Console or Router LaunchAgents. They were left untouched pending a safe cleanup window. The E2E harness now chooses free ports and builds/serves a separate `.next-staging-e2e-*` artifact, so new browser runs cannot overwrite a live production `.next`; all 13 synthetic Playwright tests, including provider discovery at mobile width, pass.

## Console backend compatibility gate

The current Runtime source exposes authenticated `/control/contracts` and read-only `/control/provider-models`. The shared compatibility revision is v13: it includes provider-owned model discovery, the typed Playtesting schema-readiness contract, the operator-only Providers reset operation, the Providers response carrying each provider's reconciliation view, the Runtime's MCP observations published on their own read path (`GET /control/mcp-runtime`) so the MCP catalog stays a configuration read, and the MCP configuration the Runtime published published on its own read path (`GET /control/mcp-applied`) and reconciled against the canonical declaration. Development and production launchers probe Providers v3, provider-model-discovery v1, and workspace-scoped Playtesting before serving; OpenLIT Usage is independently validated through the same Data client/parser used by `/usage`. An incompatible or absent contract is a startup failure, not a per-page invalid-data surprise, and no old response is accepted as a fallback.

A live read-only probe on 2026-10-13 found the installed Runtime returned `autodev-control-agents-v1` while this checkout requires v2; the previous startup checks passed because they covered Providers v2 and Playtesting only. A repeat on 2026-10-14 against the active Model Router at port 4101 found `/control/contracts` still returns 404 and `/control/agents` still returns v1. The already-running Console dev process predating the new contract preflight rendered `autodev_control_api_invalid_agents_response` at that time; the updated root launcher now rejects an incompatible Runtime before starting Next. The live OpenLIT p85 Usage endpoint returned validated v4 responses on repeated sequential and concurrent probes; `/usage` stayed free of telemetry error states during those renders. On 2026-10-14 the current Runtime source was materialized into `$CODEX_HOME/src` with `bash scripts/install.sh --materialize-only`; `runtime/src/control-api/index.ts` byte-compared equal to the installed source. The 2026-10-14 recheck deliberately did not restart the already-running Router and then still found `/control/contracts` returning 404 and `/control/agents` returning v1; a later local Console read confirms the current v10 contract and provider-model endpoint respond. Managed Runtime and Console release verification remains a separate safe-window acceptance gate.

The root test runner executes workspace suites one at a time so the Console’s ratio-based URL-performance guard is not measured under concurrent Data/Runtime CPU load. Its existing growth threshold is unchanged; the focused guard passed ten isolated repetitions.

## Console control affordances

The Console's markup asserted its own contract and its pages did not deliver it, so this pass measured the rendered pages rather than reading them. A computed-style sweep of all fourteen routes found every `<button>` rendering `cursor: default` -- "Apply filters", "Reset to defaults", the per-session steppers, the provider row's limit buttons -- while looking and behaving like buttons; the shared button vocabulary had no pointer class and twenty-one feature files spelled `cursor-pointer` inline instead, so the same role had two spellings and the shared vocabulary had none. A `getClientRects()` sweep found the same table header measuring 35.5px on twelve routes and 50.5px on two: "Active Agents" was 13px narrower than its own name, so it wrapped to two lines, and "Requests" was 2px narrower than its label plus its help marker, so the marker dropped onto a line of its own -- a bare "?" under the label it explains. The shared table contract says a column's weight must be large enough for its own header, and its own comment claimed no header needed to break, so this changes no rendered output today; it did. The agent enablement pill and the model enablement pill were byte-identical chrome, the same three tones and the same explanatory paragraph, written twice, and neither carried a pointer cursor.

Every page's heading outline also began with the sidebar's three group labels -- "Configure", "Observe", "Operate" -- ahead of the page's own title and at the same level as the page's body sections, because the sidebar is chrome and sits before the shell header in the document. The group labels are labels now, not headings: the group is still a labelled region and `aria-labelledby` names it from the same element. And a scroll region had no way to say that it scrolls: a table's declared widths are a content budget, the region scrolls when the viewport cannot provide it, and macOS hides overlay scrollbars until you scroll, so at 1440px five of eleven routes had their last column cut in half with a chip sliced mid-word -- a rendering fault rather than more content to the right. The Console's scroll regions now wear a thin scrollbar in its own border token, and `scrollbar-width`/`scrollbar-color` take them out of the overlay behaviour; the table's own geometry is unchanged with and without the rule.

A link's name also has to say what it points at. Three tables repeated one name per row: every prompt carried an "Evaluations" link, every tool repeated a filter link per exposed role, and every agent repeated a provider link. The links were correct -- each pointed at its own row -- but a links list, which is how a screen reader user scans a page, showed "Evaluations" seventy-six times and "Filter tools exposed to smart" twenty-four times with nothing to tell the entries apart. The visible text stays short and the accessible name carries the row, and the name still contains the visible text so a voice-control user can say what they see. The same rule reaches the tabs: the "Tools" tab on an MCP server and the Tools catalog are two different destinations under one name, and the navigation carries both on every page, so the shared tab primitive takes an optional accessible name and the MCP detail page names the two tabs that share a label with a top-level page. Measured in a real browser against the production build, no route -- list or detail -- has a link name that points at two different destinations.

Measured in a real browser against the production build after the change: every table header row on every route measures 35.5px, no help marker is orphaned from its label, no interactive control on any of the fourteen routes is missing its pointer, the first heading on every route is the page's own `h1`, and the scroll regions compute `scrollbar-width: thin`. The Console's own suite is 761/761, and `console/tests/control-affordances.test.ts` pins the properties rather than the class names.

**The failed-change notice was measured against the owner that ends a result, and it keeps no countdown of its own.** The Console already has one owner for "this result is over": the root-mounted feedback owner, which announces the outcome, counts the five seconds down in the words the acceptance pins (`Dismisses in 5 seconds`), and offers a keyboard-reachable close. Its own failure message is the pointer -- "The server could not save these changes. Review the notice on this page." -- and the page's own notice is where that pointer lands: it carries the reason the route observed (`confirmation_missing`, `conflicted`, `request_invalid`, ...), and each reason names a different next move, so it is the one thing the operator has to act on. A first attempt gave the notice its own five-second countdown and its own close, in different words (`Dismissing in 5s`, `aria-hidden`, a second dismiss button): it would have ended the reason before it could be read, left the owner's pointer aimed at nothing, and given the Console two spellings of one behaviour -- the drift the target state's "the same status vocabulary ... across features" forbids. It does not. The notice now carries a `data-control-refusal-detail` marker, so the two suites that read the reason address it by what it means rather than by attribute order, and `console/tests/control-failure-notice.test.ts` pins that the notice carries no countdown and no close of its own. Measured in Chromium against the installed production build, a refused write leaves the page's notice reading "The change could not be confirmed. Check the current state before retrying." followed by "This changed since the list you acted on was read. Reload it and decide again.", and it is still reading it seven seconds later, with no countdown inside it; against the current source, the owner shows the write's outcome counting down from "Dismisses in 5 seconds" to gone.

**The prompt preview took the operator's place away from them while it worked, and stayed quiet when it had an answer.** The preview island is the newest surface on the prompt page, and it had never been measured in a browser. Two things showed up. The control was disabled while the request was in flight, and a disabled control is dropped out of the page's focus order the moment it is disabled: the button had the focus, the request started, the browser moved the focus to the document, and when the answer came back the operator's next Tab started from the top of the page instead of from the control they had just used. The Console's own form owner publishes its pending state rather than disabling its controls, for exactly that reason, so the preview publishes it too -- `aria-disabled` on the control, the visible label carrying the state, and the focus left where the operator put it. And the outcome was silent in the case an operator wants: a preview that came back valid appeared without a word, while a preview the canonical parser refused spoke, because only the refusal carried a live region. The island announces through one region now -- the pending state, the ready state, and the refusal carrying the parser's own reason, each announced once. It also stopped saying two things at once: a response the route turned down used to raise the generic alert _and_ the outcome, so the operator read "The unsaved source could not be previewed." on top of the reason it was given. Measured in Chromium against the current source: the focus stays on the control from the click through the answer, the pending state is announced while the request is in flight, and the refusal is announced once, with the parser's own sentence.

**A control that is working was written as a control that is unavailable, and the rule belongs to the vocabulary.** The prompt preview's defect turned out to be one instance of a class. The Console's own islands were already right -- the auto-submit select never disables anything, and the form owner publishes its pending state on the form and leaves its controls focusable -- but every surface that fetches for itself and disabled its submit button while the request was in flight was losing the operator's focus the same way. Measured on the workspace approval form: the button held the focus, the request started, the browser moved the focus to the document, and the next Tab started from the top of the page. The shared button vocabulary now says "busy" for that state: `aria-disabled` keeps the control announced as unavailable while it stays in the focus order, the visible label carries the state, and the unavailable chrome (`aria-disabled:opacity-60`, `aria-disabled:cursor-not-allowed`) makes it look like what it says. A disabled button is still disabled -- the two are different things and the vocabulary keeps them apart -- and the prompt preview and the two workspace approval forms use the busy state. The playtesting strand's own forms still disable their controls while they work; those surfaces belong to the other session, and they now have the vocabulary to adopt. Measured in Chromium against the current source, on the workspace approval form: the focus stays on the button from the click through the answer, with `aria-disabled` and `data-submitting` published while it works.

**A table that scrolls sideways had to be reachable by a keyboard, and the permission matrix was not.** The Console's tables scroll inside their own region when the viewport cannot hold the table's content budget, which is the contract: the table keeps its proportions and its region scrolls. But a region that scrolls has to be reachable by keyboard, and the permission matrix was the case that needed it -- its cells hold no links and no controls, so nothing inside could be focused, the region was not focusable either, and its right-hand columns were reachable with a pointer and by nothing else. The shared table primitive now gives every table a named, focusable region, so the arrow keys scroll it and a screen reader says which table it is. The region is named after the table's own columns unless the view knows a better name for it, and the permission matrix takes the name its heading already gives it. Measured in Chromium at 390px on the permission matrix: the region takes focus, it shows a visible focus ring, and two presses of the arrow key scroll it from 0 to 80 pixels -- where before the arrow keys did nothing and there was nothing to focus.

## Provider model discovery

The canonical Providers contract requires provider-owned model discovery outside request/routing hot paths, with distinct observed, stale, and unavailable states; discovery never rewrites routing assignments or becomes a Console catalog authority. Runtime exposes authenticated read-only `GET /control/provider-models`; its bounded background refresher has verified sources for Antigravity (`agy models`), MiniMax (authenticated `GET /v1/models`), Claude (Anthropic `GET /v1/models` authenticated with the account's Claude Code OAuth token), and Codex (authenticated ChatGPT Codex backend `GET /models` using the existing Codex account token and account ID). Codex discovery stays unavailable when Runtime routes Codex through a different base URL, rather than sending account credentials to an unverified endpoint. Its source is the current-account endpoint used by the official Codex model provider, not the local merged picker catalog. Copilot remains explicitly unavailable because the local bridge/proxy `/v1/models` handlers return hard-coded adapter capabilities, not provider-owned account availability, and the Copilot CLI exposes no model-list command; its fallback catalogs/default IDs were removed. Codex's current source is covered by an injected-auth HTTP test, but no live Codex request was made in this implementation pass. The prior 2026-10-14 MiniMax live read returned eight provider-owned IDs while its static picker catalog contained two. The read emitted no credentials or model prompts. Discovery preserves routeability separately from provider availability, returns stale last-known results after refresh failures/restarts, and never persists credentials. The Console reads observed/stale/unavailable states and unsupported IDs, offers new role assignments only from currently observed routeable models, and preserves existing assignments unchanged during outages. Runtime rejects model enablement changes unless the model is currently observed and routeable. A current read through the local Console confirms `/control/contracts` and `/control/provider-models` respond; the rendered provider discovery state is mixed observed, stale, and unavailable, so this is not evidence of fresh availability for every provider or a managed-production rollout. Three direct read-only `agy models` probes took 5.06–8.49 seconds; the previous eight-second Antigravity deadline could expire during a valid listing. Runtime now gives this CLI source a separate 30-second bound while keeping provider HTTP-listing deadlines at eight seconds. A fake-child regression test proves a listing completing at 8.5 seconds is accepted and a stalled CLI is still terminated at the configured bound. The 12-second bound the listing first got was still too tight: `agy models` measured 3.0-9.0 seconds on an idle machine on 2026-10-22 and exceeded twelve seconds while the machine was busy, which turned a valid listing into a stale one and left the Antigravity models unselectable. The refresher runs off the request path, so the bound can afford the source's measured latency. A direct read-only call through the updated Runtime adapter observed 13 models in 5.53 seconds; this exercised the source implementation, not the already-running Runtime service, which has not yet loaded the change.

A 2026-10-21 pass fixed the two defects that made role-assignment writes fail across every provider. The installed Runtime loaded two copies of its own routing policy, so the Control API never saw a discovered model and rejected every new role assignment; the installed tree now declares the package it mirrors and materializes the Runtime's whole module closure, so one copy of each module loads. The Codex account listing exceeded the shared 256 KB provider-listing bound and left the Runtime on a stale Codex list; Codex now has its own 2 MB bound. With both in place a live read through the running Runtime reported Antigravity, Claude, Codex and MiniMax as observed, and a model assignment through the Console's own dropdown persisted for Claude, Codex and MiniMax with no error notice. Copilot remains the only unavailable provider, for the reason recorded above.

A read-only `agy models` probe on 2026-10-14 returned ten Antigravity models, while `config/catalogs/antigravity-model-catalog.json` contains eight. `gemini-3.8-flash-low` is absent despite matching the current Antigravity model-ID pattern; `gpt-oss-120b-medium` is discovered but does not match the router's current provider-ownership pattern, so Runtime marks it unsupported rather than selectable. This proves the static catalog is not a current availability source and that discovered availability and routeability are distinct facts.

Codex 0.154.0's local `model/list` returned the same 22 mixed-provider IDs as the supplied catalog, so it remains unsuitable as account-availability evidence. The official Codex model provider instead queries the authenticated ChatGPT Codex `/models` endpoint; Runtime now uses that same account-owned source with the existing auth file's access token and account ID. The implementation follows the upstream [Codex models endpoint](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/model-provider/src/models_endpoint.rs) and [Codex account backend configuration](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/model-provider-info/src/lib.rs). The Codex account listing is not a compact ID list: every model carries its base instructions, tool descriptors and message payloads, and a six-model account response measured 316,614 bytes on 2026-10-21. The shared 256 KB provider-listing bound therefore rejected every Codex refresh, which left the Runtime on a stale Codex list with no selectable Codex model. Codex now has its own 2 MB listing bound.

The Codex account listing is filtered by the client version the caller declares, so the version the Runtime sent decided which of the account's models it could see. It sent the installed Codex CLI's release, which is not a bound on what the Runtime can use: the Runtime drives the Codex backend directly, it does not spawn the Codex CLI, and it sends no client version with inference requests. Declaring the installed CLI's 0.154.0 withheld exactly the models the Runtime's own routing configuration selects -- `gpt-6-sol` and `gpt-6-luna` need a client at 0.155.0 -- while the router drove them successfully all the same, with 4,995 completed `gpt-6-luna` turns and 5 completed `gpt-6-sol` turns at HTTP 200 in the router's own event log. The Runtime now declares its own client version, above every client release, so the listing is the account's own model set; the discovery no longer needs the Codex CLI installed at all. The account also marks the models it keeps out of a model picker (`visibility: "hide"`: a reserved capacity pool and the automatic reviewer) and the ones it does not serve through the API, and the listing now offers only the models the account itself offers, which is the set an operator may assign to a role. A live read after the change reported seven Codex models -- `gpt-6.1-sol`, `gpt-6-astra`, `gpt-6-sol`, `gpt-6-luna`, `gpt-5.6-sol`, `gpt-5.6-terra` and `gpt-5.6-luna` -- and a `gpt-6.1-sol` role assignment persisted.

Anthropic's developer [List Models API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/models/list) rejected the earlier "requires API credentials" reading: the same endpoint answers a Claude Code **OAuth** token with the signed-in account's own model list. A 2026-10-21 read through the Runtime's account credential returned 14 models (`claude-haiku-5-5`, `claude-sonnet-5-5`, `claude-opus-5-5`, `claude-fable-5-1`, …), all matching the Runtime's Claude route pattern. Claude discovery now reads that account-owned listing with the same OAuth token the Claude Code bridge authenticates its turns with, so Claude role assignments are selectable from observed account availability.

GitHub's public [Copilot REST API documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/copilot) still exposes no official model-list endpoint, and the local proxy's `/v1/models` response is hard-coded. The Copilot CLI has no model-list command either, and its account token lives in a macOS keychain item that an unattended Runtime service cannot read without an interactive approval prompt. Copilot therefore remains unavailable rather than being populated from static catalogs, local defaults, or the proxy's adapter capability; its provider-owned source remains open migration work. Copilot's own route pattern admits only the single `copilot` pseudo-model, which its configured default already uses, so the unavailable state changes no effective routing.

## Installed Runtime module identity

The installed Runtime at `$CODEX_HOME/src` is a copy of `runtime/src`, and the Runtime imports its own modules through the workspace package name. Node resolves that name against the nearest package.json, so the copy did not declare the package it mirrors: every self-import escaped the installed tree and resolved against the repository checkout instead. The Runtime then loaded two copies of the same module -- one from the copy, one from the checkout -- and module-scoped state split across them. The Control API read the checkout's routing policy while provider discovery wrote the copy's, so the Runtime never saw a discovered model and rejected every new role assignment with `autodev_control_api_bad_body`, while the Console offered models the Runtime refused to accept.

The installed tree now declares the package it mirrors: the installer renders the manifest from `runtime/package.json` with the export targets rewritten to the installed layout, and the install manifest materializes the Runtime's whole module closure so a package import can never fall back to the checkout. Two modules that resolved their own data files relative to `import.meta.url` now resolve them through the shared Runtime source-root helper, because the installed tree sits one level shallower than the source checkout. A regression test materializes a miniature installed tree and asserts that a module imported by package name and by path is one module; a second asserts the install manifest is closed under package imports, which is the closure the relative-import check alone did not cover.

## Console control audit

The control-affordance pass was measured against the rendered pages rather than the source, because the Console's own contract could pass while the pages did not. The sweep covered every route -- the list pages and the detail pages -- on three axes the target state names: the pointer on every interactive control, the height of the table header row, and the link names that point at more than one destination. A second sweep covered the write surfaces: every submit control's name, every disabled control's stated reason, and the number of highest-emphasis actions in a group. A third checked the two rules that only show at a narrow width -- that discrete cell content stays atomic rather than breaking mid-token, and that a table's columns keep their declared budget instead of clipping.

After the passes, the measured Console holds: no control on any route is missing its pointer; every table header row measures 35.5px; no route has a link name that points at two destinations; every disabled control states why it is disabled; no group offers two highest-emphasis actions; and no chip, badge or model id breaks across lines at 390px or 768px. The remaining repeat is the Providers breadcrumb and its own tab item, which are the same page by two routes.

## Control API read failures

A read that the Console abandoned at its own deadline is not a misconfigured integration. The Control API already says so: it carries `autodev_control_api_timeout` rather than `autodev_unreachable`, because the service is reachable and holding the connection open. `/evaluations` drew that distinction for itself, and nineteen other routes that read the Control API told the operator to "configure the required server-side integration" anyway, which sends them to reconfigure a credential that is working instead of looking at why the query is slow. The shared failure shell now carries the timeout advice once, so every route that reads the Control API gets it; a route that knows better than the shell can still pass its own hint. Verified end to end against a Control API that accepts the request and never answers: the `/providers` page shows the timeout code and the timeout advice, and no longer tells the operator to configure the integration.

## Live instance counts

The Console reads the typed `autodev-control-runtime-v2` `liveAgents` projection for live instance counts. Runtime derives totals and role/provider/model breakdowns from the same canonical live-agent projection used by its status surface; Agents, Providers, and Models list/detail views therefore do not substitute separate health counters. Count-bearing pages refresh server-rendered Runtime evidence every five seconds. A missing source is rendered as `Not observed`, while an observed empty projection renders zero. The focused Console and Control API regression tests cover these distinctions and the rendered role/provider/model counts.

## In-place Console navigation

Internal resource and tab links use the shared Next.js `NavigationLink`; URL state remains addressable and browser history continues to work without a full document reload. The root layout's `FormNavigationOwner` handles same-origin GET/POST forms through the client router. Tools source/role filters and shared Breadcrumbs, Chips, Pagination, and drawer-close links use the same in-place navigation path; external provider/GitHub links remain ordinary external anchors. The regression target is browser navigation (the document stays mounted), not merely preserving the rendered `href` in server markup. A committed navigation moves the address bar and the page together; a page showing the destination under the previous URL is a navigation that did not commit.

The root-mounted form feedback owner keeps pending notices visible and automatically dismisses completed or failed notices after five seconds. Terminal feedback shows a visible countdown outside its live announcement and an accessible manual close control; new feedback and unmounting cancel obsolete timers.

A focused read-only Chromium smoke against the isolated staged production build covered `/agents`, `/agents/smart`, `/providers?tab=models`, `/providers/claude`, `/skills`, and `/usage` at 390px and 1280px. All six returned HTTP 200 with no document overflow, selected Control API/Usage failure code, accessible alert, or page exception. The first broad `next dev` sweep was discarded after transient request timeouts during cold route work; this staged-build sample is representative evidence only, not full visual, keyboard, mutation, or all-resource acceptance. A second pass against the same staged build covered `/mcps`, `/hooks`, `/prompts`, `/permissions`, `/tools`, `/evaluations`, and `/memory` at both widths; all seven returned HTTP 200 with no overflow, selected failure code, alert, or page exception. GitHub has separate live acceptance evidence below. Workspaces was not probed because its page reads Playtesting-owned approvals; full Workspace acceptance remains open and is left to the other session.

## Agent alias enablement

Agent enablement is Runtime-owned because pinned RuleSync 16.30.2 has no lossless `enabled` field across supported role projections. Runtime's routing policy persists disabled named aliases and per-role revision generations; `PATCH /control/agents/:role` uses an operator-authenticated `{enabled, expectedRevision}` compare-and-swap, persists before confirming, and rolls the live state back on persistence failure. Admission rejects disabled role aliases—including the dedicated orchestrator alias—before subagent/provider work begins. It does not affect concrete provider/model requests, which carry no named Agent identity. The Console uses one shared control on each Agents list row and detail page through a same-origin server route; unavailable aliases remain visible but nonmutable. Data's config repository returns configured role identifiers for Playtesting authorization rather than constructing an `AgentDefinition` with synthetic `Ready`/`Converged` Runtime state. Focused Runtime Control API and model-router tests cover authorization, stale and ABA revisions, concurrent persistence, rollback/restore, provider-assignment independence, and direct-model behavior. Data role-catalog tests, focused Console Agent tests, and workspace typecheck pass. The enablement write now has browser acceptance: `console/e2e/agents-enablement-acceptance.spec.ts` drives the shared control on the Agents row and on the agent detail view, and asserts that the write carries the revision the page loaded, that the page that comes back shows the Runtime-confirmed value rather than an optimistic one, and that a stale revision is refused with the conflict notice and writes nothing.

Agent readiness and convergence are evidence-derived. Runtime counts an Agent `ready` only when an enabled, credentialed route has a successful provider observation not superseded by a later failure, cooldown, or probe failure. Configuration with no successful health evidence remains `configured`; known failure remains `unavailable`. Core owns this readiness derivation so Provider and Agent surfaces use the same rule. Agent convergence stays `not-observed` until a successful enablement apply records an observed generation; subsequent reads compare that desired generation with the current active routing policy, returning `pending` on drift. Focused tests cover missing health, active failures, initial unobserved convergence, successful apply, and runtime drift. Live managed-Router and rendered-browser acceptance remain open.

alongside a provider-level disable toggle and per-session / across-sessions agent limits; those provider-wide controls now use the same shared `ProviderLimitsControls` on the row and provider detail page, and each model's toggle sits on its Models row, on its detail page, and in its provider's model list. Every placement renders a shared control that posts a bounded same-origin form to a typed Console route (`/api/providers/:provider/roles/:role`, `/api/providers/:provider`, `/api/providers/:provider/limits`or`/api/models/:model`), which calls the Control API and redirects back to the originating Providers page, or adds a could-not-be-confirmed notice; unchangeable or unobserved state keeps the control in place, disabled, with the reason. The Providers list is a five-column table — Provider, Status, Active Agents, Roles, Agent Limits — and provider detail reuses `ProviderLimitsControls`for the provider Disabled toggle and both agent-limit axes, alongside its role controls; the detail also shows route, credential presence (never values), tier models, priority groups, orchestrator reasoning effort, and live router health (cooldown, failure streaks, in-flight requests, active agents, attempts, last success/failure), or`Not observed`without router evidence. Agents list and detail now show read-only provider summaries for the agent's role kind that link to Providers. Priority/fallback groups and per-tier model mapping are shown read-only: they are owned by`config/model-routing.json`, and Runtime has no typed mutation or reload path for them yet. `/github`is a native read-only surface paired with authenticated GET-only`/control/github`, displaying the parsed workflow definition/event/cron catalog alongside authoritative read-only Actions runtime state (active vs disabled) and bounded 30-run sample statistics via `GithubActionsAdapter`when server-side credentials and an enabled canonical workspace are configured, or explicit`Unavailable`/`Invalid`status without synthetic zeros. Agents provider-role views render`Not observed`when provider configuration is absent rather than defaulting to enabled or disabled. MCP list/detail role columns describe configured assignments and explicitly state when no roles are assigned; they do not claim runtime exposure. The Skills view now renders the complete RuleSync skill catalog with source descriptions and paths joined to execution-contract role assignments from`/control/skills`v2; it preserves absent/invalid source state, surfaces assignments with no canonical skill, counts only catalog-backed role assignments, and keeps selection/exposure/use unknown without runtime telemetry. The RuleSync repository distinguishes an unobserved directory, a valid empty catalog, and malformed/symlinked skill sources; the catalog's source descriptions are parsed from valid Markdown YAML frontmatter. The collection GET remains a read model; role assignment and source editing are distinct mutations with separate revisions and owners. `PATCH /control/skills/:name`now assigns a skill to exactly the roles named (complete desired set, so unassigning is the same call with an empty list), guarded by the contract's own digest so two operators assigning at once produce a refusal rather than a silently discarded first write; the Console's`/skills`page carries a **Role assignment** section that posts a bounded same-origin form to`/api/skills/:name`and reports conflict, refusal and not-found outcomes. Existing skill content now has a URL-addressable editor. The typed, revision-checked source mutation validates through Data, applies the pinned RuleSync`skills`generator, then runs`--check` across configured targets; conflicts, source refusals, and projection failures remain explicit. Skill enable/disable semantics remain open because no lossless source/runtime representation is established. Prompts now use a single Data-owned RuleSync frontmatter reader for Console and OpenLIT sync; the Console gets source-authored descriptions and`/control/prompts`v2 reports absent/invalid command catalogs instead of fabricated empty lists. Prompt command detail now edits canonical Markdown and submits same-origin`POST`to typed`PATCH /control/prompts/:name`with an expected-source revision. Runtime validates/atomically updates the RuleSync file, regenerates and applies the Codex command projection, audits only bounded metadata, and reports restart-required projection changes; role prompts remain read-only. Command detail now renders the parser-owned Markdown body safely (raw HTML is not enabled), lists up to 20 committed Git versions, and shows a selected revision's bounded unified diff against the current working tree; missing Git history stays explicitly unavailable. Older-history paging, richer preview for unsaved edits, role prompt editing, and reusable operation/convergence history remain open. The shared DataTable now supports opt-in wrapped cells; long Skills/Prompts/Tools/Workflow metadata no longer forces the table wider than its viewport. Usage formats grouped counts, compact token totals, and unit-scaled percentile durations for readability, and names empty role/provider/tool groups`Not attributed`. Agent enablement is now implemented in the current worktree as a Runtime-owned named-alias admission policy: `/control/agents`reports the v2 enablement state, Agent detail reports v3, and`PATCH /control/agents/:role`requires an operator plus the current revision. | Workspaces             | **Partial: canonical source live; per-workspace health and aggregate usage shipped; role scope still unassigned** | `config/workspaces.json` is already the canonical workspace registry read by Data's `ConfigRepository`; every entry carries `id`, `baseBranch`, `enabled`, and `agentRoles` (currently `null` for every workspace in the live catalog). **The per-workspace configuration-health and runtime-availability signals now exist**: `/control/workspaces` is `autodev-control-workspaces-v2` and carries, per workspace, a `configuration` judgement (a role scope that names a role the execution contract does not define is an `invalid-role-scope` fault, naming the roles it could not place) and a `runtime` availability fact (the Runtime's live agent projection, partitioned by workspace id, is now published as `liveAgents.byWorkspace`; a workspace the source did not list is a measured zero, and a Runtime with no live source reports `not-observed` rather than a false zero). The Console renders the two facts apart: the Role Scope cell names a broken scope instead of listing roles that exclude every agent, and Availability reads the measured count, `Idle`, or **Not observed**. **Aggregate per-workspace usage now ships on the Workspaces surface**: the Usage telemetry groups logical routed requests by workspace, one read answers the whole page rather than one query per row, and the Requests cell reports a measured count, a measured zero, or the reason there is none -- a breakdown truncated by the source's row limit stays unobserved, an unread source stays unavailable, and requests that carried no workspace attribution are counted in no workspace. The workspace detail route resolves the same reading the list row does, so the two surfaces cannot drift into different vocabularies for the same fact. **A focused Chromium acceptance against a synthetic Control API and Usage fixture passed**: the Requests cell renders the measured count, the table region scrolls horizontally at 390px instead of shrinking columns, and the document itself never overflows at 390, 768 or 1280px, with no console error and one page heading. The acceptance lives in `console/e2e/workspaces-usage.spec.ts`. Remaining target gap: the `agentRoles` scope is still null/unconfigured for every workspace pending an explicit assignment. Scheduler weights/policy live separately from this registry and are not the same source. Full trace search/exploration beyond the bounded recent-attempt list remains a target gap. Patch 54 adds source-confirmed context-compaction counts, time series, scope-compatible per-request rate, and bounded workspace/requested-model/agent-role breakdowns; Provider/Skill selections fail closed for these panels and provider-level compaction breakdown remains open. Patch 55 adds ten Git output widgets through a fixed cumulative-metric query with pre-window baseline subtraction and unavailable states for invalid/incomplete series. Patch 59 adds a `requests-by-workspace` widget that groups logical routed requests by `autodev.workspace`, so the Workspaces surface can show per-workspace aggregate usage from one query instead of one query per workspace. `scripts/openlit/up.sh` deployed the exact current 58-patch hash `28c7add35b2db7ba` as `autodev-openlit:openlit-9938c6663866-p28c7add35b2db7ba` (image `sha256:a7a2477d9bb02eef6c12e2353612674630f6c2b6914ed97846d68ae2e391dcad`); the lock/hash match and the live Usage v5 verifier passed (29-widget schema). A focused headless-Chromium smoke against the local Console dev server on :3300 returned HTTP 200 at 390/768/1280, showed all six compaction labels and the explicit empty-source state, reported no Usage error code or page/console exception, and had no document overflow. This is local-dev evidence, not production-browser acceptance; broader route/navigation/mutation acceptance remains open. Active Sessions is implemented as a distinct scope over the Runtime read-only `/control/runtime` projection, has no historical window, and per-session identity remains unavailable. The Usage dashboard itself now has browser acceptance: `console/e2e/usage-dashboard-acceptance.spec.ts` drives `/usage` against a synthetic `autodev-openlit-usage-v5` source and asserts the scope control, the partial-snapshot distinction between the signals the source reported and the ones it did not, the observed and unobserved filter dimensions, the unobserved recent-attempt list, and the four distinct failure states. The fixture answers four scopes differently, because the scope is the only handle the Console's read has on the source, so the failure paths can be reached at all. The live scope has its own acceptance as well: the control fixture now serves the Runtime's read-only `/control/runtime` projection and can be taken away on demand, so the Active Sessions scope is shown to be a scope of its own -- the Runtime's counters, with no historical widget behind them and no per-session list to show -- and a Runtime that does not answer is shown to be unavailable rather than idle. | Memory                 | **Native Console operator surface + backend/JIT/governed APIs**                                                   | The unified Console now renders durable records, experiences, selected record/history and experience detail, session outcome cohorts, and governed verify/invalidate/revise/procedure-to-skill actions through the Control API. Failed experience/detail reads render explicit unavailable states; summary counts remain Not observed rather than becoming zero, and failed cohort reads no longer use the successful-empty state. Memory refuses to synthesize a default workspace or query a URL-selected scope outside the canonical workspace catalog. The workspace selector submits URL-addressable GET state while preserving the active tab, current filters, and time range; selected record/experience detail is cleared on scope changes. Memory tab links use the shared server-rendered tab navigation and retain workspace, filters, and time range across tab changes. The transitional external Memory portal bridge is retired; no OpenLIT UI URL or fallback is part of this surface. Remaining parity includes embedding/deployment acceptance, additional harness capture, and controlled real-task evaluation. The page itself had no browser acceptance: the Control fixture answered no memory read, so the whole surface could only be reached as unavailable. The fixture now answers the storage status, the records, the experiences and the outcome-cohort reads with the states the page has to tell apart -- a claim that is active, one that was proposed, one that was superseded, one that was invalidated -- and its own toggle takes durable storage away, so the page's explanation of a failed read is reachable rather than a guess. `console/e2e/memory-acceptance.spec.ts` drives the page: each row names its claim, its kind and its lifecycle state, the durable-claims card names the store's 1,204 beside the five rows on the page, the active-claims card is the Runtime's rollup over the whole filtered collection rather than a count of the two active rows on the page, and with storage not configured the page says so and names the setting to configure instead of showing an empty list that would read as nothing was remembered. | Evaluations            | **p26 trace-detail route deployed; live trace/evaluation correlation unverified**                                 | ClickHouse read adapter preserves each result's source `span_id`; the Console shows trace navigation only for valid OpenTelemetry SpanIds. `/evaluations?spanId=...` loads the selected trace through the fixed GET `/api/autodev/usage/span/:spanId` Usage endpoint with the existing server-only Usage token, rendering a bounded (200 span) privacy-filtered summary. Patch 26 is active in the current p28c7 image (hash `28c7add35b2db7ba`); the deployed manifest contains the trace-detail route, and an authenticated `OpenLITUsageClient.queryTrace` with a valid SpanId returned the typed `autodev_usage_trace_not_found` result. This verifies the live route and absent-span behavior, not cross-source correlation; the local evaluation table has no rows, so that remains unverified. Evaluation pass/fail still comes only from explicit verdicts; missing/unknown verdicts remain Not observed and do not enter the pass-rate denominator. Target selection, comparisons, and per-result detail are now Console-owned rather than delegated to a removed product: every filter axis is a URL parameter, `outcome` separates Failed from Not observed rather than collapsing them, and the pass-rate denominator counts only the runs that supplied a verdict. A column-width sweep across 390-1536 found every column in the history truncating its content at 1280 (a metric chip rendered `tool_failures: 4 - Fai...` with the verdict gone, roles cut to `docs-res...`); the fix was structural -- role and prompt merged into one Target column so Metrics can hold a whole chip, Tag gained a wrapping shape for chips that carry a reading rather than an identifier, and the weights now sum to the 864px floor the shared DataTable caps at, so narrow widths scroll rather than crush. The Duration column's minute carry works: the fixture's one span of 119.9s renders `2m 0s` beside `1.0 ms`, unclipped, with its `title`. Paging or virtualising the panel is left alone -- the bound is a product decision, and the measurement is recorded so the cost is known rather than guessed. That measurement also found the one inconsistency in that table: the Span and Parent span columns render `spanId.slice(0, 8)` with nothing behind them, while every other shortened value on the page keeps the full one -- the run-time column its full timestamp, the run detail its full run id. Measured 0 of 399 span links carrying a `title` before, 399 of 399 after. What kept it invisible is worth recording: `aria-label` already carried the full id, so the rows were distinguishable to a screen reader and not to a sighted user, which is the opposite of the usual shape of this bug. Real OpenTelemetry ids are 128-bit random, so an eight-character prefix collision is about 5 in a million across 200 spans -- that is why this was never a visible bug, and not a reason to leave it, because a source that numbers spans structurally makes the collision certain. The fixture that exposed it uses counter-derived ids, where 199 of 200 rows rendered as `00000000`. Two probes had to be corrected before these numbers meant anything: one divided a `<th>`'s padded box height by its line-height and reported a 4-character header as "3 lines", and another indexed the Duration column by position and read the Service column's values while labelling them durations. **A span's duration had two owners, and they did not agree.** This trace panel and the Usage trace tables all render the same `UsageTraceSpan.durationNs` from the same reader, through two separate functions, and the two spelled every magnitude differently -- `940 ms` against `940.0 ms`, `1.5 s` against `1.50 s`, `45 s` against `45.00 s`, `2 min` against `2m 0s` -- so the same duration read one way on one page and another way on the next. One case was more than a difference of spelling: a span of a third of a microsecond rendered `0 µs` here, which claims the span took no time at all. The two were not one formatter with a bug either. `formatLatency` read in milliseconds and switched to `min` and `h`, which reads well for a latency _percentile_; the panel's own formatter read in nanoseconds, held fixed precision per band and compounded `m`/`s`, which reads better for one _span_; and the minutes band was the one that kept a minute boundary visible (`1m 59s` beside `2m 0s`), a property the Usage spelling swallowed. There is now one owner, `console/src/components/ui/duration.ts`, and it keeps both properties: the minutes are split from the seconds and the seconds are rounded once before the split, so a duration that rounds into its next minute says so; a duration of hours reads in hours rather than in minutes; and the microsecond band is floored at one, so a span that took some time is never rendered as having taken no time. Every band carries one decimal, which is what the Usage side already read and what the seconds band stops padding (`1.00 s` is now `1 s`). The Usage p95 cards and trace tables and this trace panel now read the same duration the same way, and `console/tests/duration-format.test.ts` renders both panels and asserts that they agree, with a guard that neither view can spell a duration of its own. A count of one in this same panel was wrong while the two owners were being reconciled: it said `1 spans shown`, so the count and its noun are now read together, the way the filter bar's `1 retained result` is. The page itself had never been driven in a browser: the Control fixture answered no `/control/evaluations` read, so the whole surface could only be reached as unavailable. The fixture now answers it with a bounded window over a larger store -- sixty rows of a hundred and twenty, carrying a passed, a failed and an unobserved verdict, a run that reported no prompt, a run whose trace the Usage fixture can open and one whose trace was never retained -- and the Usage fixture answers the trace-detail read the panel needs. `console/e2e/evaluations-acceptance.spec.ts` drives the page: the retained card names the store's hundred and twenty and the window's sixty as two different facts, the filter bar's sentence and the pager's range use the same two numbers and the same words, the three verdicts are counted apart and the pass rate says how many runs carried a verdict, a narrowed view takes the filter bar's options with it (the prompt filter offers the prompts the narrowed rows report, not the prompts the excluded rows reported), the trace panel opens a run's trace and names the span it was asked for, and a span the telemetry never retained is reported as not observed rather than as a failed read. |

## Current Control API coverage

This inventory is **observed current state**, not the desired API family from the target document.

Current collection GETs (read-only unless an item detail is noted below):

```text
/control/agents
/control/providers
/control/models
/control/mcps
/control/tools
/control/skills
/control/hooks
/control/permissions
/control/prompts
/control/workspaces
/control/routing
/control/runtime
/control/evaluations
/control/github
```

Current GET detail routes include Agent, Prompt, and committed Prompt version detail. Agent detail also supports the typed enablement PATCH; Prompt version history is a read-only collection subresource. General collection resources reject non-GET methods.

`/control/providers` v2 returns each provider's route, credential presence, role enablement, tier models, priority groups, orchestrator reasoning effort, and live router health (`null` when the router has not registered evidence). `/control/models` v2 lists each model `config/model-routing.json` maps a provider tier to, with its provider, tiers, Codex-catalog display name, and enablement.

Current non-Memory mutation routes include:

```text
POST  /control/providers/reset
PATCH /control/providers/:provider
PATCH /control/providers/:provider/roles/:role
PATCH /control/providers/:provider/limits
PATCH /control/models/:model
PATCH /control/agents/:role
PATCH /control/skills/:name
PATCH /control/skills/:name/content
PATCH /control/prompts/:name
```

The skill source editor reads through `GET /control/skills/:name/content`. Provider/model operations mutate Runtime routing policy. Skill role assignment updates the execution contract; skill source editing and prompt editing use Data-owned revision-checked RuleSync writes followed by Runtime generation/apply. Each mutation is operator-authorized and audited without recording source text.

Memory is a separate governed family under `/control/memory/*`. Implemented resources include records, experiences, experience history/provenance and lifecycle actions, experience/session/use cohorts, native Codex/Claude capture paths, reporter-supplied outcome routes, curator use-assessment routes, guarded raw-experience purge, and procedure-to-skill promotion. Those operations remain subject to MemoryService authorization/governance rather than becoming generic Control API CRUD.

`/control/github` is implemented as an authenticated read-only `GET` collection returning the parsed `.github/workflows/*.yml` workflow-definition/event/cron catalog (`schema: autodev-control-github-v1`, `readOnly: true`); it strictly rejects non-`GET` methods with HTTP 405. When server-side `AUTODEV_GITHUB_TOKEN` is configured and `AUTODEV_GITHUB_REPOSITORY` is validated against an enabled canonical workspace in `config/workspaces.json`, the endpoint additionally surfaces authoritative workflow enabled state (active vs disabled) and a bounded 30-run sample with scoped statistics via the typed Data adapter (`GithubActionsAdapter`). Invariants enforced: fixed `https://api.github.com` origin, redirects denied (`redirect: "error"`), path segments encoded with `.`/`..` rejected, streamed 1MiB response body limit with active timeouts, fail-closed handling for malformed records, oversized error bodies preserving HTTP auth/rate status, workflows capped at 100 with partial status if exceeded, and `successRate` denominator = all sampled completed runs (in-progress excluded; non-success/missing conclusions in denominator; null when 0 completed runs in sample). Missing credentials, unconfigured/disabled repository scopes, or GitHub API failures render as explicit `Unavailable`/`Invalid` status without synthesizing health or zeros. No dispatch/cancel/rerun/schedule mutations are implemented (non-`GET` returns HTTP 405); local browser acceptance against both dev and an isolated staged production build is complete, while live production-credential and remote-deployed acceptance remain open. General RuleSync/runtime mutations and reusable desired/actual reconciliation are also still incomplete.

What the dependency check found was the other half: the fork still exposed the provider and model catalog as a write authority of its own. `POST`, `PUT` and `DELETE` on `/api/providers`, and the whole `/api/providers/models` tree, wrote straight into the provider metadata and per-provider model tables that the Control API owns. Patch 61 deletes it. The Vault reads that remain are load-bearing rather than administrative: `GET /api/vault/get-secrets` is what the two bundled OpenLIT SDKs call, and `getSecretById` resolves the datasource HTTP secret and the evaluation configuration's judge credential. |
