## Memory current-state snapshot

Keep implementation state here rather than in `memory-target-state.md`, which remains the durable Memory design authority.

- The PostgreSQL/pgvector store is at migration 12. Migrations 8-12 cover append-only request injection/outcome evidence, the session-key index, append-only session outcome reports, curator injection-use reports, and native trajectory source/normalizer diagnostic provenance. Historical/pre-migration values remain explicitly unknown rather than fabricated.
- Root-router JIT research, governed `MemoryService`, PostgreSQL+pgvector/full-text retrieval, current-Git validation, bounded reconstruction, the MCP facade, scoped/paginated reads, lifecycle mutations, procedure-to-skill promotion, and native Codex capture are implemented. Current `main` also implements the native Console Memory route with records, experiences, record/history detail, experience detail, session outcome cohorts, workspace/time filtering, and server-side governed actions.
- JIT research now verifies and reconstructs at most two ranked candidates concurrently; candidate/evidence/packet bounds, rank order, and the one-per-context GitHub lookup remain unchanged. Reproducible baseline/current timings are in [Memory target state](memory-target-state.md).
- The scheduled, out-of-band GitHub metrics collector fetches workflow and repository data concurrently, with each group bounded to two reads and results aggregated in input order. Reproducible fake-client timings are in the baseline evidence below.
- The time window is applied, not displayed. `?from=&until=` was parsed by `/memory`, drawn as a real window on the cohorts tab, and preserved by three filter bars, while the records and experiences reads ignored it at every layer — no request parameter, no request type, no SQL clause. That is the exact failure `console/src/components/filters/resolve-filter.ts` exists to prevent: a bounded filter reported as applied on two of the page's three tabs. `occurredFrom`/`occurredUntil` now run the whole way through `MemoryListRequest`/`ExperienceListRequest`, `buildMemoryListQuery`/`buildExperienceListQuery`, the Runtime's `parseFilters`, and the Console client. Records window on `created_at` and experiences on `started_at` — never `completed_at`, which is NULL while a session runs and would hide every in-flight session from the tab an operator reads for current work. The window is optional (a list with no window is still a legitimate request) but all-or-nothing and capped at the same 365 days the cohort reads carry; `MEMORY_OUTCOME_COHORT_MAX_WINDOW_MS` is renamed `MEMORY_MAX_TIME_WINDOW_MS` because it no longer bounds one route family.
- The list count and the list rows share one predicate. Both `buildMemoryListQuery` and `buildExperienceListQuery` wrote their filters twice by hand — once for `COUNT(*)`, once for the rows — which is how a filter added to one and not the other produces a `total` describing a different collection from the rows under it. Each now builds its `WHERE` once and applies it to both parameter sets.
- The page-scoped "Active Claims" stat said what it was not. It counted active records among the rows on the current page while reading beside a collection total as though it were a share of it; with a 25-row page it could report at most 25. The subtitle now names the scope.
- The cohorts tab can be filtered. The Runtime has accepted `memoryMode`, `injectionResult`, `reportKind`, `outcomeKind`, and `useKind` on these reads since they were written, and the tab rendered none of them — so every cohort view reachable from the Console was the unfiltered one, and the only way to narrow it was to leave the Console. All five are now URL-addressable controls resolved against the Runtime's own value lists, so a filter the Runtime would refuse is reported through the unapplied-filter notice instead of forwarded. `outcomeKind` and `useKind` are separate controls because they describe two different evidence classes: selecting `success` is a claim about reported outcomes, not about assessed use, and one filter would make the other look as though it had narrowed too.
- Reporter and curator writes are the next Console gap, and the blocker is now resolved. `POST /control/memory/experiences/:id/outcomes` and `…/use-assessments` are implemented, operator-gated, and take `exactKeys` bodies — an outcome report is `{correlationToken, outcomeKind, reportKind, evidence}` and a use report is `{injectionEventId, useKind, usedMemoryIds, evidence}` — so both are reported **per observed injection**, not per experience, which is where the evidence panel already renders them. The open question was whether a Console form may send `correlationToken` at all, since it is the key a report binds to. It may: `MemoryService.recordOutcomeReport` resolves the token through `findInjectionEventByTokenForSession` against the reporter's trusted (workspace, repository, task) scope and throws when nothing matches, so a wrong token fails closed rather than mis-binding. The token is content-free by design. Two consequences shape the UI: the Console's outcome projection is currently too narrow (it carries no `correlationToken`) and must widen before any form can post, and a non-`unknown` outcome requires at least one evidence reference, so the form cannot offer outcome kinds without an evidence kind and URI.
- The Console reads `why`. `/control/memory/records/:id/why` has existed since it was written and no client called it, so the one read that answers "why does this record exist, and what of it can I still see" was unreachable. It is not the same answer as the record's own `provenance.experienceIds`: a record cites the experiences it was derived from, while `why` returns the ones _this reader_ can still resolve, and the two sets differ whenever a cited experience has fallen outside the caller's scope. The provenance panel therefore says how many are resolvable rather than presenting the shorter list as the whole truth, and a record whose explanation was never read says neither — a failed read must not look like a clean provenance check.
- A record's sources are reachable. The "Provenance & Citations" block reported `Sources: N experiences` and linked nothing, so the one panel an operator opens to decide whether a claim still holds could not take them to the evidence. Each cited experience id is now a link that crosses to the Experiences tab, carrying the current window so the drawer closes back into the list the operator came from. A claim with no cited source says so rather than rendering an empty list under a heading that promises citations.
- Cohort filters do not follow the operator to another tab. `memory-list-url.ts` writes them only while the cohorts tab is selected, because Records has no `memoryMode` axis and carrying one there would put a bounded filter in the URL of a list that cannot honour it — reported as applied, narrowing nothing. The mode control offers only the three modes a cohort can actually be assigned (`jit`, `retrieval-only`, `disabled`); both matrices carry exactly those, so offering `invalid`/`unknown` would filter to an empty matrix and imply the tab has an axis it does not.
- An operator can see the evidence. The Console showed the experience envelope and nothing behind it: the Runtime has been storing and reading back packet injections, reporter-supplied outcomes, and curator use assessments the whole time, and no part of that reached `/memory`. So the one question a memory system exists to answer — did attaching memory do anything — had no surface. The experience detail drawer now reads `…/outcomes` and `…/use-assessments` alongside the envelope and renders them as three separate claims: observed (what the runtime attached, and when), reported (what a reporter separately claimed about the task), and assessed (a curator's judgement on use). Read-only was the first call here, on the grounds that an operator interface which lets anyone assert a task succeeded is a claim with no evidence behind it. Three separate evidence classes turned out to be the reason to build it rather than the objection to it: an unreported outcome cannot be told from a failed one, and an operator who cannot tell them apart can only guess, which is the failure the evidence rules were written to prevent. The writes are now there, and they are gated on that same separation rather than against it — a non-`unknown` outcome must name the evidence for it, and the two claims have different authors.
- Those three are kept apart because merging them is how memory evaluation goes wrong. An unreported outcome renders as unreported and says "this is not a failed outcome" rather than borrowing the injection's own verdict; `unobservable` is not folded into `not_used`, because one says nobody could tell and the other says nobody saw it used; `sessionInjectionCount` is labelled as the session's count rather than the row's, which overstates it for exactly the sessions that injected repeatedly; and a read that did not succeed renders as unavailable, never as an empty list, because "we could not look" and "there is nothing there" are the two answers an operator must not confuse. The Console validators enforce the same rule on the wire: a row that omits `outcome` is refused rather than believed, because a dropped field would otherwise render as a negative finding, and a page naming a _different_ `experienceId` is the wrong answer rather than an empty one.
- Reporter and curator writes are on the injection, not the experience. The Runtime binds an outcome to a `correlationToken` minted for one injection and a use assessment to an injection event id, so a form that reported against the experience would have to pick one and picking silently is how a report ends up bound to the wrong evidence. Each observed injection therefore carries two separate forms — a reporter's outcome and a curator's assessment — and neither is offered once its report exists, because the Runtime accepts one per binding and offering a second would be offering a submission it will refuse. `ControlApiMemoryInjectionOutcomeJoin` and `ControlApiMemoryInjectionUseAssessment` now carry `correlationToken`, which the projection previously omitted; widening the type is what made the gap loud, because every fixture missing it failed to compile instead of quietly producing a form that could never post. The curator's memory list is a text field whose placeholder is the injected set, because the Runtime holds a `used` verdict to citing all of them and a `not_used` to citing none, and showing the bound turns that rule into something an operator can satisfy rather than trip over.
- The route's subject is the action's, and it says so in one table. The identifier gate was a single `isPurge` boolean, which was wrong for both reports: it demanded a `recordId` for an action that acts on an experience, and a report with no correlation token was refused as `claim_required` — "a revision needs the replacement claim text", naming a field these forms do not have. `MEMORY_ACTION_TARGETS` now gives each action its tab, the key that tab reads, and every field it must carry, so a report that names the experience but not the injection it annotates is a malformed request rather than a refusal with a cause to report, and an action the route does not implement answers the caller with a 400 instead of redirecting to a list nobody asked about. That table also makes drift loud: an action declared but not implemented now throws rather than returning a refusal reason borrowed from a different action.
- An outcome with no evidence is refused by a code that says what is true. It carried `reason_not_accepted`, whose sentence is "the Runtime does not accept that reason for this action" — a Runtime decision on a request the Runtime never saw. `evidence_required` says the route's own check stopped it and nothing was recorded. `unknown` remains the one kind that may be filed without evidence, because that is the honest answer when there is none and refusing it would leave the form with nothing it could legitimately submit.
- Known stale reference from the window rename: `MEMORY_OUTCOME_COHORT_MAX_WINDOW_MS` became `MEMORY_MAX_TIME_WINDOW_MS`, and five comments inside the OpenLIT patch series still name the old constant (`13-autodev-memory-outcome-cohorts.patch` introduces it; `14-autodev-memory-outcome-reporting.patch` and `22-autodev-memory-injection-use.patch` carry two of them as _context_ lines). They are comments in patched files, so nothing fails to compile and the chain still applies. They were deliberately left alone: editing the `+` line without editing the two context lines that quote it would break a 51-patch series that cannot be re-applied in this sandbox (`openlit-patches-apply.test.ts` fails on `git clone` with `Operation not permitted`, a pre-existing environment failure). Renaming them belongs with the next full patch-chain verification, which has a real checkout.
- Records and experiences page. `/control/memory/records` and `/control/memory/experiences` already accepted a bounded `limit`/`offset` and returned the `total` behind the page, but the Console sent no page parameters at all, so the Runtime applied its own default of 50 and the views rendered "50 of 1,204 records" with nothing to act on — the counts were true and the rest of the collection was unreachable. Both reads now request the page the URL names, and a shared `Pagination` primitive renders the position and the two directions. `limit` resolves against the sizes the Runtime accepts (25/50/100, default 50) and `offset` is bounded and snapped to the page grid; either one the URL names badly is reported through the existing unapplied-filter notice rather than substituted. Navigation is links, so a page position stays bookmarkable and works with no JavaScript.
- Governed record actions are reachable and carry the list. `revise` existed in the Console's memory route and nowhere else: it returned null without a `claim`, and no form sent one, so the action the tracker listed as shipped could never be performed. The record panel now offers a revision with the claim pre-filled, and every lifecycle transition that records an append-only reason carries a box for it instead of always writing the route's canned sentence. The three lifecycle forms were three copies of the same block, so they are one `RecordActionForm` now — which is what makes "does this action carry a reason?" a single question with one answer.
- A Memory mutation returns to the list it was made on. The mutation route rebuilt its redirect query from scratch, so a verify made inside `kind=procedural&status=proposed` on a 25-row page 3 of a 90-day window returned the operator to an unfiltered 30-day list. Forms now submit the list's own query string as `returned`, and the route reads back only named filter keys and rebuilds `/memory?…` from them — so the value is a set of facts about the filters, never a URL to follow, and a crafted value cannot redirect off-site or smuggle in a selection the action did not make.
- One address per list. `console/src/features/memory/memory-list-url.ts` is the single owner of what identifies a Memory list, and the record/experience row links, both supersedes links, both drawer close links, the tab links, the filter forms, and the page links all build from it. Before it, opening a record and closing the drawer returned an unfiltered 30-day list: the row link carried only `tab`/`workspaceId`/`recordId` and the close link only `tab`/`workspaceId`, so the query, kind, status, and time window the operator had just narrowed the collection with were dropped on the way in and again on the way out. Submitting a filter or switching tab or changing workspace now returns to the first page — those are new lists — while a page link, a detail link, and a close link keep the position. The per-tab filter bars also carry `from`/`until`/`limit`, which they previously dropped, so applying a query silently reset a 90-day window to 30.
- Memory Control API reads/actions include records, experiences, history/provenance, cohorts, session cohorts, use cohorts, outcomes/session outcomes, curator use assessments, verify/revise/invalidate/supersede, guarded purge, promotion, and capture routes.
- Task-history/cohort reads require the explicit operator task-history grant. `GET /control/memory/cohorts` requires explicit repository/time scope with a maximum 365-day window and returns bounded exposure/report counts with explicit unreported cells rather than task success or model-use claims.
- Session cohorts derive assignment from the complete session injection set; mixed sessions remain separate rather than being coerced into an arm. Reporter-supplied outcomes, curator-assessed use, packet injection, provider-routing outcome, and downstream task success remain distinct evidence classes.
- The local AutoDev connector is configured for the observed AutoDev workspace/repository and the current local stack has verified connector health plus authenticated zero-record durable-memory/task-history reads against a newly initialized database. The external OpenLIT portal is retired: the Console Memory tab set is Durable Records / Experiences / Outcome Cohorts, and the portal tab, resolver, card, and `AUTODEV_OPENLIT_UI_URL` pass-through are deleted.
- Claude Code capture is opt-in and operator-bound; additional native-harness capture adapters remain incomplete.
- **the operator could not tell a broken memory store from an empty one.** Every `/control/memory/*` read resolves the service first, and a null service answers `503 autodev_memory_unavailable` — so the page inferred "Memory storage is not configured" from that code. The inference is right when nothing was ever configured and wrong when the database is configured and not answering, which is the case where sending an operator to set `AUTODEV_MEMORY_DATABASE_URL` wastes their time. `GET /control/memory/status` now answers that question directly, with three states the page keeps apart: `not_configured`, `unreachable`, `reachable`. It is served **before** the service is resolved and before filters are parsed, because a read whose job is to report why everything else fails cannot itself depend on everything else working, and it takes no `workspaceId` — it describes the Runtime's own storage, not any workspace's memory, so it needs no task-history grant either.
- The health read is bounded, because a health read that hangs is worse than none. The probe races a `SELECT 1` against a 1500ms deadline and reports `unreachable` on expiry, and the deadline travels in the response so "we could not reach it in time" is never read as "it is down". The pool also gained `connectionTimeoutMillis`: without it the probe would be bounded while every ordinary read still waited out the OS TCP timeout, so the Console would hang rather than say `unreachable`. This is the failure the OpenLIT fork already records once — `/api/clickhouse` hanging with no connector configured, twenty surfaces behind a ping stuck at `pending` — so the bound is the feature, not a detail.
- A reachable store with no embedding provider configured now says so on `/memory`, because nothing else ever would. Capture works, records are written, and retrieval-by-meaning silently does not — every read succeeds and memory still does not work. The banner is shown only for the two states that are wrong on their own (unreachable, embeddings missing); a green banner on every healthy page load trains the operator to read past the place that matters.
- **The use-cohort tab showed a matrix and left every question about it to the reader.** The cells are `mode x session cardinality x judgement`, and neither question an operator opens that tab to ask is answered by a single cell: _how much of what we injected was ever judged_, and _how was it judged_. Both are sums, so the view computes them once rather than each reader doing the arithmetic over a table. Two charts answer them — assessment coverage per assigned mode, and exposures by outcome across all modes.
- The folding is where that could have gone wrong, so the tests pin it. `unobservable` keeps its own bar: it says nobody could tell, where `not_used` says nobody saw it used, and merging them reports a finding nobody made. The unassessed remainder is a fifth bar rather than an absence, so the judged share can never be read as the whole — and it is deliberately ordered last, after the four judgements, so the caveat is where the eye ends. Coverage is stated against each mode's own denominator (`67% assessed (20 of 30)`) and a mode observed with zero eligible exposures gets `No eligible exposures` instead of `0%`, which would read as "every injection we sent was ignored". No share-of-used figure is offered at all: its denominator would be eligible exposures while its numerator would come only from the ones somebody chose to assess, which makes missing data look like a negative finding.
- **"Active Claims" was counting the page, not the collection.** The Console derived it from `records.filter(r => r.status === "active").length` because the records response published no total for it — the card said so in its subtitle and read beside "1,204" as a share of it. It was worse than a mislabelled count: on a 25-row page it could not exceed 25, and a page can hold zero active records while the collection holds hundreds, so the number went to zero for reasons that had nothing to do with memory.
- The records read now publishes `statusCounts`, a lifecycle rollup over the whole filtered collection. The `COUNT(*)` became `GROUP BY status` rather than gaining a second query: the rollup scans the same rows under the same predicate the count did, so it costs no more and no extra round trip, and `total` is now the sum of parts measured together rather than a second scan that could disagree with the rows under it. Every status is present, zeros included, because a partial map forces each reader to ask whether a missing key means zero or means not observed.
- `MemoryRepository.listMemories` returns `MemoryRecordPage` rather than `MemoryPage<MemoryRecord>`, so the breakdown cannot be silently dropped by a repository or a fake that never heard of it — three test doubles failed to compile the day the type widened, which is the point of widening it rather than adding an optional field. The Console refuses a records response with no rollup or a partial one, and renders "Not observed" rather than zeros; the rollup is also a chart of every lifecycle state, since the stat card answers "how many are in service" and only the breakdown answers "and what happened to the rest".
- **A claim could read "active" and "verified" while the Runtime would refuse to inject it.** `isEligibleRecord` refuses a record whose validity window has closed, and `rejectionReason` files it as `stale`, but the record detail panel rendered the state, the check date, and the verification source and said nothing about `validFrom`/`validTo`. The panel is opened to answer "is this claim actually in use?", and it answered with the two fields that make a claim look good while omitting the one that decides it.
- The window is now stated where the other validity facts are, and a closed window says the consequence rather than the fact: "Out of validity window — the Runtime will not inject this claim". The comparison is the Runtime's own (`validTo <= asOf`, string order, not a parsed timestamp) so the Console cannot come to disagree with the Runtime about which claims are live. One render instant is taken per page rather than per record, or a window closing between two records' checks would render one expired and its neighbour open on the same screen.
- An absent bound is rendered as nothing, not as a dash. It is the absence of a decision rather than "valid forever" or "expired", and an unparseable one is treated as absent rather than as expired — the Runtime would not parse it either, so refusing a claim it will inject is the worse error.
- **A promoted memory could reach the skill catalog and still be dead.** `promoteProcedureToSkill` writes the RuleSync skill and reports success, but nothing assigns it to a role: `/control/skills` is a read-only collection and role assignment lives in the execution contract. The skill lands with `roles: []`, and the skills State column — which ignored its row entirely — badged every skill `Configured`, so the memory system's own last mile sat beside "No roles assigned" under a green badge saying it was fine.
- The State column now reads the row and renders three states rather than one: `Assigned`, `Not assigned` when the eligibility entry is present and empty, and `Not observed` when there is no eligibility entry at all. Folding the last into the second would claim we checked and found nothing, which is the confusion the roles column beside it already refuses. The promotion button also states its consequence before it is pressed, because a successful promotion that produced an unreachable skill is not a success the operator was told about.
- Remaining gaps include a configured live embedding-provider acceptance test, complete RuleSync/runtime validators, skill role assignment as a written operation, deeper semantic stale/superseding-change detection beyond the cited-file and revert checks, controlled real-task effectiveness evaluation, deletion of the external portal fallback, and browser/remote/deployed acceptance.

## Current Usage baseline

The verified Usage board currently contains:

| View                           | Semantics                                                |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Logical routed requests        | one per autodev.routed_request, including final failures |
| Logical requests by agent/role | routed-request activity grouped by bounded role          |
| Input/output tokens            | summed on physical GenAI attempts                        |
| Cache-read rate                | cached input / input only where both are reported        |
| P95 attempt latency            | physical attempt duration                                |
| Physical attempts by provider  | grouped by gen_ai.provider.name                          |
| MCP tool calls                 | shim-owned tools/call round trips                        |
| P95 MCP tool-call duration     | shim-side MCP span duration                              |
| MCP tool-call errors           | errored MCP tools/call spans                             |
| MCP calls by tool              | top bounded tool-name groups                             |

Provider does not filter logical-request count because a logical route can touch multiple providers. Provider filters apply to attempt-level widgets. Context compactions are emitted by the router producer, and Usage now has structured trace-backed count, time-series, workspace/model/role breakdown, and scope-compatible rate widgets; metric-backed provider breakdown and live ingestion/browser acceptance remain open. Provider and Skill filters fail closed for this signal.

## Remaining work by dependency

This is the migration order. The gap ledger above is the status authority; do not maintain a second independent numbered backlog elsewhere.

1. **Finish the unified Console shell and design system.** Implement the target dark-only UI contract, all canonical routes, canonical edit surfaces, real loading/error/empty/unavailable states, and no foreign embedded dashboards.
2. **Complete OpenLIT product subtraction as Console parity lands.** Delete unwanted product routes/components/stores/APIs/dependencies rather than merely hiding them. The Console Memory surface (records, experiences, outcome cohorts) now owns Memory, so the temporary external Memory-page bridge is retired: its tab, resolver, card, and `AUTODEV_OPENLIT_UI_URL` pass-through are gone. The legacy additive AutoDev OpenLIT pages remain open.
3. **Finish RuleSync authority where parity is possible.** Migrate subagents/roles and permissions only after every current field has an explicit owner and deterministic supported-target parity; then delete duplicate editable authorities.
4. **Finish workspace/data integration and boundary hygiene.** Keep the four-workspace architecture, complete typed adapters, and avoid rebuilding a second telemetry/query backend.
5. **Complete telemetry cutover.** Verify a real producer through authenticated OpenLIT, separate required live-control state, then remove router-owned historical OTLP aggregation/receiver paths and direct mode.
6. **Implement reusable mutation/reconciliation.** Apply canonical edits through the Control API, validate/generate/apply where needed, observe runtime, and expose desired/actual generations, diff, operation history, and convergence.
7. **Finish retained features.** Bring Memory, Evaluations, Prompts, Usage, trace/resource linkage, Tools, and provider/model/routing detail to target parity inside Console.
8. **Finish GitHub live acceptance and context-compaction Usage acceptance.** The Console route, authenticated GET-only `/control/github`, and typed `GithubActionsAdapter` expose authoritative read-only workflow enabled state, recent runs, and bounded 30-run statistics backed by an enabled canonical workspace; GitHub dispatch/cancel/rerun/schedule controls are excluded by the target and must remain absent. Local authenticated dev and isolated production-build browser checks now pass at phone and desktop widths; remaining GitHub work is remote production-release/browser acceptance with production credentials. For context compactions, verify live ClickHouse trace ingestion and the shipped Usage widgets (including the source/scope behavior and unsupported provider/Skill filters), then complete production-credential and broader browser acceptance; the focused live compaction-panel browser check passes at 390/768/1280. Metric-backed provider breakdown remains open until a counter-safe, source-confirmed query exists.
9. **Delete transitional synchronization/compatibility paths.** Reassess OpenLIT projection syncs, singleton bootstrap, old proxies/facades, obsolete patches, stale dependencies, branches, and PRs after their consumers are gone.

## RuleSync parity gate

The pinned RuleSync 16.30.2 generator recognizes subagents and permissions, but its current target projections do not losslessly preserve AutoDev's role contract. Known gaps include orchestrator role kind, router provider alias, nickname candidates, reasoning summary, per-role skill enablement/bundling, per-role web-search policy, per-MCP enabled_tools for Claude/Copilot, and Runtime-specific provider delegation/spawn/permission-mode policy.

Generation scope also differs by target (for example Antigravity CLI permissions are global-only and Copilot permissions are project-only). Keep the current role TOML/generated execution contract until ownership/parity is explicit. Do not invent a second AutoDev declarative schema merely to force migration.

After parity:

- remove duplicate editable agent-role authority under agents/roles/;
- remove duplicate editable prompt/role authority where RuleSync can represent it;
- keep config/execution-contract.json only as a deterministic generated runtime artifact if still useful;
- update tests that currently freeze deferred RuleSync permissions/subagents.

## Telemetry cutover gate

The standalone AutoDev Collector has been removed. The router still exposes legacy direct OTLP ingress on port 4100 alongside the OpenLIT path on 4318. Before deleting router OTLP code:

- verify a real Codex/router producer through authenticated OpenLIT ingestion in the deployed stack;
- separate any required live routing/control correlation from historical aggregation;
- remove router-owned historical aggregation, metric series, lookback history, and persistence;
- remove router OTLP receiver routes and direct mode only after replacement evidence exists.

Do not delete live runtime/control state merely because it currently shares a telemetry module.

The historical Console baseline below was recorded on 2026-10-06; runtime performance measurements were added on 2026-10-09. During the 2026-10-13 continuation, Playwright/Chromium exercised the stale-v3 `/usage` fail-closed state at 1440×900 and 390×900, proving filter visibility and no document overflow only. After the p85 deployment, direct live Data-client checks validated v4 with 19 widgets and all widget queries succeeding; the same-origin `/usage` route returned HTTP 200 without the schema error. Post-upgrade rendered compaction charts, mutations, and general navigation interactions remain unverified.

- The out-of-band GitHub metrics collector now fetches independent workflow and repository groups concurrently (two reads per group, at most four total). `pnpm run bench:github-metrics -- --iterations=7 --delay-ms=25` uses eight deterministic fake reads per iteration, checks totals/order, and never contacts GitHub. On Node 25 at similar host load, seven measured baseline runs at `5596ac09` were p50/p95 `223.77/276.40ms`, peak concurrency 1; the updated implementation measured `80.89/82.43ms`, peak concurrency 4 (63.9% lower p50, 70.2% lower p95). Live GitHub API latency was not measured.

Targeted ESLint passed for changed sources except the OpenLIT patch-apply test file, whose seven findings reproduce at HEAD. Repository-wide `pnpm run lint:ci` was not rerun; do not claim it passes;
- After the fast-forward to `main`, the root/four-workspace typecheck, Core suite (318), Data suite (371 passed/9 skipped), Console suite (587), Runtime skill assignment/content routes (9), target-contract suite (19), and OpenLIT patch series/apply suite (12) passed. The Runtime skill-content tests exercise pinned RuleSync generation plus `--check` and verify the `.agents`, `.claude`, and `.github` projections. A production Console build, browser-based skill save, and live Control API write were not performed. The writer rejects static symlink paths and uses revision checks; hostile same-UID path swaps remain a filesystem race because Node has no portable handle-relative open/rename API.
- The full root `pnpm test` was not rerun in this continuation. Prior recorded full-suite attempts include sandbox `EPERM` failures and integration startup/readiness timeouts; current full-suite acceptance remains open and must be re-established in an adequately provisioned runner;
- all four workspace test scripts use Node's recursive discovery directly so root-level and nested tests are included;
- the Providers page renders against the live Control API again: the Console's `isRoleConvergence` response guard required a bare string while the Runtime returns the canonical nested `ReconciliationStatus` (`convergence`, `desiredGeneration`, `observedGeneration`, `lastApplyAt`, `lastObservationAt`, `lastError`, `explanation`), so `/providers` failed closed with `autodev_control_api_invalid_providers_response` and showed no providers at all. The guard now narrows the canonical object, and `/providers` renders all five providers with per-role enablement;
- the effective role capability matrix no longer reports a fabricated `None`: `permissionsView` hard-coded `allowedMcpServers: []` and `allowedSkills: []`, which contradicted the real per-role skill/MCP counts on the Agents page. Runtime now projects `mcp` and `skills` per role from the same execution-contract join `/control/agents` uses, Core declares both fields on `ControlApiPermissionsResponse`, and the Console validates and maps them. `fetchPermissions` had no response guard at all and now rejects a payload missing either list, so a stale Runtime fails closed instead of printing `None`. `tests/router/control-api.test.ts` asserts the permissions projection equals each agent record's `skills`/`mcps`, and the Console test asserts the mapping preserves them;
- table column weights are authored on roughly a pixel-per-unit scale, and the shared table's floor width equals the widest declared total, so a column never renders narrower than the content it was measured for. A 1024/1280/1440/1680 sweep across the list routes reports no document overflow, no clipped header, and no mid-word header break at any of those widths; below the floor the table region scrolls horizontally by design;
- the Console's source-scanning guards are now proven capable of failing, which is what makes them usable as acceptance evidence rather than decoration. A guard that never fails is worse than no guard, because this tracker cites a green run as proof the rule holds. Each guard was run against a scratch violation written in the shape a developer would actually write it, and each was confirmed to fail: `no feature view hand-types an empty state` (a hand-styled `<p className="… italic">` absent state), `no feature view calls a shared component as a plain function` (`DataTable({ … })` rather than an element), `nothing truncates text it cannot give back` (a `React.createElement` span with a bare `truncate` and no `title`), and `client behavior stays in explicitly approved interaction islands` (an unregistered `"use client"` module, a hook outside the allowlist, and an event handler outside an approved island or server exception). All four failed on the violation and the suite returned to green once the scratch files were removed. One trap worth recording: the empty-state guard exempts any file that mentions `EmptyState` at all, so a first attempt at a violation whose helper was named `ScratchEmptyState` passed the guard — the scratch file has to avoid the exempt string, exactly as a real violation would have to. The brittle-shape checks that make these guards safe to write (brace-matching a props object instead of regexing its shape, scoping to names the file actually imports so `URLSearchParams({…})` is not read as a mis-called component) are what keep them from producing false positives;
- a 1440x900 headless-Chromium sweep over all thirteen canonical Console routes reports HTTP 200, exactly one `<h1>` per page matching the resource, and zero horizontal table or document overflow. The same sweep is clean at 1280 and 1024: the 1280px layout starts expanded, while 1024px defaults to a 56px icon rail (each link keeps its section name as an accessible name and hover title, and Configure/Observe/Operate keep a visible divider), returning width to dense tables. The OpenLIT-style circular control toggles the 256px sidebar and 56px icon rail at every viewport width; narrow screens default to the icon rail, and expanding there overlays rather than squeezes page content. The preference persists across route loads. At 768 a dense table scrolls inside its own region without document overflow, which is the intended floor behaviour;
- every table now resolves column weights to percentages under `table-layout: fixed`, so a long cell can no longer push a table out of its container. Previously every table overflowed at 1440px (content area ~1061px against tables of 1196-3182px) and the Skills description cell measured 2398px because the cell's `truncate` set `white-space: nowrap`, preventing its own `line-clamp-2` prose from wrapping. Prose line clamps now apply to a wrapper box inside the cell, because `-webkit-line-clamp` needs a box display and a clamped `<td>` stops tracking row height;
- the Console renders one title block per resource: the shell header owns the resource name and an optional summary, so Memory no longer renders a second `<h1>` and description beneath its own breadcrumb title;
- selects and buttons are shared primitives: five differently styled native light selects (Usage, Memory workspace, Memory kind/status) and three different "apply filters" button styles now render through one dark-themed `SelectField` and one `Button` vocabulary, with `appearance: none` so the closed control cannot fall back to the platform's light widget;
- the Providers data model and mutation surface now follow the four-column contract in the target state, and three runtime defects surfaced while migrating it are fixed at the source. A provider role carries a priority and a model instead of a boolean (`ProviderRolePriority` is `1|2|3|"disabled"`, so a role cannot hold a priority and be disabled at once), `PROVIDER_ROLES` is the single ordered source of the four roles, and the per-role disable lists are gone from `RoutingPolicyState`. Two mutations the contract needs did not exist and are added: `PATCH /control/providers/:provider` takes only `{disabled}` and preserves every role assignment and limit so re-enabling restores the operator's configuration, and `PATCH /control/providers/:provider/limits` takes both axes, where `null` is Unlimited and anything that is not an integer of at least one is rejected at the boundary rather than normalised into an active limit. The defects: the role handler awaited nothing, putting `persistRoutingPolicy()` inside a `try` that could only see synchronous throws, so the rollback beneath it was unreachable and a failed persist left the change in memory steering routing; that rollback also only fired when a prior assignment existed, so a rejected change to an unobserved role stayed live, and it now clears the assignment instead. And the persisted state file was written with `roleAssignments`/`disabledProviders`/`providerLimits` while `restoreSection` still only knew the removed per-role disable lists, so an unknown section was discarded silently -- every operator's role configuration was lost on restart. Each new guard was mutation-checked rather than assumed: removing the clear-on-rollback, removing the limit validation, reverting the loader's `roleAssignments` branch, and narrowing the Console's per-role response check to the old two roles each turn the suite red. Verified: root suite 1416 tests, 1393 passing, the same 18 pre-existing sandbox failures (OpenLIT patch-apply/clone and bootstrap suites, `EPERM` against the sandbox temp root) that also fail at HEAD and none of which touch these files; `tsc --noEmit` clean; `eslint` clean over every touched file;
- the Providers table now renders the four columns the contract names — Provider, Status, Roles, Agent Limits — and the five removed columns are gone. `Status` is one verdict rather than a summary: `resolveProviderStatus` is a pure function of the record, so its ordering is testable without rendering and the column cannot drift into showing a summary. It reports the most _fundamental_ blocker rather than the most recently discovered one (disabled, then route, then credential, then live health), because an operator who fixes `Missing CODEX_ROUTE` must not then be told `Missing credential` while the route is still absent. Health with no evidence reads `Not observed`, never `Ready`: an unreadable health signal is not a healthy one, and Ready is the single claim the column exists to make. The Ready stat card counts through the same function, so the summary cannot disagree with the rows beneath it. `Roles` renders the four fixed roles from `PROVIDER_ROLES` in the contract's order with a white-outline icon (no crown for Default), a P1/P2/P3/Disabled dropdown, and a model dropdown of that provider's models; `Disabled` is the one highlighted priority, and a disabled role's model control stays visible and keeps its value so it remains recoverable while being disabled and marked `data-dimmed`. Three defects surfaced while building it and were fixed at the source rather than worked around. The stepper buttons originally shared a field name with the hidden state fields they were meant to override; a submit button's value is appended _after_ the control's and `URLSearchParams.get` returns the first, so the hidden state would have won and the operator's new value been silently discarded — the overrides now use distinct names. Reusing `SelectField` four times per row produced four controls sharing `id="select-priority"`, leaving every `<label for>` ambiguous: a screen reader announces whichever control the DOM resolves first and clicking either label focuses the first; `SelectField` takes an `id` for exactly this case, since it cannot come from `name`, which is the wire contract with the route. And `Button` could not express a value-carrying submit button at all, while React was dropping the `class` prop used for the Disabled highlight with a warning instead of applying it. Verified in Chromium at 1440 against a Runtime speaking the new contract, with all five providers and the disabled-role path exercised for real: four columns, five rows at a uniform 255px, no clipped headers, no cell painting outside its column, no document overflow. claude's Default role is set to `Disabled`, and its model select renders `disabled` with an `aria-describedby` explanation while keeping `sonnet` visible and selected — recoverable, which is the point of keeping the control rather than removing it. 178/178 Console tests pass, `tsc --noEmit` clean, `eslint` clean, and the four-column assertion was mutation-checked (renaming the Status header turns the suite red). Two notes on how that verification was reached, because both are traps worth recording. A first pass measured against `.next/static/css/*.css`, which is a build _output_: it only contains the utility classes Tailwind found when it ran, so measuring newly added classes against it silently measures the _previous_ design. Every number from that pass was wrong and looked entirely plausible. `WATCHPACK_POLLING=true` makes the dev server actually recompile in this sandbox; without it the file watcher dies on `EMFILE` and serves stale markup, which is a measurement that looks fine and reports the previous build. Measuring for real then exposed two defects the stale pass had hidden: `SelectField`'s inline-flex wrapper had no `max-w-full`, so a native select sized to its widest option overflowed its wrapper however narrow the caller set it, giving every row a different control width depending on that row's longest option and making row heights uneven; and the Agent Limits axis label truncated to "Across sessio…". The column weights are now derived from measured needs at the 1076px content width the sidebar leaves at 1440. Provider order still has no mutation, so the row grip renders disabled with that reason, on the grounds that a draggable-looking control that cannot drag is worse than no affordance;
- **the old role toggle survived the four-column rewrite as dead code that could not have worked.** `EnablementToggle.ts` kept exporting a `ProviderRoleToggle` wrapper that nothing rendered once the Roles column took over, and it was not merely unused: it posted `{provider, role, enabled, returnTo}` to `/api/providers/:provider/roles/:role`, while that route now requires exactly five fields and reads a priority and a model — `parsePriority(null)` returns null and `form.size !== 5`, so every submission it could still have made would have redirected to the could-not-be-confirmed notice. A control that fails on every use is worse than an absent one, because it advertises a contract that no longer exists. With the row and detail placements migrated, that wrapper had exactly one caller left (`ModelToggle`), so the file was collapsed into that single export and renamed to `ModelToggle.ts`, taking the `kind: "provider-role" | "model"` union member and the orphaned `ProviderRole` import with it; `ModelToggle` now names its route and its hidden fields directly instead of taking them as parameters no caller varied. `data-enablement-form="provider-role"` is asserted **absent** from the rendered Providers markup (`console/tests/console.test.ts:6714`), which is what makes the removal observable instead of a silent narrowing of the surface;
- **a Disabled role could never be turned back on, and two guards around that control were decorative.** The model `<select>` renders natively `disabled` while its role is Disabled, which is correct — the operator must not pick a model for a role that is off — but a natively disabled control is **not submitted by the browser**, and `console/app/api/providers/[provider]/roles/[role]/route.ts` accepts a submission only when `form.size === 5` (`provider`, `role`, `priority`, `model`, `returnTo`). The Disabled role's form therefore posted four, the route refused it, and the operator was left with a control that could set the role to Disabled and never undo it. **A disabled control and a preserved value are in direct conflict here, and the fix belongs at the form rather than at the route:** loosening the route to four fields would let a genuine malformed submission through, so the form now carries the preserved model in a hidden `name="model"` field while the select is disabled. There is no duplicate name to disambiguate, because the disabled `<select>` contributes nothing — the same shape the Agent Limits steppers already use for their current state. Exercised in Chromium against a Runtime holding `claude/default = {priority: "disabled", model: "sonnet"}`: the hidden carry reads `sonnet`, re-enabling lands on P1 with `sonnet` intact and no `?control=failed`, and disabling again is symmetric. The second defect was the mirror image: a globally disabled provider reported `mutable: false` on every role and told the operator to enable the provider first, but `patchProviderRole` never checked, so the API accepted the write and that message described nothing. The Runtime now refuses a role write against a disabled provider with **409 `autodev_control_api_provider_disabled`**, and the Console's Apply button renders disabled with the reason, because a control that can only ever fail is not an affordance. Refusing it surfaced a third defect one layer down: `findLatestAuditFor` returned `denied` envelopes as the latest evidence, so a refused request stamped the role with a `lastApplyAt` and `lastError` — reporting a failed apply for a resource that was still perfectly converged, and flipping a `not-observed` role to `error` purely because a viewer had tried to write to it. A refusal is not an apply: `denied` is now skipped, while validation and persistence failures (`error`) remain evidence. Each guard was mutation-checked — removing the hidden carry, removing the Apply `disabled`, and removing the 409 each turn the suite red. **Two measurement traps hid the first of them, and both were in the instrument.** `/\bdisabled\b/` matches Tailwind's `disabled:` variant in the class list, so a scan for the `disabled` _attribute_ reported every select and button on the page as disabled; and `formTags` yields each form's **opening tag only**, so a `matchAll` over one found nothing at all and the derived submission list came back empty. The guard now strips the class attribute before testing, and slices the element body out of the markup;
- **Providers header actions:** the shared page header now carries the target purpose statement, a confirmation-bound `Reset to defaults` form, and an `Add provider` control. The reset calls operator-only `POST /control/providers/reset`, clears only Runtime provider overrides, and preserves static `config/model-routing.json`, Agent admission, provider discovery, health/cooldown, and global Runtime concurrency. `console/e2e/providers-model-availability.spec.ts` verifies the action group and confirmation requirement at phone width. The Add provider control is visibly disabled with a reason because this Runtime has no typed adapter/provider-creation operation; completing that lifecycle remains open rather than exposing an inert mutation.
- **the hidden model carry had to be narrowed, because the fix for one unreachable control created another.** The carry exists so a Disabled role can be re-enabled at all, and it forwarded the role's stored model verbatim. The Runtime rejects a role body naming a model its provider is not configured for, and it rejects **the whole body**, not the model — so a role left Disabled while its model was removed from the configuration would have forwarded that model, been refused, and become permanently un-re-enableable: the row's one working control failing every time, in exactly the shape the carry was added to prevent. Such a model also has no `<option>` to render into, so the operator can neither see nor change what is being preserved, which makes forwarding it a claim the page cannot support. The carry now holds the preserved model only while the provider still offers it, and clears it otherwise — the operator re-enables, sees `Not set`, and chooses again. Measured, not assumed: driving the model dropdown end to end against the live Runtime confirmed the ordinary path works (choose `gemini-3.8-flash-high`, disable, re-enable, model intact), and the Runtime's refusal of an unconfigured model was confirmed against a second instance. **The general lesson is the shape of the argument:** a fix for "this control cannot do its job" should be checked for the case where its own input has gone stale, because the fix is exactly what routes that stale value into the system;
- **the whole Agent Limits column had never worked, and no test could see it.** `providerControlPath(provider, suffix)` built `${providers}/${provider}${suffix}` and its one caller passed `"limits"` with no leading slash, so every limits mutation was sent to `/control/providers/claudelimits`. **`claudelimits` is a legal provider id**, so the request matched the _single-provider_ route instead and came back as an unknown-provider 404 — not a routing error that would have looked like a typo, and not a 405 either. The Console redirected to `?control=failed`, the Runtime was never actually asked for anything, and the row kept rendering its steppers exactly as before, because nothing on the page changes when a mutation is refused. What made this survivable is that the console tests for this route asserted only that the module exports `POST`, and every other test around it stubbed `fetch` and checked the request _body_ — not one asserted the request _URL_. The single browser pass that stepped every limit axis, pressed Unlimited, left Unlimited, then disabled and re-enabled a provider, was worth more than all of them together. `providerControlPath` now joins its own segments so a caller cannot forget the separator, and the new test asserts the exact path rather than the body. Two facts from chasing it: the Runtime answers the same request with 200 once the path is right, which is what proved the fault was the Console side and not the endpoint; and `isSameOriginMutation` requires `sec-fetch-site: same-origin`, so a hand-built `Request` omitting it fails closed for a reason unrelated to the defect being hunted — the first direct-call reproduction was invalid for exactly that reason. What _does_ survive a provider disable is the stored configuration: while the provider is off the Runtime deliberately reports every role as `disabled`, and re-enabling restores the prior priorities, models and limits unchanged — measured on a role moved to P3 immediately before the cycle;
- provider role enablement is one control per role rather than a status badge beside a separate Enable/Disable button; the pill states the current value and applies the opposite, its state/target/reason live on the one button, and it stays disabled with its reason when the item is read-only or unobserved. The two near-identical role columns merged into one Role enablement column, which cut Providers row height and freed width for the model and tier chips;
- Providers rows are back to a uniform 75px. Tier priority was wrapping correctly but the column was too narrow for any adjacent chip pair to fit (widest pair `default P1` + `browser-tester P1` needs ~200px of content width against 149px available), so four tiers stacked one per line and forced 125px rows. Health was carrying ~28px of dead width (its widest badge measures 68px against 96px available); rebalancing the six column weights from measured per-column content needs funds the ~205px Tier priority needs. The weights are load-bearing and documented at their definitions: re-check them after changing any tier-name width or the table padding, because every column now sits within a few pixels of its content need and an over-generous single column silently re-truncates a neighbour;
- long identifiers truncate deliberately rather than overflow: an automated sweep of every table cell confirms that each clipped element (`/tools` tool names, `/skills` paths, `/mcps` server names) carries a `title` holding the full untruncated string, so the recoverable information is never lost. Those tables are at genuine capacity — `/mcps` in particular cannot free ~40px for its server-name column without pushing role chips, target overrides and connection badges into truncation instead, so that trade was declined rather than forced;
- truncation outside the tables was deleting information with nothing to give it back. Ten elements truncated a canonical identifier and offered no recovery: the shell `<h1>`, every skill name, the prompt source path, the Memory task and run ids, the record claim summary, the record scope, and the app-nav section label. A truncated `h1` is the worst of them, because it is the one heading on the page and it tells the operator which page they are on only partially. Two shared components now own the rule rather than fourteen views each remembering it: `Chip` titles itself with its own string content (the default chip list rendered its item as the chip's text and passed no `label`, so it truncated and offered no way to read what it had cut off), and `DataTable` titles a truncating cell whose content is a plain string. `tokens` and `prose` cells deliberately get no title — they wrap rather than truncate, so a title would claim something false — and an element cell leaves recovery to the element, because titling it as well would either duplicate the element's title or invent text that does not match what the cell shows. The `ColumnAlign` doc comment previously claimed the full value "stays reachable through the row's own detail view", which was stronger than the code delivered. A dead `truncate` on the Providers role label was removed rather than given a title: the label is a fixed literal in a `w-20` box, so it could never fire, and keeping it invited the reader to assume a recovery path it did not need;
- long identifiers now shrink inside their container instead of widening it. Every identifier the operator reads is a canonical name rather than prose — an agent role, a skill, an MCP server, a model id — so the one input guaranteed to be a single unbreakable token is also the one most likely to be wider than the panel it renders in. The mechanism is easy to get wrong and invisible in review: a flex item's automatic minimum size is its _min-content_ width, and `break-words` does not lower it, because `overflow-wrap: break-word` only breaks a token _after_ the box has been narrowed below it. `min-w-0` is therefore required at every level between the container and the text, and the entity title already said `break-words` while still overflowing, because nothing below it could narrow. It is now on the drawer header row, the identity column, the title row and the title itself; on the breadcrumb nav, list and items; and the chip list's `<li>` needs `max-w-full` as well, because the chip's own `max-w-full` resolves against the `li` — without a cap there the `li` sizes to its content and the chip is handed a container that was never narrower than itself, so `truncate` silently does nothing. Verified against a stub serving an 88-character agent role, 70-character skill and MCP names, and an RTL/CJK/emoji identifier: the agent detail page renders all ten checks green, `/skills` renders both long names with their full values on a `title`, and the emitted stylesheet confirms `truncate` and `whitespace-nowrap` agree on `white-space: nowrap` (both set it to the same value, and `truncate` is the only source of `overflow: hidden` and `text-overflow: ellipsis`), so composing the two loses nothing;
- the Console's browser verification is currently blocked, and the gap it leaves is stated rather than glossed. The shared Playwright MCP is not reachable from this session and this sandbox blocks launching its own Chromium (`bootstrap_check_in ... Permission denied` on the Mach port), so the layout claims above were verified by rendering the production build against a stub and reading the served HTML and compiled stylesheet — not by computed style. That is weaker in one specific way worth naming: a class attribute can be correct while the cascade still resolves against it differently than expected. The `truncate`/`whitespace-nowrap` case was closed by reading the emitted stylesheet directly, which is the actual cascade, but a general visual sweep at real viewport widths still needs the browser back;
- the chip list is one implementation, not several. Tier priority previously re-declared `chipList`'s `<ul>`/`<li>` wrapper and re-typed the chip class string, which meant the inline-wrapping behaviour that keeps rows short could drift from the shared one; it now reuses the shared renderer. It is a generic function rather than a component on purpose: `React.createElement` resolves a generic component's type parameter to its constraint, so a list of anything but plain strings could not type-check through `createElement`, whereas calling the function keeps the item type inferred from `items`;
- the agent provider summary is a compact chip carrying a status dot instead of a spelled-out badge per provider, with the state kept available to assistive technology and as a hover title; Agents row height dropped accordingly;
- the provider detail view now surfaces the desired-vs-actual convergence the Control API already returns for each role (verdict badge, with the Runtime explanation and both generations as its hover title), instead of carrying a status string nothing rendered;
- a failed mutation now reads the same on every resource. Every Console mutation is a server-rendered form POST, so whatever the route returns becomes the page the operator sees; the Memory route answered every failure with a JSON body, dumping `{"error": ...}` outside the Console shell with no way back. The could-not-be-confirmed vocabulary that lived inside the Providers feature is now `console/src/lib/control-failure.ts` plus a shared `ControlFailureNotice` component, used by the Memory, Providers and model routes and rendered by the Memory and Providers pages. A route cannot claim what happened to a mutation — the refreshed value it redirects to is authoritative — so the notice states only that the change is unconfirmed. Memory's route now redirects with the same relative `location` the other routes emit, preserving the tab the action came from (purge returns to Experiences), and still answers JSON to non-browser callers. Verified by redirecting a refused purge: HTTP 303 to `/memory?tab=experiences&workspaceId=…&control=failed`, rendering `role="status"` inside the Console;
- the destructive experience purge is wired to the capability the Runtime actually implements, and is guarded rather than decorative. `Purge Experience` previously posted `action=purge` with an `experienceId` field to a route that implemented only the durable-record lifecycle and read `recordId`, so the one irreversible control in the Console failed closed with HTTP 400 and told the operator nothing. The Runtime's `POST /control/memory/experiences/:id/purge` accepts exactly `{ reason }` with `privacy_request` or `retention_expired`, refuses while durable memory cites the experience, and erases only the raw envelope, so the Console now offers that reason vocabulary, calls the endpoint, and targets `experienceId`; the record lifecycle and purge are validated separately because they name different identifiers. Because purge remains a server-rendered form action, confirmation cannot depend on a `window.confirm` or a disabled-until-checked button: the form carries an explicit `confirm` field and an unticked acknowledgement checkbox, and the route refuses to act without them. This is the only irreversible Console action, and it now renders through the shared `Button` `destructive` variant rather than a hand-typed error button. Verified by route tests (forwarding shape, refusal without confirmation, refusal of an unsupported reason, refusal without an experience id) and a rendered-form test; it could not be exercised in the browser because no workspace currently holds a captured experience, so the experiences list renders its honest `0 of 0 experiences` empty state;
- the Usage breakdown widgets share one presentation. Requests by agent role, physical attempts by provider, and MCP calls by tool name all present the same "label, value" list, so they now share a single row class; the tool-name widget previously rendered each entry as its own bordered card _inside_ an already bordered panel, which read as a nested box and left one small tile floating in a wide empty panel. Its two empty states also reused the page's shared empty-state class instead of a locally retyped italic style. Values use tabular numerals so counts align down the column, as they already do in the provider list;
- a table never scrolls at a desktop width. The per-table scroll floor was derived from the sum of a table's own column weights, which is its _natural_ width — so any table whose columns wanted more than the page offered scrolled at full desktop width, with no small-screen cause: `/agents` scrolled 26px at 1440 because its floor was 1087px against a 1061px container. A floor is a legibility limit, not a target, so it is now capped at 54rem. The cap is set from measurement rather than taste: the tightest layout the Console actually produces is not the narrowest viewport but 1280 with the sidebar still expanded (about a 901px content column), with 1024 on the rail next at about 877px. A cap under both keeps every table scroll-free at those widths. Verified across all thirteen routes at 1440, 1280, and 1024: zero tables scroll and zero pages overflow the document; at 768 the seven dense tables scroll 186-243px inside their own region and the document still does not overflow. A narrow table still keeps the smaller floor its own columns need rather than inheriting the cap;
- keyboard focus is one canonical rule rather than a per-component class. `console/app/globals.css` declares `:where(a, button, input, select, textarea, summary, [tabindex]):focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--color-accent); outline-offset: 2px; }` at zero specificity, so a component may omit the utility without losing the indicator. Previously only seven files declared a focus style, all with the identical utility run, and the remaining focusables — every navigation link, table link and chip, roughly five hundred of them — fell back to the user agent's blue ring, which is not a Console token. Real `Tab` traversal now reports `2px solid rgb(34, 211, 238)` on 80/80 focusables across `/providers`, `/usage`, `/memory` and `/agents`, with no user-agent default remaining. Note that focusable controls carry `transition-colors`, so sampling computed outline colour without letting the transition settle reads a mid-interpolation frame rather than the final token;
- headings are one design system, and the document outline they produce is correct. A survey of the feature views found 29 distinct class strings for what is really two roles, so the same "uppercase label above a group of fields" rendered at 12px/400, 12px/600 and 14px/600 in `text-fg-muted` or `text-fg-secondary` with four different bottom margins — two adjacent detail pages labelled sibling panels at visibly different sizes and weights. Five files each held their own private copy of the constant, three of them spelled differently. `console/src/components/layout/Heading.ts` is now the single definition of `SECTION_HEADING_CLASS`, `ENTITY_EYEBROW_CLASS` and `ENTITY_TITLE_CLASS`, and `EntityTitle` owns the entity heading's tag level. Three structural defects fell out of the same sweep: `/tools/[name]` emitted a second `h1` under the shell's, which `AppShell`'s own contract forbids; `/memory` skipped from the shell `h1` straight to an `h3` at a third of the size; and a prompt whose Markdown opened with `# H1` injected a page-level heading midway down `/prompts/[name]`, below Console sections and above the shell title, so the prompt body is now demoted three levels as content within the page. `AppShell` remains the only owner of the `h1`. Verified in the browser: every one of fifteen routes now reports exactly one `h1` (the shell resource title), and the surviving eight distinct heading class strings each correspond to a different job — the shell title, the nav group label, the prompt author's own document, a data-bearing diff header, and a warning callout heading;
- the Console fits a phone-width viewport. The shell was sized `w-screen`, and `100vw` includes the classic vertical scrollbar gutter, so the shell was always wider than the width the document actually had and every page carried a 15px horizontal scroll wherever a scrollbar was shown; it is `w-full` now. Separately, a native select takes its intrinsic width from its widest option, so a workspace select labelled with a long repository id pushed its row past the viewport and carried the Apply button off-screen with it — on `/memory` the Apply button was unreachable at 390px, and on `/usage` the whole filter row was clipped. `SelectField` and `FIELD_CONTROL_CLASS` now carry `max-w-full min-w-0`, and the filter groups that hold them wrap, which fixes every current and future call site rather than the two rows that happened to break. Entity titles carry `break-words` because a canonical tool name is a single unbreakable token that otherwise ran off the edge with no indication anything was missing, and step down below `sm` because a 24px identifier needs three lines in a phone column. Verified across fifteen routes at 1440, 1280, 1024, 768 and 390: zero document overflow, zero elements extending past the usable width outside a deliberate scroll region, and zero clipped titles;
- panels and callouts are one design system too, and the same sweep exposed the same defect twice more. The feature views held 17 spellings of three surface boxes between them, one of which wrote the identical classes in a different order, so two panels that are the same object compared unequal by eye. `console/src/components/layout/Panel.ts` now names the three roles a region can have — `DETAIL_PANEL_CLASS` for a detail page's primary panel, `LIST_PANEL_CLASS` for the box that wraps a dense table, and `NESTED_PANEL_CLASS` for a box inside another panel, which carries no shadow of its own because a second elevation inside an already elevated panel reads as a mistake. Two empty-state panels also lost their shadow only when their region had no data, so a region changed elevation the moment it loaded; they now match the populated sibling they replace. Separately, 20 callout literals across 9 files expressed the same idea — "tell the operator a condition" — in four geometries, with `rounded-lg` against `rounded`, `p-3` against `p-4` against `p-5`, `text-xs` against `text-sm`, and a 20% tint against 10%, so moving between pages changed how loud the same condition looked. `console/src/components/layout/Callout.ts` gives them one treatment with a severity. The single fixed opacity is also the legible one: `--color-error` and `--color-warning` are already light foreground colours, so stacking a 20% tint behind them lowers their contrast. Verified in the browser: only two callout class strings now render anywhere across fifteen routes, both canonical;
- tags and badges are two named shapes, not twenty-one hand-typed ones. The last layer of the same drift sat inside single table rows: on `/agents`, a provider tag rendered at a 4px radius with 8px of horizontal padding directly beside a status badge at a full pill radius with 10px, because `StatusBadge` was a designed system with documented semantic variants while every tag around it grew organically at `px-1`, `px-1.5` or `px-2` and `text-xs` or `text-micro`, with borders appearing and disappearing. `console/src/components/status/Tag.ts` now defines `TAG_SHAPE`; colour, monospace and truncation stay with the caller because those carry meaning rather than form. The two shapes are deliberately different — a badge is a state word and is fully rounded, a tag is an identifier or category and is squared — so a dense table can tell them apart at a glance while each stays internally uniform. `ControlFailureNotice` also carried its own geometry as a fifth callout shape; it now uses the shared warning callout, so a mutation that could not be confirmed looks like every other warning the Console shows. Verified in the browser: the tag geometry resolves to the same radius, padding and size on every page that renders one, and the badge geometry is single-valued everywhere;
- the dark-only palette holds its contrast, measured rather than assumed. The target state requires readable contrast without naming a ratio, so every element carrying its own text was measured on all seventeen routes at 1440: foreground composited over the accumulated alpha of every ancestor background up to the first opaque one, then scored with the WCAG 2.1 relative-luminance formula against the 4.5:1 normal-text and 3:1 large-text thresholds. Zero elements fall below their threshold; on `/agents` the 137 measured elements span 5.71:1 to 18.80:1, with the floor held by `text-fg-muted` on `bg-surface-raised` and the ceiling by the page title. The auditor is self-checked rather than trusted on a zero result — a sweep that cannot fail is indistinguishable from one that measures nothing. The same sweep over semantics reports one `main` and one `h1` per route, no duplicate `id`, every `nav` named, every form control and button with an accessible name, and every `section` either named or containing a heading;
- browser-rendered Console acceptance remains partial: this sweep covers layout, overflow, heading structure, control theming and keyboard focus on the local production build against the live Control API, not full visual/accessibility/mutation acceptance. Table headers specifically satisfy the target-state rule that a header rendering as an ellipsis is a layout defect: a sweep of every `thead th` at 1440 and 1280 reports zero, and zero interactive elements lack an accessible name;
- **the Console is server-first, not client-free.** Server components remain the default for page data, Control API access, and mutations; prefer native links and forms when they provide the needed interaction. Small client islands are appropriate when immediate browser state is essential, as with the persistent sidebar toggle. AppNav is the only currently approved island and does not own page data or API credentials. Additional islands must be narrowly scoped, registered with a rationale in the Console test allowlist, and covered by interaction and accessibility tests.
- **responsive behaviour was re-checked at the breakpoints themselves, not only at the usual widths.** The earlier sweep used 1440/1280/1024/768/390, which are Tailwind's own breakpoints — the widths _between_ them were untested, and those are exactly where a grid flips column count. Sweeping 639/640/641, 767/768/769, 1023/1024/1025, 1279/1280/1281 and 1535/1536 reports zero document overflow, zero elements past the usable width outside a deliberate scroll region, and no clipped heading at every boundary. At narrow widths the sidebar defaults to a 56px icon rail; the OpenLIT-style circular control remains visible at every width and toggles between that rail and the 256px layout. At narrow widths, the expanded panel overlays the page rather than creating horizontal overflow. The rail keeps every navigation item clickable, with its section name as accessible name and hover title, and group dividers remain visible.
- The compact navigation closes after a primary same-tab destination selection or Escape below 1280px; modified link-open gestures preserve the current view state. Console unit tests cover the dismissal predicates, and `console/e2e/navigation-acceptance.spec.ts` now drives the navigation itself in a browser: the rail is the default at a narrow width, the expanded panel overlays the page rather than squeezing it, a destination selection and Escape both collapse it, and a modified link-open gesture leaves the current view state alone. After p85 deployment, the live Usage API and server-rendered route pass; a focused post-upgrade compaction-panel check now passes in headless Chromium at 390/768/1280, while destination navigation and mutations remain unverified.
- the remaining primitives named in the target state now exist, and each one closed a real defect rather than only removing duplication. **Charts**: `/usage` drew its three breakdowns as rows whose left accent bar was a fixed four columns wide and never varied with the value, so it encoded nothing the number beside it did not already say; `console/src/components/charts/BarChart.ts` is a horizontal bar chart built from elements rather than SVG, because the chart remains server-rendered, and an SVG chart is the only way to draw one — it would cost the labels and values their selectability and their accessibility. Bars scale to the largest value in the set and floor the bar width, so an observed zero is a bar and a number rather than a missing row. **Filters**: four surfaces each had their own filter row, in four geometries, one of which rendered no panel at all; the experiences bar bypassed `Button` and the shared control chrome entirely, and its search input had no accessible name because it relied on a placeholder, which disappears the moment the field has a value. `console/src/components/filters/FilterBar.ts` owns the form, its GET method, the panel, the accessible name, the query state that must survive a submit, the submit button, and the trailing result count; `FilterSearchField` makes the accessible name a required prop. **Drawers**: the two Memory selection panels shared four hand-copied class strings and the only thing keeping them identical was nobody editing one; `DetailDrawer` owns the surface and header, and a test asserts both the absence of `<dialog>` and of any dismissal handler so a modal is not introduced by accident. **Code surfaces**: seven spellings of a block of source, disagreeing on radius, padding, height cap and background — most visibly, the prompt version diff and the committed source directly beneath it were two blocks in the same section, one bordered and padded and the other with none of it. `CodeBlock` and `CodeEditor` own the chrome; height is a closed set rather than a caller-appended `max-h`, because Tailwind resolves same-property utilities by stylesheet order, so appending one to a base that had another would silently lose. **Empty states**: rendered three ways, and one of the inline ones had silently lost its `text-xs`, so the same "nothing here" line rendered at two sizes on two pages; `EmptyState` names the two real treatments — `box` replaces a whole region and keeps the table's border, `inline` fills a slot inside one — and finally uses the `empty` icon, which had been defined in the icon set and never rendered anywhere. It never synthesizes a message: "no rows" and "source not wired" are different facts, and only the caller knows which it is rendering;
- two defects found in that pass were about how components are _used_, not about how they look.
