- **patch 43 clears tenancy residue that only a literal scan could see.** Four things: the telemetry datasource page branched a link onto `/organisation/project/<id>/connectors` (patch 32); it carried an 81-line `SignalRoutingSection` that no caller ever rendered, because both of them passed `showRouting={false}`; the database-config page and the same file's source dialog both fetched `/api/project/environment` — a route patch 32 deleted — and each `.catch` turned the 404 into an empty environment list that merged straight back into the single entry it was meant to fill, so the failure was invisible and the UI was unaffected by the fix; and `RESTRICTED_DEMO_ACCOUNT_ROUTES.DELETE` still named `/api/prompt-hub`, which has no route file and no rewrite. The two fetch sites now derive their single environment from the config they are editing.
- **patch 44 removes route config for products that no longer exist, and restores a page the logs signal already linked to.** `utils/breadcrumbs.ts` still carried configs for `/home`, `/d/<uuid>`, `/dashboards`, `/dashboards/{board,explorer,widget}`, `/settings/profile`, `/evaluations/manual`, `/agents`, `/agents/<key>` and `/coding-agents/users/<userId>`, along with two `extractRouteParams` branches that existed only to serve them — and the coding-agents config rendered breadcrumbs pointing at `/agents?tab=coding&codingTab=users`, three dead links in one component. `getActiveApp` still special-cased `/dashboards` + `/d/` and returned null for an `/onboarding` prefix that no longer exists anywhere. `ONBOARDING_WHITELIST_ROUTE_PREFIXES` / `ONBOARDING_WHITELIST_API_ROUTES` gated nothing: `check-auth.ts` computed `isOnboardingWhitelisted` and never read the result, so both constants and that branch are gone, along with `/api/user/complete-onboarding`, which had no caller in the fork or in AutoDev. Separately, `/memory` shipped outside `config.matcher`, so the whole middleware chain skipped the fork's own page. The tests that pinned the removed configs were inverted rather than rewritten: `ROUTE_CONFIGS` must match no removed path, and every surviving breadcrumb href must match a config that still exists.
- **the logs signal linked to a detail page that was never created, and the page rendered blank when it could not read the log.** `registry.tsx`'s logs entry returns `/telemetry/logs/<rowId>` from `getDetailHref`, which `signal-list.tsx` pushes on row select and again from the sheet's "Full screen" button — but no `app/(playground)/telemetry/logs/[id]/page.tsx` existed, so both paths 404'd, while the sibling traces, exceptions and metrics detail routes did. `log-detail-page.tsx` already exported a `LogDetailPage` component with nothing mounting it. Chromium now renders `/telemetry/logs/<id>` as HTTP 200 with a "Log entry" heading. The second defect is why it rendered an empty body even once the route existed: `LogDetailView` read the failure from `(data as any)?.err`, but a 503 `TELEMETRY_SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE` never reaches `data` — `useFetchWrapper` clears it and puts the message in `error` — so the page showed a title over nothing. It reads `error ?? data?.err` now, and distinguishes a readable request that returns no record ("No log entry with this id in the selected source and time range") from an unreadable one. Verified in Chromium against this stack, which has no ClickHouse connector: the page shows **"No connector is configured or routed for logs."**
- **the ClickHouse connectivity banner's page allowlist had outlived the pages it named.** `ALLOWED_CONNECTIVITY_ALERT` permitted the alert on `/home`, `/dashboard`, `/telemetry*`, `/observability*`, `/requests`, `/exceptions`, `/d/<uuid>`, `/prompt-hub`, `/vault` and `/dashboards*` — six of which no longer exist — while `/evaluations`, `/costs`, `/memory` and `/connectors`, which the banner's own text describes as unavailable, were not on it. The wrapper mounts only from the `(playground)` layout, so the list was pure residue with a real cost: the warning was silent on exactly the surfaces it described. The list is deleted and the alert renders wherever the shell renders. A nine-route Chromium pass after the change confirms the wrapper's container does not disturb the layout on any page; the alert's visible state could not be exercised here, because this stack has no ClickHouse configuration and `pingDetails.error` is therefore never set.
- **the trace detail page had the same two defects as the log one, and Chromium is what surfaced them.** Visiting `/telemetry/traces/<id>` for an id this stack cannot resolve returned HTTP 200 and then sat there: the title settled on the raw span UUID, the body stayed on its loading skeleton at t=4s, t=10s and t=20s, and `/api/telemetry/request/span/<id>` was answering 500 the whole time. Same root cause as patch 44's log page — `useFetchWrapper`'s `error` was never destructured, so a failed read and a finished one looked identical — plus a title fallback that treated "nothing loaded" as "title it with the identifier". It now reads `error ?? data?.err`, separates a readable request that returns no span ("No trace with this id in the selected source and time range"), and titles the page "Trace unavailable" over the API's own reason rather than a UUID. Re-verified in Chromium: **"Trace unavailable — Request failed (500)"**, with no loading line left behind. This is patch 45, and it is the case for keeping the browser in the loop — the page was HTTP 200 the whole time, so no status-code check or unit test would have flagged it.
- **the metric detail page reported an unreadable metric as "Loaded Points 0".** The third and last of the three signal detail siblings, and the worst of the three answers: the trace and log pages rendered an empty body, this one rendered a number. `metric-detail-page.tsx` destructured neither `error` nor `isFetched` from `useFetchWrapper`, so a 500 left `points` as `[]` and the summary tile confidently reported **0** — the exact "unreadable ≠ empty" failure the target state names, on a tile whose whole job is to be a count. It now distinguishes an unreadable metric (the API's reason), a metric with no points in range, and a load in progress.
- **a currency rendered as `$0.0041000000`, and only the browser could see it.** `normalizeTrace` runs lodash's `round()` and then forced `.toFixed(10)` on the result, which re-adds exactly the trailing zeros the rounding had removed. `cost` is the only `type: "round"` mapping and both its consumers read the value as-is — the trace detail's Cost tile and the requests table's cost column — so a $0.0041 call rendered as `$0.0041000000`. Two more sites did the same with `toFixed(10)` on a currency, in the cost-recalculation toast and the span hierarchy's total, while the rest of the client (`columns.tsx`, `signal-records.tsx`, `grouped-table.tsx`, `trace-governance-panel.tsx`) uses four decimals. The fix is at the mapping rather than at each consumer, and the assertion pins the mapping's output (`0.0041`→`"0.0041"`, `12`→`"12"`, and a longer value still rounded to the mapping's precision). It is mutation-tested: restoring `.toFixed(10)` turns the suite red.
- **half the product can only be seen down its error path here, so a fixture stub is how the rest was inspected.** This stack has no ClickHouse connector, so every `/api/telemetry/*` read answers 500/503 and the traces list, log list, metric list and all three detail pages can only render their failure states. `.tmp/telemetry-fixture-stub.mjs` serves fixtures for the unreachable reads and proxies everything else to the dev server, which is what made the currency defect visible: the Cost tile only exists on a page that loaded a span, and that page only loads with a connector. Two things followed from pointing a browser at it. The **ClickHouse connectivity banner now renders** on the metrics list and the detail pages — pages its old allowlist excluded, so patch 44's change gets the visual acceptance it could not get from the unconfigured stack. And the trace detail page was confirmed to still render its real content (status, duration, tokens, cost, model, trace/span/service/environment pills, Overview/Resource/Span Attributes tabs, and an honest "Span hierarchy is not available for this span") with the new error branch in place rather than displacing it.
- **the first 32-route sweep was measuring the harness, not the product.** It reported `text=22` and `alert≥1` on all 32 routes including `/login`, and classified 31 of 32 as `partial`. Two instrument bugs: the volume selector matched a nested header element instead of the content column, and the alert count included the toast host's permanently empty `role="alert"` region. **A metric with zero variance across every sample is the strongest possible evidence that the instrument is stuck, not that the product is fine.** Re-measured on `<main>`'s `innerText` with non-empty alerts only, the sweep discriminates: 15 `product`, 12 `partial`, 1 `EMPTY`, 3 `stuck?`. That mix is what located the remaining work — `/prompt-hub` is honestly empty over a successful read, while the three `stuck?` routes are the landing page and two analytics tabs reporting zeros or a permanent Loading state over failed reads, still open below.
- **patch 45 verified as a chain, and the 44-patch verification extended to it.** All 45 patches apply to `9938c666` in order, the applied result is byte-identical to the tested working tree (the same three leftover empty directories from patches 30 and 39 excepted), `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean and the suite is 271 files / 4117 tests. The trace-detail assertion fails on a 01-44 tree and the whole helper — every pre-existing assertion plus the patch 43, 44 and 45 blocks plus the wired-in literal scan — passes on 01-45.
- **the landing page reported unreadable counts as `0`, and the analytics surfaces waited on a ping that may never settle.** The corrected sweep left exactly three `stuck?` routes, and all three were one defect wearing two faces. `StatCard` gates its read on `pingStatus === "success"` and never reads the hook's `error`: when the ping succeeded and the read failed, `data` was null and the `|| 0` defaults rendered a confident **`0`** with a `0%` trend beside it — on the landing page, eight times. When the ping _failed_, `isFetched` never became true and the tile sat on **"Loading..."** for the life of the page with the stat never attempted. One component carries nine callers (the dashboard's llm/costs/evaluations/vector stat rows, the evaluator detail page, the memory page), so patches 48 and 49 fixed it there rather than at each call site.
- **the ping gate is systemic, and a failing ping is the mild version of it.** Twenty components gate a fetch on `pingStatus === "success"`. On a stack with no connector configured this is not a fast failure: `/api/clickhouse` can hang, the ping stays `pending`, the read is never issued, and the surface waits indefinitely — exactly the "stuck?" the sweep recorded on `/evaluations` and `/costs`. The ping was never a precondition for the data; the read's own error already says whether a connector is reachable. The four components behind those two routes (`stat-card`, `pie-chart-card`, `evaluation-analytics`, `cost-per-time`) now run the read as soon as the filter is valid, and each distinguishes a failed read from an empty one. Verified in Chromium: `/evaluations` goes from **9 permanent Loading states** to the real "evaluations not configured" onboarding; `/costs` from 5 Loading states to **11 Unavailable**; and against the fixture stub the dashboard tiles still render real values (1.28K / 0.42s / $41.28 / $0.0321) with their trends, so the success path is intact rather than merely unblocked.
- **closed by patch 50.** The sixteen remaining `pingStatus === "success"` gates — `request/grouped-table`, `observability/{signal-list,agent-loop-bar,generation-health-bar}`, `dashboard/{vector/operations,evaluations/metrics-per-time,llm/requests-per-time,llm/token-charts,costs/auto-pricing-runs}`, `costs/costs-auto-pricing-banner`, `evaluations/evaluators/[id]`, `prompt-hub/[id]`, `filter/traces-filter` — are gone from the client tree, and the guard now proves it by scanning that tree rather than by naming the files. The two UI-affordance gates (`prompt-hub/header`, `context/header`) keep theirs deliberately.
- **patches 48 and 49 verified the same way.** All 49 patches apply to `9938c666` in order, byte-identical to the tested tree (the same three empty directories from patches 30 and 39 excepted), `npx tsc --noEmit` clean, 271 files / 4118 tests. Each block is proven red on its own predecessor: patch 47 on a 01-46 tree (`round() must not be followed by a fixed precision...`), patch 48 on a 01-47 tree (`a stat tile that never reads the hook error cannot tell a failed read from a zero count`), patch 49 on a 01-48 tree (`pie-chart-card.tsx must not gate its read on a ping that can never settle`). - **patch 50 closes the ping gate, and seven of its sixteen sites were still lying after the ungate.** The two-part change was ungate the read, then add the distinct unreadable state, and the second half is the half that does not come for free. A failed read settles as zero rows, so every ungated surface became a candidate for reporting "no data" — and seven were. `grouped-table` said "No data found for the selected filters"; `signal-records` said "No traces found for the selected filters" **while its own sibling rendered the read's error banner**, so `/requests` showed "No connector is configured or routed for traces." directly above "No traces found for the selected filters." — the page contradicting itself, which is what the browser pass found and reading the code did not; `token-charts`' area chart reported an empty series; `auto-pricing-runs` offered the **"Enable Auto Pricing" call to action** for a failed read, sending the operator after a setting that was not the cause; `agent-loop-bar` and `generation-health-bar` printed "0 of 0"; `prompt-hub/[id]` said "No such prompt exists!" for a prompt it never read. `IntermediateState`'s `nodata` arm now accepts `children`, as its `loading` arm already did, so a surface can say "Unavailable" without a second shared component. The two affordance gates (`context/header`, `prompt-hub/header`) keep theirs — hiding "New prompt" while the connector is unreachable is correct.
- **ungating a read made the outcome nondeterministic until the honest state existed, and the probe had to be fixed too.** `/costs` alternated between a settled page and one stuck in a loading skeleton, and the first probe run blamed the product. It was sampling: with no connector each read hangs 8–15s and a cold Next.js compile pushed first paint past the fixed delay, so a transient skeleton was read as the final answer. Polling until the surface stops claiming to load (rather than sleeping) made it settle reproducibly — **0 Loading, 11 Unavailable on `/costs`; 5/5 routes honest** (`/costs`, `/requests`, `/dashboard`, `/evaluations`, `/prompt-hub/<id>`), each asserting the specific false claim is absent **and** the honest state is present, not merely that the page rendered. `/evaluations` is the one route whose correct answer is not "Unavailable": no evaluation engine is configured here, so it short-circuits to its own onboarding, and the probe asserts that instead of the guess I first wrote. The fetch counts are also recorded because ungating exposed them: `/evaluations` issues 11 analytics reads inside the first 1.4s and `/costs` 6, all from React StrictMode double-invoking effects across the mount cycle, all bounded, none runaway.
- **the guard derives its scope from the client tree, and mutation-testing found two of its own assertions could not fail.** `clientSourceModules` walks `src/` rather than taking a list, so a module added later is covered — a literal array is green for the files it names and blind to everything that grows into it. Two assertions were initially unfalsifiable and the probes said so: requiring the bare word `unreadable` matched a renamed declaration (`_droppedUnreadable`), and requiring `unreadable={` on `signal-list` matched `unreadable={false}`. Both now require the identifier to be _used as a condition_ (`/unreadable\s*\?/`) and, for the prop, to actually reference the read's error. All six mutation probes are caught: a gate introduced into a module no assertion names, the `signal-records` false claim, `signal-list` passing a constant, the `nodata` arm losing its override, the CTA returning to the unreachable arm, and a chart losing its unreadable arm entirely.
- **patch 50 verified as a chain, 01-50.** All 50 patches apply to `9938c666` in order; the applied result is byte-identical to the tested tree (the same three empty directories from patches 30 and 39 excepted); `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; 271 files / 4118 tests. - **the OpenLIT patches were not the blocker this entry predicted, and the one place the old contract still appears is a mock that cannot drift.** The measurement behind the original claim was right about the work and wrong about its widest edge. `PROVIDER_ROLES` really was `["orchestrator", "subagent"]` (`core/src/routing/types.ts:1`), `RoutingPolicyState` really did carry only `disabledOrchestratorProviders` / `disabledSubagentProviders` / `disabledModels`, and a repository-wide search really did find no per-role priority, no per-role model and no agent limits anywhere — which is why the change had to be atomic across **Core** (`PROVIDER_ROLES` to the four roles; `RoutingPolicyState` to per-provider per-role `{priority: 1|2|3|"disabled", model}` assignments, a provider-level `disabledProviders` list, and per-provider `{perSession, acrossSessions}` limits where `null` is an explicit Unlimited), **Runtime** (`setProviderAssignment` / `setProviderLimits` / `setProviderEnabled`, a changed `runtimeState()`/`restoreRuntimeState()` shape, three `http.ts` state snapshots, and a `PATCH /control/providers/{provider}/roles/{role}` body that changed from boolean `enabled` to `{priority, model}` — a boolean cannot express "restore this role at P2 with that model"), **Core's Control API types and the Console validator**, **the Console API route**, and **the view**. All of that shipped, and a partial migration was correctly never committed. What did not survive measurement was the sentence claiming `02-autodev-pages.patch` and `28-remove-autodev-pages.patch` "must be regenerated or the fork series stops applying": all 51 patches apply to `9938c666` in order (`APPLIED_OK`, re-verified against a fresh checkout). The old two-role example _does_ survive into the final tree, at `src/client/src/__tests__/lib/autodev/control-api.test.ts:193`, and it is inert for a reason worth stating rather than assuming: patch 28 **modifies** that test instead of deleting it, and the test never imports Core's provider types — it declares its own generic argument at the `forwardToControlApi<{...}>` call site, mocks `fetch`, and asserts only that the body passes through. A fixture that owns its own type cannot drift from a contract it does not reference. The same holds of `tests/openlit-control-proxy.test.ts:326`, which mocks an `autodev-control-provider-role-v2` body — two schema versions behind the live `v3` — while asserting nothing but the forwarded `X-AutoDev-Actor` header; the stale literal is mock input, never an assertion. **The tempting fix is worse than the residue:** editing patch 02's fixture shifts that file's line numbering and fails patch 28's hunk context for the same file (`patch failed: .../control-api.test.ts:380`), so the pair would have to be regenerated in lockstep to keep a documentation example honest. The fork's transient Providers page and types are left alone for the same reason — patch 02 creates them and patch 28 deletes them, so they never coexist with the final state and no consumer can observe them. `tests/openlit-patches-apply.test.ts` reports 4 failures in this sandbox, all from the checkout being unable to create `.claude/commands/*.md` and `.gitmodules`, which kills the clone before any patch runs; identical at HEAD and unrelated to the series.
- **the AutoDev Console is clean across all twelve list surfaces, and finding that required fixing the sweep twice — each time the instrument, not the page.** Measured in Chromium against the Console on `:3300`: 12 routes, all HTTP 200, `load=0`, no horizontal overflow, no console errors, content volumes from 312 to 12,747 characters (so the instrument discriminates), and no route that claims an empty result while also saying it could not read. The classifier was calibrated against eight known page states first, so the all-clear is a measurement rather than a single bucket. Three defects were in the sweep: its loading pattern included `…`, and `/skills` truncates 14 skill descriptions, so a settled page with 14 ellipses in it read as `STUCK` — it was not stuck; its settle loop waited for the **loading count** to hold at zero, which a **server-rendered** page satisfies immediately, so `/permissions` was classified before its error state rendered and lost the honest-state flag it does carry; and, carried over from the fork sweep, the contradiction test had to learn the Console's vocabulary rather than one product's word for it.

The runtime snapshot on the Agents landing page is the other half of the same idea: **READY AGENTS / CONVERGED AGENTS read "Not observed"** because no reconciliation has run, while **IN-FLIGHT REQUESTS reads 0** because that number comes from a live runtime snapshot. Those two are different evidence and both are rendered at their own strength, which is the distinction a single `|| 0` would have erased.
- **the fixture stub backed the stat tiles but not the charts, so patch 50's success path had never actually been seen.** Every probe so far asserted that a _failed_ read is reported honestly; none asserted that a _successful_ read still renders its data, which is the regression an added `unreadable` branch can cause. Pointed at the stub, `/dashboard` showed real stat values (`1.28K`, `0.42s`, `$41.28`, `$0.0321`, `7`) beside **eight charts reading "Unavailable"** — honest failure, since those endpoints were proxied to a server with no ClickHouse, but it meant the charts' success path was unverified. The stub now serves the series endpoints (`/request/time`, `/llm/{token,model}/{top,time}`, `/llm/{category,endpoint}`, `/llm/cost/{environment,application}`), with shapes taken from each component's own mapping rather than guessed — including `/llm/endpoint`, which is what "Generation by provider" actually reads, distinct from the cost-by-provider series. - **patch 51: the chart time axes printed the raw stored timestamp, and it was only visible once the charts had data to draw.** `request_time` arrives as "2026-10-05 20:18:07.020" and the XAxis drew it verbatim; six ticks across a card's width collided into `2026-10-05 20:18:07.0202026-10-05 23:18:07.020`. This is a defect of the _rendering_, not of the honesty work, and it could not be found before this pass because an empty chart draws no ticks at all — the failure was invisible for exactly as long as the surface was unreadable for a different reason. Four axes draw that value (requests-per-time, two in token-charts, metrics-per-time), so `helpers/client/chart-axis.ts` owns the tick text once: it compacts to "Oct 5 20:18" and normalises both shapes the reads use (a ClickHouse datetime string, a unix timestamp in seconds or milliseconds) rather than letting an axis print "Invalid Date"; an unparseable value is echoed unchanged, so a malformed tick degrades to its input instead of becoming noise. The full value still belongs in the tooltip. Six unit tests, and the guard asserts that the number of formatted axes equals the number of `request_time` axes **per file**, so a fourth chart added later cannot skip it silently. Measured in Chromium against the stub: twelve evenly spaced ticks reading `Oct 5 19:18 … Oct 6 18:18`, real stat values intact, zero Unavailable.
- **patches 51 verified as a chain, 01-51.** All 51 patches apply to `9938c666` in order; the applied result is byte-identical to the tested tree (the same three empty directories from patches 30 and 39 excepted); `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; **272 files / 4124 tests**. The new block is proven red on a 01-50 tree (`the chart tick formatter must exist; four time-series axes depend on it`) and green on 01-51, and four mutation probes against it are caught — including one that removes the formatter from exactly one of token-charts' two axes, which the per-file count assertion reports as `draws 2 request_time axis/axes but formats 1 of them`.
- **the route sweep was rebuilt, and its own classifier needed calibrating before its all-clear could be believed.** The previous sweep waited a fixed 4.5s against reads that hang 8-15s, so its `stuck?` verdicts were sampling artifacts; worse, it classified a route `partial` whenever any alert was present, and the shell's **"ClickHouse connector unavailable"** banner renders on every `(playground)` route — so 12 of 32 came back `partial` on a banner that says nothing about the route. The rebuilt sweep settles by polling, separates that banner from route-level state, and classifies on what the route itself claims. It then reported **`MIX {"ok":31}`** — a single bucket, which is the same tell as the zero-variance metrics: a classifier with one bucket is indistinguishable from a classifier that never discriminates. Calibrating it against ten known page states found a real bug: `CONTRADICTS` tested for the literal word "Unavailable", but the signal list's honest failure says **"No connector is configured or routed for traces."** and nothing else, so the contradiction — the defect class this sweep exists to catch — was the one it could not see. Every bucket is reachable after the fix. **One defect class remains deliberately invisible to this sweep: a bare confident `0`.** Detecting it from page text would flag every legitimate zero, so it is caught by the per-surface probes instead, which know which tile is meant to hold a count.
- **a sweep detail that looked like an authentication gap is not one — the API-key path is checked first, and the check is worth not skipping.** The four telemetry detail routes render their own content beside an **"Unauthorized user!"** alert, which is `getCurrentUser()` returning null (`lib/db-config.ts`, `lib/scope.ts`, `lib/rbac/route.ts` all throw it) and looked like a contradiction with target-state §Account/auth, which removes the account product and forbids the auth middleware from recreating an OpenLIT account gate. It is not a contradiction. `withDbConfigAccess` resolves identity API-key-first: when the middleware has verified a Bearer key it sets `x-database-config-id` (`middleware/check-auth.ts:155`) and the handler proceeds with no user at all; `getCurrentUser()` is only the fallback for a browser session (`lib/rbac/route.ts:54-63`). A headless browser has neither, so the 401 is the correct answer, and in the deployed shape — AutoDev calling the fork with its bearer token — telemetry reads never require an account. `/login` and `/register` are compliant for the same reason: both are bare `redirect("/dashboard")` with no UI, which is what that section requires. Recorded because the wrong reading was the plausible one: **a dev stack with no seeded session produces a 401 that looks exactly like the removal having broken the read path, and the fix is to trace the identity resolution before believing it.**

These were the same root cause patches 45 and 46 fixed in the detail pages — `useFetchWrapper`'s `error` and `isFetched` ignored — but in the list and stat-tile components rather than the detail pages. All four now render an unreadable state instead, re-measured in Chromium on the 01-50 tree: `/dashboard` 0 Loading / 17 Unavailable / 1 no-data, `/costs` 0 Loading / 11 Unavailable, `/evaluations` the real onboarding, `/requests` 0 Loading with the honest connector alert and no contradictory empty beneath it.
- **an unrecognised URL filter was resolved into a default and then drawn as the reader's own choice.** Every list page read its filters out of the query string, where each value is arbitrary text — a bookmark outlives the option it names, a shared URL gets edited, a value gets typed — and every page answered a value it did not accept the same way: substitute the default, then render that default as though the reader had chosen it. Measured in headless Chromium, `?source=bogus` on `/tools` answered with the whole 41-entry catalog and the `all` chip rendered as selected; `?kind=bogus` on `/memory` drew a select reading "All Kinds" while the request carried `kind=bogus` to the Runtime, so the control reported a filter the request never contained; `?tab=bogus` drew "Durable Records" as the current tab. Three surfaces, one behaviour: the page asserts a filter state it never observed, which is the same failure the rest of this tracker records for evidence, only about a control rather than about a count. The fix is that a coercion is not a resolution — `console/src/components/filters/resolve-filter.ts` returns the value to apply _and_ the request it could not use, and `FilterNotice` names that request in the shared warning callout (`role="status"`, no icon, because the icon set is closed and deliberately carries no warning glyph). `MEMORY_KINDS`/`MEMORY_STATUSES` from Core now decide the Memory value lists, so the filter the page applies and the options the select renders cannot drift apart. Two deliberate exclusions: `role` is free text, so an unmatched role is a filter that honestly matches nothing and says so in the table's empty message rather than a refused one; and the notice is reported on whichever `/memory` tab rendered, because `tab` chooses the surface and the `kind`/`status` selects are preserved across tab links, so no filter can be named from a place that may not render — a rule holding on only one tab is a fourth thing to remember about filters. Measured across 17 URL cases and seven viewport widths (390–1536): the notice appears exactly when a bounded filter is refused, never otherwise, and produces no document or internal overflow at any width. The guard is asserted on **rendered output** rather than on imports, because `app/memory/page.ts` resolves the filters and hands the list to `MemoryView`, which is what renders it — a source scan reading "does this file mention `FilterNotice`" fails that legitimate split while an unused import would satisfy it. Both halves are mutation-tested: restoring the silent coercion in `resolveFilter` reddens the unit assertion, and dropping the notice from `ToolsView` reddens the DOM assertion, each with its own message rather than a parse error;
- **every page put fourteen tab stops in front of its content, and a keyboard user had no way past them.** The sidebar is a persistent fourteen-link `<nav>` that precedes `<main>` in the document, and nothing skipped it. Measured in headless Chromium across eight routes: exactly fourteen focusable elements before `<main>` on all of them, which is most of the page wherever the page is not a dense table — `/mcps` has 22 focusable elements in total and 8 inside `<main>`, `/tools/find_code` 23 and 9, `/providers/antigravity` 25 and 11, `/memory` 29 and 15. `AppShell` now renders `SkipLink` before the nav, visually hidden until focused and then revealed over the viewport's top-left with a focus ring, pointing at a `<main>` that carries `id="main-content"` and `tabIndex={-1}`. The `tabIndex` is load-bearing rather than decorative: a browser scrolls to a fragment target with or without it, so without it the next Tab resumes from the nav and the fourteen stops are still there — the guard asserts the attribute exists for exactly that reason, and removing it reddens the suite. The link lives beside the `<main>` it targets instead of in the root layout, because the nav is the thing being skipped and a route that renders outside `AppShell` has none to skip. The focus ring is the one shared `:where(a, button, input, select, textarea, summary, [tabindex]):focus-visible` rule in `app/globals.css`, so the guard asserts the link is an anchor and that the rule still covers anchors, rather than asserting a `focus:ring-*` utility this product does not use. Re-measured across six routes: the first `Tab` lands on the link (1x1 hidden, 126x38 revealed), `Enter` moves focus inside `<main>`, and no route gains document overflow. The same sweep found the rest of the keyboard path already consistent — no focusable element on any of eight routes lacks a visible focus ring;
- **a cross-page accessibility structure sweep is clean, which is worth recording as a measurement rather than an assumption.** 23 routes (13 list surfaces plus the three Memory tabs and seven detail routes) at 1280: exactly one `<h1>` per page, no heading-level skips in document order, no duplicate `id`s, no `input`/`select`/`textarea` without an accessible name, no link with no accessible name, no `svg` that is neither `aria-hidden` nor named, and no `role="tab"` outside a `role="tablist"`. `aria-current="page"` appears once to three times per route (sidebar; plus the breadcrumb on detail routes; plus `/mcps/cocoindex-code`'s third) and is left as-is: `TabNav` documents the choice deliberately, declining the `tablist`/`tab`/`tabpanel` roles because it does not implement the roving-tabindex contract they carry, so the plain link semantics are a considered answer rather than an oversight, and nothing measured here contradicts it;
- **the truncation guard was scanning from the wrong offset, so it had been half blind since it was written.** `nothing truncates text it cannot give back` walked the source by setting `at = propsEnd + 1` at the end of each iteration and then computing the next props object from that offset as though it were a `React.createElement(` position. Every props object after the first was therefore read from an arbitrary origin and attributed to the wrong line. Fixing the advance to `source.indexOf("React.createElement(", propsEnd)` took the offender count from 5 to 11 — the guard had been reporting some of the sites it should have been reporting all along, and missing the rest. **A guard that reports real findings at the wrong line numbers is still worth reading, but it cannot be cited as evidence that the rule holds.**
- **a tag cut a value with no marker and nothing to give it back, and 14 more could.** Measured in headless Chromium at 390px, `/github`'s `workflow_dispatch` trigger chip was capped by `max-w-full` at 116px against a 131px identifier and rendered the name cut mid-word with `text-overflow: clip` and no `title` — `inline-flex` blockifies to `flex` as a flex item, and `text-overflow` does not apply to a flex container, so the cut carried no ellipsis at all. Widening the guard to the second form of truncation exposed the root cause: fourteen call sites were assembling the same shape by hand from `TAG_SHAPE`, and a title has to be added per site, so it was added at none of them. That is the `NOT_OBSERVED_LABEL` failure again — composing the constant left it decorative. `TAG_SHAPE` is now a block box, which is what makes the ellipsis work, and `Tag` owns the shape and the title together the way `Chip` already did; the two non-`span` sites (a role link in `ToolDetailView`, an inline `code` span in `PromptDetailView`) title themselves with a comment saying why they cannot be a `Tag`. `whitespace-nowrap` is spelled out beside `truncate`, which already implies it, because it is a decision and not a default: an earlier round fixed a collapsed drawer title by adding `flex-wrap` to the row rather than letting badges squish, and that guard asserts the literal. Re-measured across eight routes at 390px: 15 tags cut on `/github` and 23 on `/tools`, every one now with an ellipsis and a title, none without. The one deliberate waiver is `Reported`/`Unreported` in the cohorts table, a fixed pair of short words with `title: null` and `cut=0`; the guard's two exemptions are `StatusBadge`, whose title is spread conditionally as `{ title }` rather than `title:`, and `Chips`, which titles from its own child — both held by the assertions on those components directly. `Tag` is deliberately _not_ exempt, so it has to keep passing the rule itself.
- **the guard could not resolve a composed shape, and then could not resolve one that explained itself.** Two follow-on holes, both found by mutation-testing rather than by reading. Shapes declared in one module and _imported_ into another are invisible to a scan of the call site's own `className`, so the resolution has to run across modules first — and a shape constant is allowed to carry a comment between its `=` and its string, which `TAG_SHAPE` does precisely to explain the `whitespace-nowrap` decision. Without stripping comments before matching, the one constant whose rationale most needs reading was the one the scan could not resolve, and a guard quietly stops covering everything that composes it in. Verified by mutation: reverting the advance offset, removing `Tag`'s own title, and reverting the `workflow_dispatch` chip each redden the suite with the guard's own message and the offender's file and line.
- **the drawer's dismiss control was four pixels under the minimum target height.** `ClosePanelLink` measured 58x20 on every width with zero padding — 20px is its line box, and WCAG 2.5.8 asks for 24. `py-1 -my-1` reaches the floor and gives the space straight back, so the drawer's title row does not grow. Measured false positives from the same sweep, recorded so they are not re-investigated: the purge confirmation checkbox renders as a 13x13 input, but it is wrapped in a `<label>` whose measured box is 252x32 and clicking anywhere on the sentence toggles it, so the real target clears the floor; and the filter chips inside table cells measure 20-22px tall because the target state specifies that density (`th` 16/10 12px/15, `td` 16/12 14px/20). The sweep that found all of this also over-reported on 171 of 230 measurements before its instrument was tightened to leaf elements only — a flex parent reports its overflowing child and a native `<select>` reports its widest option, and neither says anything about whether a reader can reach the text.
- **the Console has no motion, so no `prefers-reduced-motion` block is warranted.** Measured rather than assumed: zero `@keyframes`, zero `animation` declarations, zero `animate-*`/`transform`/`translate-*`/`scale-*`/`rotate-*` utilities across `console/app` and `console/src`, and twelve `transition-colors`. Adding the block would be dead CSS against a product that does not animate.
- **one detail surface read flat where every sibling read nested, and "no heading skips" is the opposite condition.** A cross-surface outline sweep of the six detail routes found `/tools/[name]` emitting its entity title as the canonical `h2` and its four section headings as `h2` as well, so Source authority, Role exposure, Description and Historical use were siblings of the thing they belonged to. `/providers`, `/prompts` and `/mcps` all render the same sections at `h3` under an `h2` title, so the outline was flat on one surface and nested on three. The existing 23-route sweep reported this page clean because it tests for _skips_, and `h2` followed by `h2` skips nothing — a guard for the opposite defect cannot catch this one. `every detail view titles its resource with the one canonical entity title` had the same hole from the other side: it asserted each view's _title_ was the shared `h2` and never looked at what followed. It now asserts that no section shares the title's level, and mutation-tested by restoring one `h2` (`ToolDetailView nests a section at h2 (levels present: 2, 3); the entity title is the h2, so its sections must be h3 or they read as siblings of their own title`). Two things the new assertion has to get right, both found by writing it wrong first: sections are identified by the **shared class they render**, not by the name of the constant supplying it — markup carries the value, so matching `SECTION_HEADING` against the output finds nothing and the check passes vacuously — and an empty match must be reported as _vacuous_, not as clean. Demotion is semantics only: `/tools/find_code` and `/mcps/cocoindex-code` section headings measure identically afterwards (12px/600, 0.6px tracking, 12px margin, 16px tall).
- **the icon surface is clean, measured rather than assumed.** No `<svg>` element and no `createElement("path")` literal exists anywhere in `console/app` or `console/src` outside `components/icons/Icon.ts`, so every mark in the product comes from the one closed set. The seven arrow characters in the source are all truthful or properly decorative: `View ↗` on `/github` really does carry `target="_blank"` and `rel="noopener noreferrer"`, the `→` separating provider tiers in `ProvidersView` is `aria-hidden`, the `→` in `Open Usage →` and `Evaluations results →` is trailing label punctuation rather than an icon, and the `✕` that survives is inside the comment in `ClosePanelLink` documenting its own removal.
- **no route fetches anything it does not render, and every multi-read route already fans out in parallel.** Measured through a logging proxy in front of the Control API across 23 routes: eleven list surfaces make exactly one call, `/agents` three (agents, providers, runtime — each feeding a rendered projection), `/providers` two, and every detail route two or three. Then measured for _serialisation_ rather than count, by injecting a fixed 150ms per upstream call and reading wall clock: `/agents` (3 calls) 211ms, `/providers` (2) 195ms, `/prompts` (1) 253ms, `/mcps/cocoindex-code` (2) 263ms — one round trip each, so the reads are parallel. `/memory` was the only serialised route in that fixed-150ms sweep (565ms over four to six upstream calls). The required gate is `resolveMemoryWorkspaceScope`, which must complete before workspace-scoped Memory reads. Within that scope, the unscoped status read and records read are independent and now start in parallel; the status result is still retained when records fail, and a records failure still short-circuits the remaining reads. A separate seven-run `MemoryPage` render against the same five fixture endpoints, each delayed 150ms, measured a warm median of 617.3ms before and 461.8ms after (155.6ms / 25.2% saved) with no change in upstream call count. These route numbers isolate server render. A separate single-run production-mode headless Chromium check against the same 150ms Control API stub measured a Memory tab click at 599ms without a prefetch dwell; after hovering for 1.2s, click-to-selected-tab was 49ms, with the completed intent prefetch reused and no extra RSC/API request on click. The fixture produced no browser console errors. This is synthetic single-sample evidence, not a live-backend latency percentile. `use-cohorts` is fetched only on the cohorts tab while `session-cohorts` is fetched on every tab, which is also correct rather than accidental: the first backs a table that renders on one tab, the second backs the "Cohort Sessions" stat that renders on all three.
- **a section heading shared a non-wrapping row with a badge and collapsed into a three-line column.** Found by looking at `/mcps` at 390px rather than measuring it: "Model Context Protocol Servers" rendered stacked three deep in a 129px box beside the `RuleSync source valid` pill. Measured: 3 lines, 129x48, parent `display: flex`. A flex row that spaces its children apart has a minimum intrinsic width set by whichever child refuses to shrink, and `whitespace-nowrap` on a pill means no wrapping _inside_ the other child reduces it — the same shape this tracker already records for the Providers role row. `/prompts` had it on "Edit Canonical Markdown Source", and `AppShell`'s header had it one level up, where no page fills the `actions` slot yet so it costs nothing today and would have cost the title its width the first time one did. All three now wrap; `/mcps` measures 1 line at 252px. The new guard asserts no row that spaces a heading against a sibling can fail to wrap, with **no exemptions** — `AppShell` was the reason there are none, since making it wrap cost nothing and removed the need for a carve-out. Mutation-tested by reverting one `flex-wrap`.
- **the primary key was the narrowest column on `/mcps`, so every server name rendered as eight characters.** The table's floor is 864px (`tableMinWidthPx` caps the declared sum), which is what every viewport under 864 sees, and column `weight` is only a share of that floor rather than a pixel measurement. Server Name was declared at 150 — tied with the RuleSync declaration column and below `Configured roles` at 192 — so at 390px it resolved to 105px against roles' 135. Measured, every name rendered truncated: `cocoind…`, `codegra…`, `openaiD…`, `playwri…`. Server Name is the row's primary key and its link target, so it now declares 230, taking the width from `Configured roles` (192→180) and `Overrides` (224→196, the widest column on the page for what is usually one chip). Result at 390px: 156px, and five of seven names fit whole — `autodev_spawn`, `cocoindex-code`, `codex_app`, `context7`, `lsp`, `playwright` — with `codegraphcontext` and `openaiDeveloperDocs` still truncating recoverably. This was a deliberate trade against row height: a 6-role server still stacks one chip per line at 122px, so those rows remain tall, and widening the role column enough for two chips would need roughly 129 weight taken back out of the name, undoing the fix. Reading the row beats scanning it faster.
- **the failure shell rendered an error code that does not exist.** `/usage` and `/permissions` both drew `autodev_openlit_usage_unreachable` as `autodev_openlit_usage_unreachabl` + `e` and `autodev_control_api_invalid_permissions_response` as `autodev_control_api_invalid_perm` + `issions_response`, because the code span carried `break-all`. That was a deliberate decision — the comment argued that an unbroken machine token "has nowhere to break but mid-word" — and the argument is the bug: `break-all` does not make an arbitrary cut a last resort, it makes it the _only_ option on every render. The resulting strings are not the code, and neither matches a line in a log. The repo had already settled the opposite rule for this class of value in three places (`Heading.ts`, `AgentsView`'s router instance id, `DetailGrid`), all of which use `break-words` and say why; this site was the exception. Note that `break-words` alone does not fix it either: CSS has **no break opportunity at `_`**, so a snake_case token is one unbreakable word and the browser must still cut it at an arbitrary character. What fixes it is making those positions real break opportunities — a `<wbr>` after each separator, so the token wraps only between its own groups and each line is a true prefix of the value, with `break-words` kept solely for a single group too wide for the card. `<wbr>` renders no characters, so the element's text is still exactly the code. Measured in headless Chromium at 390px: `/permissions` now reads `autodev_control_api_invalid_` / `permissions_response` and `/usage` reads `autodev_openlit_usage_` / `unreachable`. The old guard asserted `assert.match(markup, /break-all/)` — **a fixture pinning the defect** — so it was green for the life of the bug; it now asserts the rendered text equals the code exactly (which passes on both the broken and the fixed shell, since `break-all` leaves the text intact too) _and_ that every separator group is followed by a `<wbr>`, _and_ that `break-all` is absent. Mutation-tested both ways: restoring `break-all` without the `<wbr>` elements and keeping the `<wbr>` while truncating the value each redden the suite with their own messages.
- **three candidates from this round measured clean, recorded so they are not re-investigated.** (1) _Table row height._ `/agents` rows measure 99px at both 390px and 1280px because the Providers column wraps its chip list to three lines, which reads as a defect against the one-line rows elsewhere — but a census of all twelve list surfaces at 1280 shows `/agents` is among the tightest: `/workspaces` and `/evaluations` are flat at 48px, `/prompts` 65–73, `/github` 61–77, `/tools` 67–125, `/skills` 79–125, `/providers` a flat 123, and `/mcps` 48–**177** for a six-role server. Multi-line cells are the application norm and `/agents` is not the outlier. The target state settles this explicitly: "Discrete cell content (chips, badges, model ids, environment variable names) stays atomic and wraps between items, never mid-token", which is what the wrapping chip list does and what truncating it to one line would violate. (2) _Column headers._ The same paragraph names a real defect — "a column's weight must be large enough for its own header: a header that renders as an ellipsis is a layout defect" — so all 66 distinct headers across thirteen routes were swept at six widths (390–1536) for ellipsis, clipping and under-width. Exactly one was flagged, `VALIDATION` on `/memory?tab=experiences`, and measuring it cleared it: `thOffset === thScroll === 101`, so the usual overflow probe reports nothing, but a `Range` over the header's contents measures the text at 81px with `overflowWrap: normal`, so the word overflows its 69px content box by 12px — into the **neighbour's 16px padding**, leaving 20px before the next header's text. It renders whole and collides with nothing. The flag was the instrument, not the product: the sweep estimated 7.4px per character and `tracking-wider` makes it 8.1px. (3) _The `/github` workflow path._ At 390px the path reads `.github/workflows/_` / `agent-open-pr-and-` / `ping.yml`, which looks like a mid-token break — the underscore is real: the file is `.github/workflows/_agent-open-pr-and-ping.yml`, and the breaks land on hyphens, which _are_ natural break opportunities, so every line is a true substring. A repeat sweep should measure with `Range.getClientRects()` rather than estimate per-character widths, and should compare the widest line box against the _neighbour's text_ rather than against the cell box, because a `th` reports `scrollWidth === offsetWidth` even while its content overflows;
- **a status badge was cut with no ellipsis, no marker and no title, in four places, and two of them had already been "fixed" by widening the column.** Measured in headless Chromium at 1280: `/skills` drew "Configured" with its right border and last glyph gone on all fourteen rows, `/agents` cut it by 9px, `/prompts` cut "Role prompt" by 11px, and `/providers` cut a 297px environment variable name inside a 143px cell. Three of the four carried no title at all. The component's own comment claimed the opposite — "a column that cannot fit a badge is a column-width problem, and the word stays legible" — and the rendering contradicted it, because the badge is an `inline-flex` box and **`text-overflow` does not apply to a flex container**: the box simply ran out. `StatusBadge` now puts the ellipsis on the label, in a `min-w-0 truncate` span (`min-w-0` is what lets a flex item shrink below its `white-space: nowrap` min-content at all), and titles itself with `title: title ?? displayLabel`, so a caller's own longer explanation still wins.
- **a `weight` cannot be tuned for a pill, and two columns' comments recorded a previous attempt at exactly that.** A weight is a share of a table whose width is whatever the container gives it, while the pill's pixel width is fixed, so one number cannot serve every viewport. Worse, the number itself was wrong twice over: `/providers`'s Health column was documented at "the widest health badge measures 68px" when the pill is 70px with its dot and padding and needs 102px of column, and my own first pass measured the badge's _already-clamped_ `scrollWidth` rather than its natural width, understating it by 8px. Measuring the pill with its clamp removed in place, then comparing against the **table's 864px floor** rather than the viewport the badge was measured at, gave the real budget: `/agents` Status 131 / Convergence 147, `/skills` State 131, `/providers` Health 102 / Credential 162, `/mcps` RuleSync 123 / Default State 144 / Connection 144, `/prompts` Type 137, `/evaluations` Outcome 144 / Trace 163. `/evaluations` turned out to be a different regime entirely: its weights total 600, which is under the cap, so its floor is the sum itself and **a weight there is the column's pixel width directly** — sizing it against 864 would have been wrong twice. After the change, measured across nine routes and six widths (390–1536): every status pill renders whole at every width except the one deliberate case, `/providers` Credential, which names a 297px environment variable in a 162px column, is documented as expected to truncate, and now truncates with a title instead of silently. Width came from the cheapest column on each page, in this order: a chip list that wraps between items (costs height, not legibility), a clamped description, then a truncating identifier. **`/mcps` Overrides is the one place that order ran out** — it is now 105px against a 130px chip, so every override reads `codex…` / `copilo…`. It is titled and recoverable, and it was not shuffled into Server Name or Configured roles, which are the primary key and already wrapping one chip per line; the honest fix is the one `AgentProviderSummary` already uses on `/agents` (a chip carrying a status dot instead of a spelled-out suffix), which would bring the column to roughly 70px.
- **the truncation guard now reads ancestors, which retired an exemption rather than adding one.** `StatusBadge` had been exempt from `nothing truncates text it cannot give back` because its title was spread conditionally (`{ title }`, not `title:`) and the scan reads the ordinary form. That reason is gone, so the file exemption went with it — and the scan immediately flagged the new label span, because the title is on the badge and the ellipsis is on its child. A per-file exemption would have re-opened the hole for the next `truncate` anyone adds to that file, so the scan keeps a stack of the calls open around the scan point instead: truncation is recoverable from anywhere above it, and an enclosing element carrying the title covers its descendants. Mutation-tested both directions: dropping the badge's `title:` reddens both the badge and the label span, and an unrelated untitled `truncate` with no titled ancestor is still reported, so the rule is a real narrowing rather than a blanket pass. An exemption kept after its reason has gone is a hole waiting for the next change to use it;
- **`/mcps` is over budget at its own floor, and the arithmetic is worth recording because it constrains every future weight on that table.** Widening the three pill columns in the previous round was paid for out of Overrides and Transport, and looking at the result showed the damage plainly: `STD…` on five of eight rows, and the two headers rendering as `TRANSPORTOVERRIDES` with no gap between them. Both are named defects in the target state, so the weights had to be solved rather than nudged. Measured in the browser rather than estimated — and the estimate is what caused it: I had assumed 8.1px per uppercase character with `tracking-wider`, and the real figure is 9.1, which is the whole difference between "TRANSPORT" fitting at 105px and overrunning at 82px of text. Each of the seven columns needs this much of the 864px floor: **84** for Server Name's own header, **120** for the longest role chip, **123** for the "Canonical" pill, **144** for each of the two "Not observed" pills, **114** for "TRANSPORT" (wider than the cell it labels), and **108** for "OVERRIDES". That is 793px before the primary key takes a pixel, so Server Name takes the 111px that is left. Every other column is therefore at its own minimum and the primary key is the one that gives — which reverses the previous round's fix on purpose, because a header that runs into its neighbour is a defect and a truncated name is a title. The cost is stated rather than hidden: at 390px `autodev_spawn` now renders `autodev_s…`. Raising `TABLE_FLOOR_CEILING_PX` would resolve it and was **not** done, because its measured reason for existing is sound (a derived floor made a table scroll at full desktop width for 26px) and the spec only promises core workflows at desktop widths, where the table is 958px and none of this binds. Re-measured across nine routes and six widths: **zero header defects**, and the only remaining pill cuts are the six deliberate `/providers` Credential ones.
- **`/mcps` Overrides now spends its column on the name instead of the state, via a shared component.** The spelled-out state was costing more than the name did: `antigravity-cli: enabled` is a 175px chip where `antigravity-cli` with a status dot is 130px, and at 105px every override on the page read `codex…` or `copilo…`. That chip-plus-dot shape was already hand-written on `/agents`'s provider summary, so a second site needing it is where the duplication stops being acceptable — `StatusChip` now lives beside `Chip` and both sites use it, which is also the only way the dot and the `target: enabled` title stay the same thing in both places. `/mcps` passes typed `items` with a `renderKey` rather than pre-joined strings, so the enabled flag is a value rather than text that has already been flattened into a label;
- **the shared-component changes regress nothing, measured across 22 routes and recorded with the two sweeps' own defects.** Re-run after `StatusBadge` and `StatusChip` landed, since both are on every page: exactly one `<h1>` per route, no heading-level skips in document order, no duplicate `id`s, no control or link without an accessible name, no `svg` that is neither `aria-hidden` nor named. The detail surfaces were also reviewed by eye at 390 and 1280 (`/tools/find_code`, `/prompts/abstraction-layer`, `/mcps/cocoindex-code`, `/providers/antigravity`) and carry no document or internal overflow at either width. **The two findings the sweep produced were both its own**, which is worth writing down because a sweep that only ever finds defects in itself is not yet evidence of anything. (1) _It flagged two Memory search inputs as unnamed._ They carry `<label for="filter-query">Search memory claims</label>` — the sweep checked `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, `title` and text content, and `label[for]` is the most common naming mechanism in plain HTML and the one it forgot. A correctly labelled control reported as unlabelled is the worst kind of false positive, because acting on it would mean deleting a label that is doing its job. (2) _It flagged a `<label>` overflowing by 203px at both widths._ That label is `sr-only`: a 1px box whose `scrollWidth` is its intrinsic text, which is what a screen-reader-only element is supposed to measure. Any clipped-element sweep will find these; the filter has to exclude `sr-only` by name, or better, check the rendered box's visibility.
- **the stale Router is still stale, re-probed rather than assumed.** `/control/agents/orchestrator` still answers `schema: "autodev-control-agent-detail-v1"` where the Console requires v2, and `/control/providers/antigravity/models` answers 404, so `/permissions`, `/agents/[id]` and the model detail page continue to fail closed by design. Restarting it was still not the right move: other agents were mid-edit under `runtime/src/router/`, and a restart would load their unfinished work into a process they share. The three surfaces stay covered by the throwaway stub serving the exact v2 shape the Runtime source emits, which is recorded above;
- **two of seventeen list views inherited a sentence that named no resource, and the default that let them is now gone.** `DataTable` defaulted `emptyMessage` to `"No items to display."`; fifteen views overrode it and `/agents` and `/permissions` did not, so the two pages whose whole job is answering "what exists here" rendered a generic nothing on their empty state. `EmptyState` already documents that it "only ever renders a caller-supplied message and never invents one" — the default was `DataTable` inventing one on its behalf, so the prop is now **required** and the typecheck refuses a list view that skips it. That immediately earned its place: it caught two call sites that invoke `DataTable({...})` directly instead of through `createElement`, which a source scan for the `createElement` form had missed. The same round removed two hand-copied `DataTableProps` interfaces in the memory views — shadow copies that sat between the real type and three call sites and had already drifted to `emptyMessage?`, so the contract was not actually being enforced there. Verified in Chromium at 390 and 1280 against a stub whose catalogs are genuinely empty: both pages paint a box that names its own resource, fits the viewport, keeps one `<h1>`, and leaves no horizontal page scroll;
- **the capability matrix sorted roles alphabetically, so the four fixed roles appeared in an order the target state does not use.** Measured in Chromium: `/permissions` listed `default, orchestrator, smart, subagent` because the adapter sorted with an `Intl.Collator`, while the target state fixes the sequence as "Default, Smart, Orchestrator, Subagent" and calls them the canonical roles. An operator had to re-learn the sequence per page. The first attempt ranked by Core's `PROVIDER_ROLES`, which is wrong twice over: it models the two roles a _provider_ can be enabled for (`orchestrator`, `subagent`), not the agent roles a matrix row is about, and the file is currently being rewritten by another agent — it read as four roles and as two within the same session. The order is now declared next to the adapter with the spec as its authority. `AgentRole` is an open union, so a Runtime may legitimately report `worker` or `explorer`: those rank after the canonical four and stay ordered among themselves by the collator, because dropping a role the API sent would hide evidence and an arbitrary order would churn between reads. Both properties are asserted;
- **one card in a row of four rendered a raw enum in display-sized type.** `/permissions`'s stat row reads "Workspace write", "Allowed", "Enabled" and then `on-demand` — `sandboxMode` has always been mapped to prose by `sandboxLabel`, and `approvalPolicy` was not. It is now a `Record` keyed by the policy union rather than a switch, so a fourth member fails to compile here instead of quietly rendering as itself;
- **`/permissions` and `/agents/[id]` have now been audited in a browser, which they never had been.** Both fail closed against the live Router, so until now they had only ever been seen as a failure shell — the two routes most likely to hide a layout defect were the two never rendered. A contract-accurate stub (every field the Console's own response guards check, built field by field) brings both up: one `<h1>` per route, no heading skips, no duplicate ids, no value cut with nothing to recover it, and no horizontal page scroll, across six widths from 390 to 1536. **The sweep's one finding was its own**: it flagged the table's `overflow-x-auto` wrapper at 390 and 640, which is precisely the behaviour the target state requires below the floor ("the table region scrolls horizontally rather than shrinking columns"), and the obvious "fix" would have been a `title` on a scroll container. Anything inside a horizontal scroll container is now excluded, and the revised predicate was calibrated against four injected states before its clean result was believed: it reports a clipped untitled value in a non-scrollable box and ignores the scrollable, titled and `sr-only` cases. Looking at the pages also checked one suspicion that turned out to be wrong: `/permissions`' Sandbox Mode wears the same chrome as the token lists beside it, but `Tag` for a single short value is the house pattern (`WorkspacesView`, `GithubView`, `MemoryRecordsView`, `MemoryCohortsView`), so it was left alone;
- **Historical 2026-10-13 audit of the prior four-column Providers implementation.** Audited in Chromium against a stub built to stress it -- five providers covering Ready, missing credential, provider-disabled, in-cooldown, and no health observed, plus the longest id in the catalog. The column set is exactly Provider, Status, Roles, Agent Limits, and Status resolves correctly in every case: `Ready`, `Missing CODEX_API_KEY` (the spec's own example), `Disabled`, `Cooling down (upstream_5xx)`, `Not observed`. The findings at that time, all in `console/src/features/providers/`, were measured rather than eyeballed: (1) **the Provider cell cuts the id.** `antigravity-cli` measures 144px in a 118px box and renders `antigravity-cl`. The column comment says it is "sized to never truncate it (longest observed id renders ~92px)", which was measured against a shorter id than the one the grip leaves room for -- the grip is inside the same box, so the name does not get the whole column. `ProviderLink` carries an `aria-label` but no `title`, so the id is fully reachable by screen reader and invisible to a mouse, and the one hover title a sighted operator _does_ get in that cell is the grip's "Reordering providers is not settable yet", which explains something other than the text under the cursor. (2) **`null` limits claim two contradictory things in one cell.** `core`'s `ControlApiProviderRecord` documents `agentLimits: null` as "the explicit Unlimited choice", and the Console's own guard agrees -- "`null` means Unlimited and is a decision the operator made, so it is distinguished from an absent key". `ProviderLimitsControls` renders `null` as an `EmptyState` reading "No limits configured", directly above steppers that render `∞` for the same value and an `Unlimited` button whose own title says "This is not the same as a provider that was never configured". Three statements of one fact in one cell, two of which are false by the contract that validated the payload. (3) **A static "Provider disabled" caption sits beside the Disable/Enable button on every row**, including the four that are not disabled -- so it reads as a state claim and is wrong on four rows of five. It is also pure duplication: `resolveProviderStatus` checks `provider.disabled` first, so the Status column already carries that verdict and always will. (4) At that time, all six files in that directory were Prettier-dirty. Those historical findings were recorded rather than applied during that iteration; they are not current acceptance evidence.
- **Provider table recheck (2026-10-14):** The canonical target and current view now agree on Provider, Status, Active Agents, Roles, Agent Limits. Provider links retain the full identifier in a `title`; `null` limits render as explicit Unlimited (`∞`) and the disabled caption appears only for a disabled provider. Repository formatting is clean. A current rendered-browser sweep of the five-column layout at narrow and desktop widths remains open; no visual pass is inferred from the earlier four-column measurements.
- **the three blocked routes each fail closed for a different, now-named reason, and the fix is on the publishing side.** Re-probed against the Control API actually serving on 4202 (the earlier throwaway stub has been replaced by a real one, which also explains why a probe that omitted `x-autodev-actor` started returning `autodev_control_api_actor_missing` instead of data). Each failure was traced to the exact field, because "the Router is stale" is not actionable and these three need different things: (1) **`/permissions`** — every `rolePermissions[*]` entry publishes only `readOnly, sandbox, networkAccess, approvals`. The Console's guard also requires `mcp` and `skills` arrays per entry, and its own comment gives the reason: "The capability matrix must be a real projection. An absent list is missing evidence, not 'no MCP servers'." The eight roles the Runtime does publish, including `worker` and `explorer`, fail on those two absent keys alone. (2) **`/agents/[id]`** — serves `autodev-control-agent-detail-v1` with no `reconciliation`; the Console requires `autodev-control-agent-detail-v2` carrying `reconciliation: { status, history }`. (3) **Model detail** — every one of the 8 `/control/models` records publishes `enablement: { enabled, mutable }` and **no `convergence` block**, so all 8 fail `isEnablementWithConvergence` and the entire response is rejected as `invalid-response`. The guard is not the thing to relax in any of the three: loosening it would let a response render a convergence verdict nobody reported, which is the one thing this Console must never do. Restarting the serving process was still not the right move — other agents are mid-edit under `runtime/src/`, and a restart would load their unfinished work into a process they share;
- **`/evaluations` was never in a sweep, and real ClickHouse rows hid a defect three fixtures could not.** The route list was carried forward from an earlier session and named thirteen surfaces; `/usage`, `/evaluations` and `/memory` were missing from it. With live data the METRICS cell rendered `to…` and `to…` on the same row — `tool_calls: 14` and `tool_failures: 4`, two metrics whose names share a prefix. The container was `flex gap-2`, which cannot wrap, so both chips were clipped inside their own boxes and both read `to…`: two readings that were the same reading twice, which is worse than either one being cut. `flex-wrap` is the fix the target state names directly ("discrete cell content ... wraps between items, never mid-token"), and it is what makes the column's budget legible at all, since the budget now has to fit one chip rather than half of two. **The widths were also measured against live rows for the first time** — the previous round solved them from fixtures whose values were shorter than anything the store actually holds. Needs at 1280: Target Role 130, Model 184, METRICS 216, Outcome 144, Trace 163, Run Time 190 — **1027px of content into 959px of table**, so this table cannot show six columns whole at that width and the question is only where the cuts land. Three allocations were tried and measured before settling, which is the point: ranking the columns and spending everything on the top two left `Not ob…` on four badges and `2026-10-05T0…` on Run Time, a _worse_ reading than before. What shipped puts METRICS and Model whole and pays proportionally from the three whose cuts still read their own value, because a cut role is still `docs-res…` while two identical chip prefixes are not a reading at all. The per-chip verdict stays: it is the metric's own `pass`, which the Outcome column does not carry (that is the evaluation's result), and it is also the chip's accessible form of its colour, so removing it for width would have taken the information with it. At 1536 every column but one chip renders whole; at 1280 the cuts are 10-35px each and every one keeps its full value on hover. The declared sum is 840, still under the 864 cap, so the floor stays the sum and this table adds no horizontal scroll at desktop width. The guard is mutation-tested: removing `flex-wrap` reddens it;
- **every internal link in the Console resolves: 247 distinct targets crawled, zero broken.** A link to a route that does not exist renders Next's own 404 page, which an operator cannot tell from a broken deployment -- and one had already been found by accident, when a sweep route id I invented turned out to have no page at all. What made this checkable is that it separates the two ways a page can fail: an HTTP 404 or a `next-error-h1` body means the target does not exist, while an HTTP 200 carrying an `autodev_control_api_*` code means the route exists and failed closed on purpose. Thirteen targets are in that second class, and they are listed rather than counted as sound so a failure-only page cannot quietly read as "all links work". The crawler was calibrated before its zero was believed, against two paths that certainly do not exist and one that does -- a checker that can only pass is the same failure wearing a lab coat. `/skills` has no detail route at all, and `/skills` links nowhere: 13 internal links, which is the sidebar;
- **the fork had dead code of its own, and one import of it could not resolve.** `60-remove-dead-client-modules.patch` deletes six modules nothing imported any more -- `components/common/code-block.tsx`, `components/ui/alert.tsx`, `components/ui/alert-dialog.tsx`, `lib/autodev/index.ts` (a one-line `export * from "./control-api"` barrel), `types/fleet-hub.ts` and `utils/hooks/use-database-setup.ts` -- and takes the dependency with them: `@radix-ui/react-alert-dialog` had exactly one consumer, the deleted alert dialog, so it leaves both the manifest and the lockfile. Regenerating the lockfile also prunes the two stale root entries the manifest never declared, `next-themes` and `tiny-cookie` (416 deleted lines, no additions), which leaves the lockfile root agreeing with the manifest exactly. The `tiny-cookie` entry was not merely untidy: `src/client/src/__tests__/utils/hooks/hooks.test.ts` imported `get`/`set` from it and mocked the module, but no source file reads or writes a cookie, the manifest never declared the package, and the fork's own suite installs from that same lockfile -- so the import could not resolve and nothing inside the fork was able to see it. The vestigial import and its `jest.mock` are removed, the fork carries `src/client/src/__tests__/platform/dead-client-modules.test.ts` so that a later patch reintroducing a removed module has to say so deliberately, and `controller-removal.test.ts` now also asserts that `types/fleet-hub.ts` is gone. The AutoDev side owns the contract: `tests/openlit-client-dependencies.ts` reads every import in the patched client with the TypeScript parser -- a regex would mistake a string literal for an import and would miss `export ... from` and dynamic `import()`, so it would lie in both directions -- and asserts both that every package the client imports is installed by its own lockfile and that every package its manifest declares is installed too. `tests/openlit-patches-apply.test.ts` applies the whole series and runs that audit against the patched tree, so a later patch that adds an uninstallable import fails the suite rather than the image build. The removal also exposed a stale expectation of the fork's own: the apply test still listed `lib/autodev/index.ts` as a file that must exist after the series, which is corrected rather than the module kept.
- **the Tools detail page now has browser acceptance, and the acceptance is what found the page's heading contract.** The detail page is the one place the wire name is the whole subject, and nothing had ever driven it in a browser: the list's filters and links were accepted, the detail page was not. `console/e2e/tools-detail-acceptance.spec.ts` drives the synthetic Control API's two catalog entries -- the native `read_file` and the MCP-owned `mcp__lsp__lsp_goto_definition` -- and asserts what each one may claim. The MCP entry reports `mcp` as its source, `lsp` as its server and `RuleSync MCP` as its authority, and links its canonical edit surface to `/mcps/lsp`; the native entry reports `Not configured` for a server it does not have and an absence note rather than a link that goes nowhere. Role exposure is the projection the catalog observed, so the MCP entry shows one chip and the native one shows two. The Usage fixture observed no calls for either, and the page says so: the status is `not-observed`, the count is not rendered as zero, and the `Calls (24h)` and `Errors (24h)` fields are absent rather than present and empty, because a labelled field with a blank value reads as zero to anyone scanning the page. All three catalog identities address the same entry, so the source-qualified form is driven too. The document fits 390, 768 and 1280 without overflowing, and the page produces no console errors -- a check that earns its place, because a stale build serves markup whose JavaScript chunks no longer exist and the result is a page that reads right in a fetch and throws on hydration. Rendering first and asserting second is what corrected the spec: the tool's name is the `h2` beneath the shell's single `h1`, not an `h1` of its own, so the spec asserts the document outline rather than the heading the first draft assumed.
- **the fork still had a second provider and model authority, and nothing had been looking for it.** The gap ledger's only open product-subtraction row was the generic Vault/secrets/model administration, and the dependency check it was waiting for turned up more than the Vault. The Vault's own administration was already gone -- patch 35 deleted the `/vault` page, its `POST/GET /api/vault` routes, the sidebar entry, the middleware matchers and the token-allowlist entries -- and the Manage Models page had gone with the Settings and dashboard work. But the fork's `/api/providers` route still carried `POST`, `PUT` and `DELETE` next to its `GET`, and the whole `/api/providers/models` tree sat beside it, and every one of those wrote straight into the provider metadata and per-provider model tables that AutoDev's Control API owns. A repository-wide search found no page, no caller and no SDK behind them: the only reference to `/api/providers` anywhere in the fork was the evaluations configuration page's single `GET`, which lists providers and their models so a judge can be picked from them. So the writes were a second authority that nothing could reach and nothing could undo -- a provider created through them would have existed in OpenLIT and nowhere else, with no way to remove it again. `61-remove-provider-model-administration.patch` deletes them, and with them the `models-service` module that only those routes and their own test imported. The read stays, and the catalog behind it stays too: the ClickHouse migrations seed both tables from the default provider and model lists, so removing the writes leaves the evaluations picker with exactly the catalog it had. `62-fix-stale-fork-test-assertions.patch` then fixes what the search turned up next -- two assertions in the fork's own test suite that earlier patches had made stale, the `PRICING_CONFIG_UPDATED` event that patch 56 deleted and the `cumulativeCounterDeltas` capability that the counter-deltas work added to the ClickHouse adapter. With them fixed, and with `npm install` and `prisma generate` run in the patched client, the fork's own suite is green: 259 of 259 suites and 4,024 of 4,024 tests. Nothing in this repository ran that suite, which is why two stale assertions could sit in it across many patches -- so the AutoDev side now asserts the removals against the patched tree instead, and the fork carries its own guard for them in `provider-model-administration.test.ts`.
- **the ledger's own quality-gate evidence had stopped matching the ledger, and the guard that watched it was watching the wrong thing.** Two of this repository's own earlier slices had left five committed files unformatted, so `pnpm format:check` failed on them while the tracker still claimed it failed only on three concurrently modified Playtesting files. The five files are formatted now and the tracker records the truth. The guard that reads the tracker was also pinning the exact numbers the other sessions' in-flight work moves every day -- a lint count, a root-suite count -- and it matched the table separators with a single space, so a markdown formatter padding one cell was enough to fail it.
