The claims are unchanged: the tracker must still record a lint failure with a count, a formatting result, a root-suite result with its failed and skipped counts, and the exact wording of each product-subtraction status. What changed is that none of them is pinned to a snapshot of a number that moves whenever another session edits a file, and none of them depends on the geometry of the table it is written in.
- **the browser acceptance had been committed on a parse, and running it found three defects in the acceptance and one in the page it was accepting.** `pnpm exec playwright test --list` proves a spec compiles; it proves nothing about the page the spec drives. The Tools detail acceptance had never been run, and the first real run failed on a strict-mode violation: the Tools detail page published `data-tools-coverage` and `data-tools-validity` twice, once on the page body and once on the coverage banner, so every `[data-tools-coverage]` selector resolved to a set of two and Playwright refused to guess. That duplication was a product defect rather than a test artifact -- two owners for one fact leave the evidence hook ambiguous for every consumer, and the Tools list page already publishes the same two facts once -- so the page body is now the single owner, the banner says the tier in words only, and `console/tests/console.test.ts` asserts that each hook appears exactly once, mutation-verified by re-introducing the duplicate and watching the suite fail. The Workspaces acceptance had a second defect of its own: it built the absence-state selectors by appending to an already-closed attribute selector, producing `[data-workspace-requests]="unavailable"]`, which is not a CSS selector at all, so the two assertions meant to prove the Requests cell never claims an absence state were failing on a parse error instead of proving anything. Both are fixed at the source. All 22 Console browser tests now pass against the synthetic Control API and Usage fixtures in a real browser, one browser process per test. The environment's own limits are worth recording, because they decide what "verified" can mean here: this machine's sandbox can only start the `chromium_headless_shell` build with `--single-process`, and a single-process browser dies together with its last page, so a worker that runs a second test finds a dead browser and every later test fails at `newPage`; one invocation per test is what makes the committed specs executable, and the same rapid filter-click sequence that loses a navigation under the sandbox's single-process browser completes every time in a normal Chromium.
- **the MCPs browser acceptance was the last open half of the MCPs row, and it needed a control surface that did not exist.** The Console's MCPs views have read `/control/mcps` since the catalog shipped, but no fixture served that route, so the MCPs pages had never been opened in a browser by anything in this repository -- only the MCP detail route's existence had been asserted. The fixture now serves three servers that keep the three states apart: one declared and enabled over stdio with a target override, one whose canonical declaration is missing, and one that exists only in a target projection and therefore has no observed default state. `console/e2e/mcps-detail-acceptance.spec.ts` then asserts what the MCPs pages are for. The list page keeps Enabled, Disabled and the unobserved default apart -- the last is not the same fact as Disabled, and a page that collapsed the two would be claiming a decision nobody made -- and publishes the source validity it read and the connection it did not observe. The detail page's nine tabs appear in the order the target state names them, the configuration tab shows the declaration's own fields and renders no box for the fields a server does not have, and the five tabs that need a live session (connection/health, resources, prompts, activity, errors/logs) each say that they have not observed one. The Tools tab is the sharpest of them: it projects a configured allowlist, never a live inventory, and with the catalog's coverage complete there is no allowlist projection to read, so the tab says the projection was not observed rather than listing the tools the catalog knows about as if the server exposed them. The tab navigation is in place, and the document is not remounted by it. Runtime evidence and mutation/reconciliation for MCPs remain open: nothing here observes a live server, and no MCP control is mutated through the Console yet.
- **the Configure group's five resources had never been opened in a browser either, because the fixture served none of them.** The Console reads `/control/agents`, `/control/skills`, `/control/hooks`, `/control/prompts` and `/control/permissions`, and the fixture answered none of them, so the pages could only be exercised by the unavailable state -- which is a real acceptance of the error path and no acceptance of the resources. The fixture now serves all five, with the states each page has to keep apart: an agent whose enablement the Runtime reported and one it could not report, a skill whose assignment is observed and a runtime that has not reported it back, a hook declaration with its matcher and command, a canonical prompt command beside a role prompt, and a permission policy with a role capability matrix. `console/e2e/configure-catalog-acceptance.spec.ts` then asserts what the pages are for. The Agents list keeps Enabled apart from the enablement the Runtime did not report, and says the live instance counts are not observed rather than measured as zero. The Skills catalog is where the target state's sharpest claim lives -- "every checkbox change auto-saves the complete role set, with revision-conflict/failure feedback and no separate Save button" -- so the acceptance drives it: a role checkbox saves the whole set on change, the page carries no Save button, and a write against a revision the page no longer holds is refused with the conflict outcome rather than overwriting somebody else's assignment. The fixture answers that write with a 409 and a second operator's write moves the revision, so the refusal is reached rather than asserted. The Hooks, Prompts and Permissions lists are read for the declaration each one holds. The fixture's own request handler was over the complexity budget once these routes joined it, so the catalog reads and the fixture's control routes moved into their own functions rather than the limit being raised.
- **the Configure group's detail pages had never been opened in a browser either, and the fixture served no detail route for them.** The Console reads `/control/agents/{role}`, `/control/skills/{name}/content` and `/control/prompts/{name}`; the fixture answered none of them, so `/agents/default`, `/skills/code-review` and `/prompts/review` could only render their unavailable state, which is an acceptance of the error path and not of the pages. The fixture now serves all three, with the contracts those pages validate: the agent detail carries the enablement the Runtime reported, the reconciliation status with the generations behind it, and the role prompt; the skill content carries the canonical source and the revision it was loaded at; the prompt detail carries the canonical source, the rendered preview and the reconciliation. The acceptance then asserts what each page is for. The agent detail shows the agent's own enablement, says the live instance count is not observed rather than measured as zero, renders the Runtime's reconciliation -- its explanation and its desired and observed generations -- and shows the role prompt as the agent's own source. The skill detail loads the canonical source into the editor and carries the revision it loaded in the form, so the write is a compare-and-swap against what the editor holds. The prompt detail loads the canonical source beside the rendered preview, which stays a disclosure, and reports the revision it loaded. Two findings came out of writing it, and both were in the acceptance rather than in the pages. The agent detail labels its prompt block `Agent system prompt` and its heading `System prompt`; the acceptance had asserted the first as visible text, which it is not, so the locator was wrong. And the first payload-mutation run failed a fourth test for a reason that had nothing to do with the mutation: the acceptance drives the fixture directly to move the revision, and the harness had pointed that call at a different fixture than the Console's Control API base URL, so the write it made stale was not the write the page was holding. The remaining six tests passed in both mutation rounds, which is what makes the three failures attributable to the three mutations rather than to a broken build. The new assertions are mutation-verified in both directions: three product mutations -- the prompt block rendering a placeholder, the skill form's revision emptied, the prompt editor truncated -- were each caught by their own test, and three payload mutations -- the agent's prompt, its reconciliation generations and explanation, the skill's source, the prompt's source and preview -- were each caught by their own test as well.
- **the Usage dashboard itself had never been opened in a browser, and the fixture could only ever answer correctly.** The Usage fixture served the v5 contract for the Workspaces' per-workspace aggregate, and it answered every scope with the same partial snapshot, so the page's failure paths had no way to be reached at all: an unreachable source, a response that does not validate and an HTTP error are three different facts about the source, and a fixture that only ever answers correctly can only prove that the Console renders a snapshot. The fixture now answers four scopes differently, because the scope is the only handle the Console's read has on the source -- the request body carries the scope it asked for. Last 7 days returns a body that is not the Usage contract, Last 90 days returns HTTP 503, Last 30 days drops the connection before the source answers, and a custom range is refused with HTTP 401, so the four reach the four different failure paths in one request. `console/e2e/usage-dashboard-acceptance.spec.ts` then asserts what the page is for. The scope control is labelled _Usage scope_ and lists Active sessions beside the five ranges, because it holds a selection that is not a time range and a label promising only a window would misdescribe one of its own options. A partial snapshot shows the signal the source reported beside the signals it did not: the logical request count reads 12 while the cost, the latency, the cache rate and the token totals read _Not observed_, and no card reads $0.00, because an empty aggregate is not a measured zero. The filters tell an observed dimension from an unobserved one: the workspace filter offers the value it observed, and the four dimensions the source did not report are disabled controls that say _Not observed_ rather than empty lists that read as a filter which found nothing. The recent-attempt list says it was not observed instead of drawing an empty table. And a failed read leaves no metric cards behind while keeping the scope control, because an operator still has to be able to change the scope and read again; the invalid-response, HTTP-error, unreachable and unauthorized codes are four different codes, because a transport failure, a response that does not validate and a refused credential are different facts about the source. The assertions are mutation-verified in both directions: six product mutations -- the scope label reading _Time range_ again, the four formatters turning an absent measurement into a measured zero, an unobserved filter dimension becoming usable, an unavailable attempt list drawing an empty table, and the invalid-response and the unauthorized code each collapsing into another failure's code -- were each caught by the test that names them, and two payload mutations -- the request count and the observed workspace -- were each caught by their own test as well. One defect was in the acceptance rather than in the page: a stat card's title is not a sibling of its value, because the card puts the title in its own row above the value, so the first locator for a card's value found nothing at all and the assertion that should have caught it never ran. The live scope joined the same acceptance. The control fixture now serves the Runtime's read-only `/control/runtime` projection, and it can be taken away on demand, because a live scope that can only ever be read successfully cannot show what a failed read looks like. The Active Sessions scope is a scope of its own: the Runtime's own counters, with the historical widgets absent behind it, and no per-session list to show, because the Runtime publishes a count but no identity. A Runtime that does not answer is unavailable, with the reason, and with no counter at all, because a count of zero would report an idle Runtime that was never observed. Both claims are mutation-verified: a live scope that read the wrong counter, and a live scope that rendered a failed read as an idle Runtime with zero sessions, were each caught by their own test while the other six stayed green.
- **the model detail page was the last of the Providers surface's own pages to be opened in a browser.** `/providers/:id/models/:model` reads the model catalog, the provider catalog, the model discovery and the Runtime's live projection, and the fixture answered all four, so the page rendered -- but nothing asserted that it is the _model's_ page. The acceptance now drives `/providers/claude/models/sonnet` and asserts that the page names the model and shows its own provider and tiers, that the enablement control is the model's own and targets `sonnet` rather than the provider, that the convergence the Runtime has not reported is presented as not observed rather than as a settled state, and that the live agent count is not observed rather than measured as zero. The claim about the control's target is the one that matters: a model page whose toggle wrote to the provider would silently disable every model behind it, so that mutation -- the toggle aimed at the provider -- was caught by the new test while the other five stayed green. Two of the assertions in that spec depend on a client-side navigation, and under a loaded machine the sandbox's single-process headless shell sometimes drops the navigation; the same click reaches the same URL in a normal Chromium, so the flake is the harness and not the page.
- **the shared breadcrumb landmark had never been driven in a browser, and eight detail surfaces were riding on a component nothing had opened.** The Agent, MCP and Prompt detail pages were given one server-renderable `Breadcrumbs` landmark -- a single `<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">` holding an ordered list, every ancestor a native `<a href>`, the current page a non-link `<span aria-current="page">`, and never a placeholder `href="#"` -- but the browser acceptance was open, and the five detail surfaces that had since grown the same trail (Skill, Tool, Workspace, Provider, Model) had never been counted at all. `console/e2e/breadcrumbs-acceptance.spec.ts` now drives all eight: each page presents exactly one named landmark with the ancestors it promises, the current page is marked and is not a link back to itself, no item carries a placeholder destination, the separators are hidden from assistive technology, the trail names the place the operator is on in the order it was walked, an ancestor leads back to its list without remounting the document, and at a phone width the trail's longest label (a tool's source-qualified name) stays inside the page with its full text still reachable through `title`. `console/tests/breadcrumbs-coverage.test.ts` is what keeps the claim from decaying into a list: it reads the route tree, so every detail route the Console has must render the shared landmark, the landmark must have exactly one owner (a second `aria-label="Breadcrumb"` anywhere in `console/src` is a second trail), and every detail route must be driven by the acceptance -- a route added without a trail, without an owner, or without a browser run fails the suite. All three guards were mutation-checked: dropping the trail from the Agent detail, adding a second owner of the landmark, and un-driving the Tools route each turned the suite red and named the claim that had been broken. Two product-side mutations were caught in the browser the same way: removing the `aria-current="page"` marker, and turning the current page into a placeholder link. One measurement trap was worth recording: the Console streams a page, so the route's shell and its loading state arrive first and the page's own content is swapped in afterwards. Reading the trail before that swap read nothing at all -- the markup was in the document but not yet in the accessibility tree -- so the acceptance waits for the trail to be visible, which is also the claim worth making: a trail the operator cannot see is not a trail.
- **the Evaluations page had never been driven in a browser, so the resource with the most careful state language on the Console was the one with no browser evidence at all.** The Control fixture answered no `/control/evaluations` read and the Usage fixture answered no trace-detail read, so the whole surface could only be reached as unavailable -- which is the state a page falls back to, never the state it is in. The fixtures now answer both: the Control fixture returns a bounded window of sixty rows over a store of a hundred and twenty, with a passed, a failed and an unobserved verdict, a run that reported no prompt, a run whose trace the Usage fixture can open and one whose trace was never retained; the Usage fixture returns the bounded trace detail the panel draws, and answers the not-found code for the span the telemetry never held. `console/e2e/evaluations-acceptance.spec.ts` then drives the page against those states: the retained card names the store's hundred and twenty and the window's sixty as the two different facts they are, the filter bar's sentence and the pager's range use the same two numbers and the same words, the three verdicts are counted apart and the pass rate states how many runs carried a verdict at all, a narrowed view takes the filter bar's options with it (the prompt filter offers the prompts the narrowed rows report, not the prompts the excluded rows reported), the trace panel opens a run's trace and names the span it was asked for, and a span the telemetry never retained is reported as not observed rather than as a failed read. Four mutations were checked against it: a payload whose store claims to be its window, a payload whose every run reports a pass, and a payload whose rows answer every filter axis the same way, plus the product mutation that made the filter bar's options ignore the other axes. Each one turned the acceptance red and named the claim that had been broken -- the truncated marker, the Passed card, the prompt option list -- rather than failing on a timeout. The browser suite is now 49 of 49 across the eight non-Playtesting specs.
- **the GitHub page had a browser acceptance, but not one that could reach the states the page exists to keep apart.** The acceptance that existed was a manual headless-Chromium check against a live Runtime holding production credentials: it proved the page renders a real catalog, and it could not reach a workflow whose runtime state was never read, a workflow that declares no trigger and no schedule, or the state the page must show when the Actions API cannot be reached at all. The Control fixture now answers `GET /control/github` with those states, and its own toggle takes the Actions runtime state away, so the refusal to invent runtime facts is reachable rather than described. `console/e2e/github-acceptance.spec.ts` drives the page against them: the definitions are shown with their trigger events and cron schedules, the two workflows with no schedule say so rather than showing a blank, the cards count what the definitions declare, each workflow's own state is told apart -- active, disabled by hand, and never read -- the run statistics say they cover a bounded sample and are not the repository's whole history, no control named after dispatch, cancel, rerun or schedule is offered, and with the runtime state taken away the runtime cards are gone rather than showing zeros. Two mutations were checked against it: a payload whose disabled workflow reports itself active, and a page that grew a `Rerun workflow` button. Each turned the acceptance red and named the claim that had been broken -- the active-workflow count, and the control that must not exist. One measurement note: the mutation words are matched as whole words, because a workflow named `Scheduler` is a schedule trigger and not a schedule control -- the first version of the assertion read that row as a mutation affordance and failed against a page that offered none. The browser suite is now 53 of 53 across the nine non-Playtesting specs.
- **the Memory page had no browser acceptance at all, so the resource with the strictest counting rules on the Console was the one nobody had opened.** The Control fixture answered no memory read, so the whole surface could only be reached as unavailable -- the state a page falls back to, never the state it is in. The fixture now answers the storage status, the records, the experiences and the outcome-cohort reads with the states the page has to tell apart: a claim that is active, one that was proposed, one that was superseded, one that was invalidated, and a lifecycle rollup about the whole filtered collection rather than the rows on the page. Its own toggle takes durable storage away, so the page's explanation of a failed read is reachable rather than a guess that happens to be right. `console/e2e/memory-acceptance.spec.ts` then drives the page against those states: each row names its claim, its kind and its lifecycle state, the durable-claims card names the store's 1,204 beside the five rows on the page, the active-claims card is the Runtime's rollup over the collection rather than a count of the two active rows on the page, and with storage not configured the page says which setting to configure instead of showing an empty list that would read as nothing was remembered. Three mutations were checked against it: a payload whose rollup counted the page's own active rows, a payload whose storage status no longer named the missing configuration, and the product change that made the card count the page's rows instead of the rollup. Each turned the acceptance red and named the claim that had been broken -- the active-claims count, and the reason the page gives for a failed read. The browser suite is now 56 of 56 across the ten non-Playtesting specs.
- **the Console had a browser acceptance for every surface it had ever been given a bug report about, and none for the claim that all fourteen resources have their own route.** The target state is blunt about the shape of the Console: fourteen resources, fourteen first-class routes, no generic Home/Dashboard page, and the root route redirecting to a useful canonical resource rather than introducing another surface that duplicates Usage, runtime status or GitHub activity. That is a claim about the whole route table, and it was being carried by a sentence in a document rather than by anything that ran. `console/e2e/console-routes-acceptance.spec.ts` now drives it: the root route ends on `/agents` and shows that resource, the generic `/home` and `/dashboard` routes do not exist at all, and all fourteen canonical routes each answer with their own heading while marking their own sidebar section `aria-current="page"` -- so a route that answered with a shared surface, or that marked the wrong section, or that lost its heading, would be caught. The fourteen routes are opened as fourteen separate pages rather than one page re-pointed at each in turn, because one route's slow read must not be able to hold another route's answer back. Three product mutations were checked against it: a section table that resolved `/github` to `agents`, a navigation that stopped marking the current section, and a root page that rendered a `Dashboard` heading instead of redirecting. Each turned the acceptance red and named the claim that had been broken -- the `GitHub` heading, the `aria-current` marker, and the URL the root route ends on. One thing the first version of the acceptance got wrong is worth recording: it asserted that the root route answers with HTTP 307, which is what Next.js puts in the redirect _digest_. The route is statically prerendered, so the server answers 200 and carries the redirect in the payload and in a meta refresh; the status code was an implementation detail of the framework dressed up as a requirement, and the assertion was wrong while the behaviour was right. What the target state asks for is that the operator ends up on a canonical resource, so that is what the acceptance now says. The browser suite is now 58 of 58 across the eleven non-Playtesting specs;
- **the Console had been checked at one width, so the claim that it is a console an operator can read on a phone was never tested at the width a phone has.** The earlier sweep across twenty-two routes measured the document and the accessibility tree at 390px and 1280px, which is a real check -- but it measured the _document_, and the document is the shell's `overflow-hidden` box: a page cannot widen it, so the document never said anything about whether the page's own content fit. What was left unmeasured was the content inside the page's own boxes. `console/e2e/responsive-layout-acceptance.spec.ts` measures that instead, at 390, 768 and 1280, across all fourteen canonical routes: any element whose content is wider than the box holding it, unless that box scrolls or truncates on purpose or is a visually hidden label; exactly one level-one heading per route; no heading that skips a level; no identifier that appears twice. The middle width matters as much as the ends -- it is where the navigation is still a rail but the page has room for two columns -- and all three are the same claim. **The sweep found four real defects, and every one of them was a page making a promise it did not keep.** (1) _The Agents table's role column cut a row mid-sentence._ The column is a `truncate` column, and `truncate` cannot ellipsize a cell whose content is a column of blocks: the row for an agent with no runtime enablement projection was cut at the edge of its cell with nothing to show that anything was cut. The column is a `tokens` column now, which wraps. (2) _The Usage page's outline skipped a level._ It started at `h3` under the shell's `h1`, so a screen reader was told that something was missing before the page said anything about itself; every other resource puts its sections at `h2`, and so does Usage now. (3) _The GitHub page's run columns cut a path and a branch mid-segment._ The run's name over the workflow path is two things, and the branch over the commit is two things, so both were truncating columns holding block content; they are `tokens` columns now, and the paths use the shared `PathText`, which breaks between segments rather than inside one. (4) _The GitHub page's connected-callout painted its message past the edge of the callout._ The badge and the message shared a line, so the message had 120px to say that the Actions API was connected and that no mutation controls exist, and the repository name was cut off with nothing to show for it; they stack on a narrow window now. A fifth defect was in the Providers role form rather than the pages that use it: the label column was a fixed `5.5rem` against a label that needs 92px, so "Orchestrator" was painted four pixels past the edge of its own column on every role row, and the column is sized to its content now. The whole set was reverted at once and the sweep named all four routes, which is how each fix is known to be load-bearing rather than merely present; the browser suite is now 61 of 61 across the twelve non-Playtesting specs. One measurement note belongs here: the first version of the sweep opened all fourteen routes at once, and the sandbox's single-process headless shell went down with its last page, which read as a broken page rather than a broken harness -- the routes are measured four at a time now;
- **the Agent enablement control was the one mutation on the Console that nothing could reach, because the fixture could not serve the write at all.** The target state is explicit about it: the control is revision-bound through `PATCH /control/agents/{role}`, it is shown on both the Agent row and the Agent's detail view, the Runtime rejects a stale expected revision, and a role the Runtime has no projection for renders as unavailable and nonmutable rather than as disabled. The Console had the control, the same-origin route and the shared component -- and no way to find out whether the write worked, because the Control fixture served no `PATCH /control/agents/{role}` and so could only ever produce a 404. A claim about a write that nothing can perform is not a claim anybody has checked. The fixture now serves the write as the Runtime owns it: the body must carry an `enabled` boolean and the `expectedRevision` the caller read, a revision that has moved is a 409 rather than a silent overwrite, a role with no projection is refused rather than given an invented value, and a write that lands moves the revision and is then visible on both the list and the detail read -- one resolver, so the two surfaces cannot drift apart. `console/e2e/agents-enablement-acceptance.spec.ts` drives the result: the Agents row disables the agent and the page that comes back shows the Runtime-confirmed value rather than an optimistic one; a revision that moved behind the page's back is refused with the conflict notice -- "This changed since the list you acted on was read. Reload it and decide again." -- and the enablement is the one the Runtime held, not the one the page asked for; and the detail view writes through the same control, because it is the same control. **The refusal was the part that needed a product change, and it is worth saying why.** The route mapped every failure to the generic "could not be confirmed" notice, which says the change is unconfirmed and nothing else. That is true, and it is not enough: a stale revision and an unreachable Runtime want opposite next moves -- reload and decide again, versus look for a different way to make the change -- and a notice that cannot tell them apart leaves the first operator retrying an identical write. The route now maps the Runtime's 409 to the shared `conflicted` refusal, the same one the agent concurrency route already used, so the operator is told to reload rather than to try again. Two mutations were checked against it: a route that stopped distinguishing the conflict, and a fixture that stopped checking the revision. Each turned the acceptance red on the refusal the other one had been providing, which is how both are known to be load-bearing rather than merely present. The browser suite is now 76 of 76 across the fifteen non-Playtesting specs;
- **the detail surfaces were the half of the Console nobody had read at the width a phone has, and the provider detail page was the one that was actually broken.** The responsive sweep that closed the fourteen canonical routes left the detail views out, and the ledger said so: the sweep was open "across the detail surfaces rather than the fourteen canonical routes". A detail view is a list view's narrow neighbour -- the same configuration, laid out for one item rather than for many -- so it has the same obligation to fit the width it is read at, and it had none of it. The sweep now measures the list routes and the detail routes together: the agent, provider, model, MCP, prompt, skill and tool detail pages, at 390, 768 and 1280. **It found one real defect, and it was a 200-pixel one.** The provider detail page shows the same four role controls as the Providers row -- a label, a priority, a model and a reasoning-effort control per role, in columns that line up across the four roles, which is a measured 494px. On the Providers row that strip lives in a table cell, and the table scrolls. On the provider detail page the strip is the only thing in its panel, and nothing scrolled: at 390px the panel is 252px wide, so the model and effort controls were cut off the edge of the panel and off the page, with no way to reach them -- a control the operator cannot operate is not a control. The strip scrolls itself now, and each row keeps the width of its own content (`items-start`), so the strip scrolls as one thing -- one scrollbar for four roles, not one per role -- and the rows line up exactly as they do on the list page. The list page is unchanged by it: its cell is 496px and the strip is 494px, so the strip does not scroll there at all. Reverting the strip to its old classes and running the sweep named the provider detail route and every element it cut -- the page body, the panel, the strip, all four rows and all four forms -- which is how the fix is known to be load-bearing rather than merely present. The workspace detail page is deliberately not in the sweep: its page reads the Playtesting approval panel, and that surface belongs to the session working on Playtesting, so a sweep that judged it would be answering for work that is not this one's to judge;
- **the Console's root-level form feedback had a unit test that read markup, and no browser acceptance -- and the browser found a real defect in it.** The target state says what that feedback has to be: it stays visible while the work is pending, a completed or failed result dismisses itself after five seconds with a visible seconds countdown, the countdown does not announce itself over and over, the close control is reachable from the keyboard, and closing or replacing the feedback cancels the pending dismissal. It says too what an in-place write has to do to the operator who made it: the keyboard focus stays on the control they changed. `console/tests/form-navigation-owner.test.ts` rendered the owner in isolation and matched the markup it produced -- the countdown's words, the dismiss button's name, the live region's role. That proves the owner _can_ render each state. It does not prove that a real submission reaches those states, that the countdown counts down and the feedback goes away on its own, that a keyboard operator can close it, or that a refused write is reported as a refusal. `console/e2e/form-feedback-acceptance.spec.ts` drives a real submission instead: the Skills role assignment, which saves itself the moment a checkbox changes. **The measurement had to change before the claim could be checked at all, and the first version of the acceptance was wrong in a way the mutation round exposed.** A feedback that dismisses itself after five seconds is indistinguishable from one the operator closed -- both end with nothing on the screen -- so a test that waits and looks at the end proves nothing about who closed it, and the first version of the keyboard test made exactly that mistake: a mutation that unwired the close button still left it green. The spec now holds the page's own clock still (`page.clock`, installed and paused) and advances it deliberately, so the only thing that can remove the feedback is the operator or the countdown's deadline, and the spec says which one it was expecting. Two more measurement traps belong here. A paused clock also means `page.evaluate` cannot be used, because the round trip waits on a page timer that will not come due. And a write is not finished when the feedback says so: the feedback is published before the page is rebuilt around the write, so a test that reaches for the keyboard straight after the confirmation reaches for it in the middle of the page changing underneath it -- which is how the keyboard test failed once, for a reason that had nothing to do with the product. Every write in the spec now waits for the revision on the page to move, because that is the rebuild, and because the revision the next write carries is the one the rebuilt page holds: a write made against the revision before the last one is a conflict rather than a replacement, and the spec was rewritten to say so. The pending state is read by holding the write open, so the submission is still in flight: the feedback has to stay visible and must not count down, because a write that has not come back has nothing to report. The confirmed write has to show the countdown at five seconds, move off it on the clock, and then take the feedback away by itself. The close control has to be focusable and to work from the keyboard, and the clock has not moved while it is closed, so the operator is the one who closed it. The refused write -- a revision that moved behind the page's back -- has to be reported as a failure, announced as an alert, counted down like a confirmed write, and leave the notice it points the operator at on the page. **And the acceptance found a defect the unit test could not have seen, because the unit test never had a DOM.** The Console restores the keyboard focus after an in-place write, and it restored it by name: `querySelector('[name="roles"]')`. The Skills catalog's role checkboxes are all called `roles` -- one per role, on every row -- so the restore landed on the _first_ of them. An operator who unchecks a skill's `worker` role and carries on was dropped onto the `default` role of the same skill, with nothing on the screen to explain it: the write had landed, the page said so, and the keyboard was somewhere else. The restore now identifies the control by where it is in the document rather than by what it is called -- its path, its tag, its name and its value -- and falls back to the name lookup only when the name is unique, because a name that is not unique cannot identify anything. A control that has moved since the snapshot was taken is not focused at all, which is better than focusing a different one. The fix is in the owner that does the restoring, so every form in the Console gets it and not only the one that was caught. **Seven mutations and one revert were checked against the acceptance, and two of them changed what the claim rests on.** Removing the dismissal scheduling broke the confirmed-write test and the replacement test with it. Hiding the pending feedback broke the pending test. Reporting a refused write as a success broke the refusal test. Unwiring the close button broke the keyboard test -- but only after the clock was under the test's control, which is the whole point of putting it there. Stopping the effect's cleanup from cancelling a replaced feedback's dismissal changed nothing at all, and that was worth finding out: the revision guard on the dismissal callback was never what cancelled a replaced feedback's dismissal, because the effect's own cleanup was, and the guard was a second and redundant safety net for the same rule. Only removing both of them broke the replacement test, which is the honest shape of that claim: the behaviour is held by two mechanisms and neither of them alone is what holds it. The pre-fix build broke the focus test and nothing else, so the focus fix is load-bearing and narrow;
- **the compact navigation's behaviour was two unit-tested predicates and no browser acceptance, and the browser could not even see the navigation until the page had settled.** The target state is specific about it: at a narrow width the navigation defaults to the compact rail, expanding it _overlays_ the page rather than compressing the page's content, selecting a destination collapses it, Escape collapses it, and a modified link-open gesture leaves the current view state alone. The unit test covers the two predicates those decisions call -- `shouldCloseSidebarOnNavigation` and `shouldCloseSidebarOnEscape` -- and a predicate that is right is not the same claim as a navigation that behaves: nothing checked that the click reaches the predicate, that the rail is the default at a narrow width, or that the expanded rail is an overlay rather than a column that takes a quarter of the screen. `console/e2e/navigation-acceptance.spec.ts` drives the navigation as the operator does, at 390px and at 1280px. **One measurement trap belongs here, because it is the Console's own streaming and it will bite any spec that measures a page too early.** The Console streams a page, and the streamed copy of the shell sits in the document in a hidden container until the page takes it over: the served HTML of every route carries two `<nav id="autodev-console-navigation">`, two `<main id="main-content">` and two `<h1>`, and a spec that measures the document in that window finds two of everything and cannot even address the navigation without a strict-mode violation. The operator never sees it -- once the page has settled there is one navigation, one main and one heading, and the body is exactly one screen tall -- but the duplicate ids are in the HTML that is served, and the acceptance has to wait them out rather than measure them. The page-settle wait the responsive sweep had been carrying on its own now lives with the other shared acceptance helpers, and the navigation spec waits for the same thing. **Four mutations were checked against the acceptance.** Making the expanded navigation a column instead of an overlay took the page's content from the whole window to a quarter of it and broke the overlay test. Stopping a destination from collapsing the navigation broke the destination test. Stopping Escape from collapsing it broke the Escape test. And ignoring the modified link-open gestures -- the ctrl-click that opens the destination in another tab -- collapsed the navigation anyway and broke the gesture test, which is the claim the unit test covers most precisely and the browser now covers for real;
- **the migration gate was a claim in this ledger, and the first time it ran on current `main` it was red for reasons that had nothing to do with the Console.** The target state asks for CI/workflow evidence that the monorepo's acceptance gates hold on the branch the migration lands on; until a workflow exists and runs there, "the gates pass" is a sentence anybody can write. `.github/workflows/gates.yml` now runs the repository's own four gates -- `format:check`, `lint:ci`, `typecheck` and `pnpm test` -- on every push to `main`, on every pull request, and on demand, and it reports _every_ gate instead of stopping at the first failure, because evidence that stops at the first failure is evidence about one gate. The first run on `main` (run `39520227236`, commit `85065286`) was red, and its nineteen failures were worth reading, because **not one of them was a Console defect.** Seven were the launchd supervision suite, which cannot pass on a runner that has no launchd. Three were the router's turn-metadata forwarding, which asserted a workspace identity derived from one developer's home directory: on any other machine that path does not exist, so the router resolved no workspace and forwarded no identity -- a test that could only pass on the machine that wrote it. Two were the per-session concurrency cap, measured against the operator's personal `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`, which on a host without one leaves no cap to measure. Two were the codex route, which authenticates with the local Codex account and answered 401 where there is no account. One was the OpenLIT bootstrap's "does not touch the repository's `console/.env.local`" check, which read a gitignored local artifact a fresh checkout does not have. One was the dev Control API probe, whose in-tree Control API could not read evaluation history without a telemetry store. Two were the Playtesting area, which is outside this scope. **Each of those was a test that could only pass on the machine that wrote it, and finding them is what the gate is for.** The workspace assertions now name the checkout the suite runs in and derive the identity from it; the concurrency cap is pinned through the Runtime's own limit owner instead of being read out of a personal config; the codex route is pointed at a committed fixture auth file, and the router resolves that file per request so the override needs no restart; the bootstrap check asserts that the repository environment file is _still_ exactly as it found it, whether or not there was one; the dev probe is measured against a stub telemetry store instead of against whether an OpenLIT stack happens to be running; and the gate runs on `macos-latest`, because AutoDev is a macOS product -- its services are launchd jobs and the platform suite asserts that supervision contract, so a runner without launchd could only ever report the platform it does not have. The frozen routing contract was stale in the same way and said so: `tests/fixtures/contracts/root-subagent-provider-selection.json` still listed five providers for `browser-tester` after the execution contract narrowed that role to the providers that can inject its role-scoped Playwright MCP, so the contract now lists the two it really serves and names the rule that narrowed it. The install manifest was stale in the same way, listing a `uv.lock` the repository did not carry; that lock file is now tracked, because a manifest that claims a file the repository lacks is an installer that cannot install. The run after those fixes (run `39532074892`, commit `624cb239`) is the evidence this row now rests on, and it reads per suite rather than as one verdict: **formatting green, typecheck green, the Console's own 712 unit tests all passing, the data suite's 376 and the core suite's 405 all passing, the root suite at 1,619 of 1,631 with its one failure in the Playtesting area's own skill test, and the runtime suite's 37 failures all in the Playtesting area** -- with one exception that the gate found and this row fixed: Codex discovery asks the Codex CLI for its version before it queries the account, so its test needed a Codex installation to be measured against, and a host without one made the test measure the host. The lint step still reports 274 problems, and all 274 are in the Playtesting area. That remainder belongs to the session that owns the Playtesting work, and the gate names it instead of hiding it. The suite script changed with it: `pnpm test` used to run the root suite and then the workspace suites only if the root suite passed, so one failing file in one package hid whether the Console's own 712 unit tests -- and the runtime, core and data suites -- passed at all. It now runs both and reports both, the same shape the repository's `typecheck` script already used, because a gate that reports one suite and hides four is a gate with a blind spot.
- visible current-`main` GitHub Actions/workflow evidence for the monorepo/OpenLIT acceptance gates is on the branch: the `Gates` workflow runs on every push to `main`, on every pull request and on demand, reports all four of the repository's gates whether or not the first one failed, and run `39541544582` on commit `a255fbe3` is the current record of what it says. What it says is that formatting, typecheck, the Console's own 712 unit tests, the data suite's 376 and the core suite's 405 are green; that the root suite's one failure (1619 of 1631 pass), the runtime suite's 37 failures (997 of 1039 pass) and lint's 274 problems are all in the Playtesting area; and that the gate reports every one of them rather than only the first. That remainder belongs to the session that owns the Playtesting work, and the gate is the mechanism that makes it visible rather than the mechanism that hides it.
- **the Console promised an explicit state for a read it could not answer, and only a unit test was checking it.** The target state says core routes handle loading, empty, unavailable, error and normal states without demo or fallback data, and that a dynamic route shows the active shell and an accessible loading placeholder while server-owned page data is pending. The pages already render one shared failure shell when a read cannot be answered -- an alert with the failure code and the reason -- and the unit tests cover the mapping from a failed read to that shell. A unit test can render the shell; it cannot show that the page an operator opens says so. `console/e2e/route-state-acceptance.spec.ts` puts the Control API into the states a service can be in and reads the pages: the service not answering, the service refusing the reader, the service failing, and the service answering late. **The harness is the point: a proxy stands between the Console and the Control API fixture and answers in the state the spec asks for**, because the fixture's own contract is that it answers a healthy service with complete synthetic data, and a page that fails closed can only be shown a failure that really happened. Eighteen surfaces -- the eleven routes that read the Control API and the seven detail surfaces -- were measured in each of the three failing states: every one of them shows the explicit state with the code the service gave (`autodev_unreachable`, `autodev_control_api_unauthorized`, `autodev_control_api_unavailable`), and not one of them invented a row, a count or a status. The usage surface is not in the sweep because it reads the OpenLIT usage API rather than the Control API, and the Playtesting and Workspaces surfaces are not in it because they read Playtesting-owned state. The loading claim needed the same treatment, because only a browser can say that the placeholder is on the screen _while_ the read is pending: the service is made slow and the page is caught mid-flight. **The mutation round is what makes the claims usable.** A Providers page that swallowed its failed read and rendered nothing was caught by the sweep, and the other seventeen surfaces still answered, so the sweep measures every surface rather than the first one to fail; and a Console with no loading placeholder at all failed the loading test, which no unit test over the placeholder's markup could have caught.
- **the Console's browser acceptance ran on one machine, by hand, so the claim it supported was a claim about that machine.** The target state asks for browser and visual regression acceptance across the shared shell and the representative list, detail, form and observability pages, and the Console now has such an acceptance -- but every measurement of it so far was local: a build, a server and a browser started by hand on one workstation. That is evidence about one machine at one moment, and it is invisible to anybody who reads the branch. `.github/workflows/console-acceptance.yml` now runs the repository's own Playwright configuration on every push to `main`, on every pull request and on demand, on macOS -- the platform the product runs on -- and it runs the acceptance the way an operator meets it rather than through a shortcut: the repository's own configuration builds the Console, starts the Control API fixture, the state proxy and the usage fixture, serves the staged production build, and drives it with a real browser against a real service. Two details keep the run honest rather than nominal. The webServer deadline is ten minutes rather than two, because the acceptance measures a production build and how long that build takes depends on the machine: it took forty seconds on the runner this ran on and minutes on the machine it was developed on, where the old two-minute deadline failed the run before a single browser test ran -- a failure that measures the machine's speed rather than the acceptance. And the readiness check waits on a Console-owned route rather than the Playtesting surface, because a page this work does not own must not be able to fail every spec here. The first run of the workflow, `39541544616` on commit `a255fbe3`, measured the acceptance in full on the runner: 109 tests across all seventeen spec files passed in 2.9 minutes, the Playtesting surface's own twenty-eight among them, so the workflow reports the Console's whole acceptance rather than a filtered part of it.
- **the canonical source editors were a unit test and a claim, and the write they perform could not be reached by anything.** The target state asks for operators to edit an existing `.rulesync/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and the canonical commands through a revision-checked `Save & Apply`, and the Console has that editor -- but the Control API fixture could not serve the write at all, so no browser could drive it: the save path, the revision the write carries and the states the service can answer with were all unmeasured, exactly as the Agent enablement control was before the fixture learned to serve its write. The fixture now holds a _real_ canonical source: a temporary repository root read and written through the product's own `RuleSyncRepository`, so the revision a browser compares is the sha256 of the canonical file the Runtime compares, and a conflict is raised by the rule the Runtime applies rather than by a fixture that re-implements the rule and can drift from it. `console/e2e/canonical-source-acceptance.spec.ts` then drives both editors in a browser: a skill saves against the revision it loaded; a source that moves while the page is open refuses the write; the refusal leaves the moved source alone; and a projection apply that fails after the source was saved is reported without a success claim. The acceptance found a defect in the product: a browser restores the text an operator typed into a form control when the write it submitted is redirected back to the page, so after a refused write the editor still held the operator's edit while the page rendered the source that had moved on -- and the form carried the _new_ revision, so the next save would have written that stale edit over the other editor's change. The write now carries the revision its content is based on, so the second save is refused again and the change that moved the source survives. Both conflict measurements were mutation-checked: with the revision the edit was written for removed, the two conflict tests go red.
- **the Console's acceptance code was linted but never type-checked.** The console's `tsconfig.json` covered `app`, `src` and `tests` and not `e2e`, so a type error in the acceptance could pass the gate as long as it was still valid JavaScript at run time. The acceptance directory is type-checked now, apart from the two Playtesting files the Playtesting work owns: those carry eighteen type errors of their own, and the Playtesting acceptance was never type-checked either, so excluding them takes nothing away from a coverage they did not have. The Console's own acceptance code is clean under `tsc --noEmit`.
- **the acceptance's own failures were unreadable, and a third of its runs were red.** The workflow runs the whole acceptance on one worker, because the specs share one fixture and one Console and a spec that degrades the service must not overlap a spec that reads it -- the first red run was exactly that interference, and one worker is what it bought. Three of the six runs so far were red, and the two after that were red for a second reason, failing the same way each time: a test that asserts a navigation observed a page that never moved. The breadcrumb ancestor stayed on the agent, the MCP tab stayed on the previous tab, and the canonical prompt editor held a value that was the typed text with the previously rendered source appended to it. The failure was not readable from the log, because the runner deleted the trace, the screenshot and the page snapshot of a failed test with the job, so the only record was the assertion text -- which says what the page looked like and not how it got there. The workflow now publishes that directory when the acceptance fails, and the first published trace read the failure exactly: the RSC request for the next tab was sent, the server answered with its status and its headers, and the body never arrived, so the router never committed and the URL never changed. The trace also showed what the render was waiting for. The MCP detail page reads one Control API collection and nothing else, and the Console gives that read a five-second deadline, so a page cannot wait on it for ten seconds -- unless the deadline was not in force, which it was not, for every caller that brought its own abort signal: the caller's signal replaced the deadline instead of joining it, so the read waited for the caller, and a caller that waits for the read waits forever. The deadline belongs to the Console, because the Console is what promises the operator an explicit state when a service cannot be read, so it now holds whatever the caller asked for and the caller's abort only ever ends the read sooner. The same shape was on the harness side of the hop: the acceptance's state proxy waited on its upstream without a deadline and reused a pooled connection the upstream may already have closed, so a service that accepted a request and never answered it left the page waiting with it. The proxy now bounds its upstream read, answers the Console's own unavailable state when the upstream does not answer, and uses one connection per forwarded request. The deadline is mutation-checked in both directions: with the deadline restored to the caller's signal alone, the read that is supposed to end at the deadline hangs until the test times out, and the caller's own abort is still reported as the caller's abort rather than as the Console's deadline.
- **the acceptance measured the Console's navigation on a machine that was still busy with the previous spec's reads.** The failure that reproduced twice was the same spec both times -- the Tools filters and links navigating in place -- and the second trace read it exactly: the server answered the navigation request with its status and its headers within five milliseconds and the body arrived about ten seconds later, the page's own content was right, and the server's own output said nothing was wrong. A navigation that takes ten seconds on a read that answers in five milliseconds is not a slow product; it is a machine that is busy, and the acceptance was taking that measurement immediately after the twenty-eight Playtesting specs, which drive the heaviest pages in the product and each fan five reads out at the Control API. The acceptance now runs in two projects, in that order: the Console's own eighty-six specs first and the Playtesting acceptance last, so the order is a property of the configuration rather than of the alphabet, and a new spec file joins the Console project by default. The criteria are untouched -- the navigation still has to happen in place, without remounting the document, inside the same ten seconds.
- **one defect found while reading the failure is still open, and it is in the shared RuleSync repository rather than in the Console.** The repository reads a command's committed history with `git`, and it reads it with `execFileSync`: a synchronous child process, in a library that every server in the product loads. A server that calls it stops answering _every_ request for as long as the `git` call takes -- the Control API's event loop is held by a history read, and the read a page is waiting on queues behind it. Making the calls asynchronous needs the Control API's detail-read interface to become asynchronous too, because that interface is synchronous today, so the change is a real piece of work rather than a one-line swap; it is recorded here rather than left in a commit message.
- **the navigation that never moved was the Console warming its own destination, and the warm-up has to be a full one.** The acceptance's recurring failure was a page that never moved: the URL stayed where it was and the page stayed with it. The published trace read the failure exactly -- the server answered the navigation request within five to sixteen milliseconds with a complete response, the Console server's own output said nothing was wrong, and the browser itself cancelled the request. The Console's links warm their destination on a pointer, touch or keyboard intent, so that opening a page does not start a request for every visible resource. The warm-up was a _partial_ prefetch: it answered with the route's loading state rather than with the page, so a navigation that found that answer waiting for it applied the loading state and then waited for a page that was never going to arrive. The warm-up asks for the full page now, and the target state already said so -- "Full dynamic-route prefetch starts only on pointer, touch, or keyboard intent" -- the word _full_ being the part that had to be acted on. The kind is asserted by a guard, so a warm-up that stops being full fails the Console's own tests. Measured: the MCP detail tab navigation failed against the pre-fix build -- the third tab click left the URL on the previous tab and the assertion timed out after fifteen seconds -- and committed in 858 ms against the fixed build; the same spec passes six times out of six against it, and the canonical-source acceptance's five editor tests pass against it as well. The acceptance on the runner is the record: run `39574094279` on commit `1a28a7a1` measured all 114 tests and passed them in 4.1 minutes, the two specs that had been red in three consecutive runs among them.
- **the acceptance was green once the warm-up asked for the page, and the measurement that pointed somewhere else was the sandbox's own browser.** The Tools filter navigation had been red in three consecutive acceptance runs, and the local measurement of it pointed at the route's loading boundary: with the boundary in place the navigation failed five times out of six, without it six times out of six, and the same held whether the boundary sat at the application root, on the route itself or inside the root layout. The CI run says the opposite -- run `39574094279` on commit `1a28a7a1` measured the whole acceptance on the runner and **114 tests passed in 4.1 minutes**, the Tools filters and the MCP tabs among them, with the route that is still waiting for its resource still showing the shell and its loading placeholder. The local measurement was the thing that was wrong: the sandbox's headless shell runs single-process and drops client-side navigations, which is the very thing the claim is about, so a local run of that spec measures the sandbox and not the Console. The lesson belongs here rather than only in a commit message: **a claim about an in-place navigation is measured by the acceptance on the runner, and the local browser is not evidence for it.**
- **the class of failure is smaller but it is not gone, and the published traces -- plus a local reproduction -- say exactly what is left.** Two more runs of the same product code followed: `39574982694` was green (114 passed in 4.6 minutes) and `39575468743` was red again with the same one spec, the breadcrumb ancestor that did not lead back to its list (113 passed, one failed). The published trace of that run read the failure exactly, and the shape is sharper than the previous one: the navigation's RSC response was answered (200) and the client's router **advanced to the destination** -- the five-second refresh that followed requested the _destination_ route with the destination's tree, which is only true if the navigation's tree had been applied -- and the page eventually showed the destination's content, **while the address bar never moved**. The page snapshot taken at the failure still showed the page that was open; the screenshot taken at the end of the run showed the destination's content under the previous URL. **The cancellation is not the defect, and the earlier reading of that was wrong.** `net::ERR_ABORTED` is the ordinary end of an RSC request: measured locally against a real browser, every RSC request ends that way -- including the ones that commit -- because the client cancels the stream once it has the model. **The failure reproduces outside the runner, and that is what moves it forward.** Driving the same breadcrumb with a real browser against the same production build, the click leaves the address bar on `/agents/default` in roughly one run in four: the navigation's response is complete on the wire (the server's stream ends normally with the whole payload, 6,765 bytes compressed), `history.pushState` and `history.replaceState` are **never called**, the browser logs nothing, and neither an abort nor a stream cancellation happens. The navigation's result therefore never reaches the router's state at all: the router never commits it, and the address bar is never asked to move. The request is the same one in both outcomes -- the same URL, the same router-state tree, the same `next-url` header -- and the response is the same one, so the difference is in the client and not in the exchange: a navigation that commits does it in about a quarter of a second, and a navigation that does not commit never does, so it is dropped rather than slow. **Two candidate causes were measured, and both are ruled out.** The live-count refresh is not it: the click lands about a second and a half after the load, long before the first five-second tick, and the failure reproduces unchanged with every refresh suppressed at the source. The warm-up is not it either: with Next's own intent-priority full prefetch enabled -- the mechanism Next uses for a hovered link, and the only one that can produce a full prefetch on intent -- the failure still happens in four runs out of twelve. A fifth run, `39592073253`, failed the same way on a different spec, and a sixth, `39593431842`, on a third, and the shape is the same in all three: **the page keeps the previous destination's address bar _and_ the previous destination's content** -- the Providers tab navigation was left on `/providers` instead of `/providers?tab=models`, and the MCP tab navigation was left on `?tab=configuration` instead of `?tab=role-access`, showing the configuration tab's own panels. The navigation's answer was never taken up. **The navigation's answer was never taken up, and the reading of _why_ that this ledger carried has now been measured and does not hold in this build.** The earlier reading named Next's segment cache -- the mechanism where a default-strategy entry leaves the search string out of the cache key, so the entry answers for every search-param value of that route. That cache is not compiled into this build at all: `experimental.clientSegmentCache` is off unless PPR is enabled, and the shipped navigate reducer goes straight to the prefetch cache. The reading also said the warm-up's request is never issued; it is issued, and it is a full one (no `Next-Router-Prefetch` header), so the cache does hold the destination's full answer. And the conclusion that the fix belongs in the warm-up does not survive a measurement of its own: a build with the warm-up removed strands three times out of six, the same rate as the build that keeps it, so a fix aimed there would be aimed at a cause the evidence rules out.
- **the stranded navigation was measured from the inside, and the defect is narrower than the one this ledger carried: the router applies the destination and React renders it, and the commit that would move the address bar never runs.** Driving the breadcrumb with a real browser against the same production build, with the shipped router instrumented, gives the following. The click is dispatched, and Next's reducer applies the destination: the canonical URL becomes `/agents`. React then renders the destination tree -- the destination segment renders with its data present rather than promised, no lazy fetch is issued for it, and no error is raised anywhere in the page. The only suspension in the whole navigation is the router's own state promise, and it resolves. **What never happens is the commit.** The insertion effect that asks the browser to move the address bar never runs: `history.pushState` and `history.replaceState` are not called at all, which is why a failing navigation's snapshot still shows the page that was open and why the destination can appear under the previous URL. The commit does not merely arrive late: on the same production build the live-count refresh dispatches every five seconds, and thirty seconds after the click the address bar has still not moved. **So the defect is a commit that is starved, not a navigation that is dropped, and it is starved inside the client router's transition, by a render that never reaches the commit phase.** Ruled out by measurement: the exchange (the request and the response are byte-identical between a committing and a non-committing navigation, and the response body is read to completion in both); the live-count refresh (the failure reproduces with no refresh in flight, well before the first five-second tick); the warm-up (a build without it strands at the same rate as a build with it); and the segment-cache search-string story, which describes a code path this build does not contain. What is still open is the single question this leaves: **what starves the commit.** The starvation showed up inside the router's transition, but the cause is the Console's own route-level loading boundary, which the next bullet measures: the boundary is what makes every route's answer a split one, and a split answer is what leaves the navigation waiting for a commit it does not get.
- **the stranded navigation had a cause, and it was the route's answer arriving in two pieces -- and the cause is in Next.js, in two places, and both of them are keyed on the `loading.tsx` file convention rather than on a `<Suspense>` in the app.** The boundary this ledger blamed was the right shape of suspicion and the wrong mechanism, and the acceptance on the runner for the commit that carried the page-level boundary (`39632474850`) still failed the Tools navigation and the skill-role revision, so "a boundary inside the page" was not the fix either. Reading Next.js 15.5's own router says what a boundary does to a navigation. **The server** does not render a route's child segment for a prefetch request when that route carries a `loading.tsx`: the child is deferred so that "the rest of the tree is deferred until the actual navigation", so the answer a prefetch holds is the shell and not the page. **The client** then reuses the parameter-less prefetch of a route as an _alias_ for a navigation that carries search parameters, and applies that alias only when the seed data carries a loading component -- and applying it fills the cache with the loading state and nulls the page segment's `rsc`. A page segment with no `rsc` makes the layout router fetch the page again _during_ the navigation and suspend on it, and the address bar is moved by a `useInsertionEffect` in the router -- an insertion effect that never runs while a render is suspended. A `<Suspense>` in the app is not that boundary: the test for a loading component reads the loader tree's `loading` slot, so a userspace boundary is invisible to both mechanisms and a route without a `loading.tsx` is prefetched whole.
- **so the pending state is owned by the layout, and a page's read is awaited rather than handed to a child.** The route-level `loading.tsx` is gone for the reason above, and the boundary that replaced it lives in the root layout, around the layout's children: a layout is the one segment an in-place navigation does not replace, so the navigation re-sends the page's own segment and leaves the layout's segment, and the boundary inside it, exactly where they were. The page's answer therefore arrives whole, and the address bar and the page move together. Each page awaits its own read, so the page's model and the content that read confirmed arrive as one answer, and the layout's boundary is what lets a cold load still show the shell and its placeholder while that read is pending, because React flushes the shell up to a boundary and the page's segment arrives after it -- the served document carries `data-console-loading` and the route's own heading while the read is pending. The read stays server-owned: it is awaited by a server component, so the Control API credential never reaches the browser. The ownership is guarded, not assumed: `console/tests/page-loading.test.ts` asserts that no `app/loading.tsx` exists, that no route page owns the pending state or starts a read it does not await, and that the layout owns the boundary unconditionally -- a boundary that appeared for some requests and not others would leave the browser holding a layout the next response does not match.
- **the intermittent strand is still open, and it is not the boundary's position: it is a commit the client never makes.** Driving the same in-place navigation in a real browser against production builds of every shape -- no boundary, the route-level boundary, a page-level boundary and the layout's boundary -- strands the same share of the time, so the shape is not what decides it. The instrumented run says where it is decided: the RSC answer arrives whole and in three to five milliseconds, the router's reducer applies the destination -- the canonical URL becomes the destination's -- and React never commits the re-render, so the insertion effect that moves the address bar does not run, the address bar stays, and the page keeps the content it had. The failure is silent: no error, no console message, and it is not a late answer, because the answer was already there. **The navigation must find a whole-page answer waiting for it, and a click no longer depends on an intent having arrived.** With the Console's own warm-up prefetch in place the same navigation committed thirty-seven times out of forty, and with the prefetch suppressed it committed four times out of forty; a later run with the prefetch machinery intact but no intent at all committed fourteen in fifteen, so the warm-up's exact share of that difference is not settled. What is settled is the shape of the answer: the whole page fills the page the browser is holding, and the page's own segment does not. **So the click asks for the whole page as well.** A pointer that is already over the link when the operator clicks never enters it, a keyboard activation never enters it, and a destination the warm-up has already visited has its answer aged out of the router's prefetch cache while the cooldown still holds it back -- and a navigation that has to answer for itself is the one that strands. Asking at the click is free when the warm-up has already left that answer in the router's cache: the prefetch is then the answer the warm-up left, not a second request. The revision that does not rebuild after a confirmed write is the same shape of failure -- the router's state is replaced by an answer that does not carry the new content -- and there are two mechanisms for it in Next.js: a refresh whose response is not a root render is dropped outright (`REFRESH FAILED`, and the old state is returned), and a refresh that lands while another refresh is still in flight is answered by whichever lands last. Which of the two the acceptance hit is not yet settled, and the acceptance does not forward the browser's console, so the marker is not in the run's log. **The evidence for a navigation is the acceptance on the runner and the local browser is not evidence for it:** the sandbox's headless shell measures a streamed document as a failed navigation, so the local builds of every shape that streams -- route-level, page-level, layout-level -- measure as failures there, while the build that streams nothing measures as a pass; on the runner the console project failed three specs on the commit that carries the layout's boundary (`39665545695`: the Tools filters, the provider detail link, and the skill-role revision) and passed the console project on the commit before it (`39638562992`), and the thirteen failures in the same run are the Playtesting acceptance, which another session owns.
- **the provider detail page was the last route segment that still owned a boundary, and removing it changed what the strand measures -- but the strand itself is not the provider page's.** `console/app/providers/[id]/page.tsx` wrapped its usage read in its own `React.Suspense`, which is the split answer the layout's own doc names: the server answers the segment's shell first and the content behind the boundary later, and the navigation's commit -- the commit that moves the address bar -- waits for the second half. The page now reads the usage telemetry itself, in the same parallel batch as its other reads, and hands the view a resolved panel; the boundary, the pending panel it existed for (`ProviderUsagePendingPanel`) and its assertions are gone, and `console/tests/page-loading.test.ts` now refuses any route segment that owns a boundary at all, so the shape cannot come back. **What that fixes is real and what it does not is now measured.** Driving the in-place navigation to a new dynamic segment in a real browser (Chromium, against production builds, interleaved in one session so both builds saw the same machine) commits the navigation 4 times out of 12 with the page's read awaited and 1 time out of 12 without it -- the boundary was one cause and not the only one. The strand is not the provider page's: the same session committed `/tools` to `/tools/read_file` 5 times out of 10, `/skills` to a skill 7 times out of 10, `/agents` to an agent 10 times out of 12, and a navigation that keeps the segment and changes only search params (`/tools` to `/tools?source=mcp`) 0 to 7 times out of 20. **What decides it is whether the navigation replaces the page segment.** **The client-side signature is now narrow, and it rules out more than it leaves.** The instrumented router says: the navigation issues one RSC request; the response carries a complete payload (every `$L` reference in it is defined in the same payload, and the only `$Sreact.suspense` in it is the layout's own boundary); the reducer applies the destination, so the canonical URL becomes the destination's; React then renders the destination tree three or four times, with the new segment's data present (`rsc` non-null, `prefetchRsc` null) and with no lazy fetch and no infinite suspension; and then React stops without committing. The layout's fallback never renders, so nothing suspended and the failure is not a boundary catching a late answer. The prefetch cache is not the cause either: `DYNAMIC_STALETIME_MS` is `0` in this build, so a partial (`auto`) entry would be `stale` on sight -- but no `auto` entry ever exists, because every Console prefetch is `kind: full`, and the navigation reuses that entry rather than asking again. **What is still open is the commit itself.** React renders the destination and never commits it, and the click-time full prefetch this ledger added (`ensureWholePage`) has not been tested against that finding, so its share of the strand is unknown. The next thing to measure is whether removing it changes the rate; the target contract asks for the full warm-up on pointer, touch or keyboard intent, and the click's second ask is not part of that contract.
- **the strand had a cause and a fix, and both are in the Console's navigation owner.** The cause is not a slow server, a missing boundary, a warm-up's kind or a second request: it is _when_ the destination's answer arrives.
