Driving the same production build in a real browser (Chromium, one session, the same machine) with the router instrumented gives a clean comparison: a navigation whose destination answer was **already in the router's prefetch cache** when it was dispatched committed every time (4 of 4), and a navigation that had to answer for itself did not (0 of 4); a navigation that found the answer still on its way committed 1 of 4; a navigation that found a _partial_ answer committed 2 of 4, which is the loading state rather than the page; a delay on its own changed nothing (0 of 4), while the answer in hand plus a delay committed 4 of 4; and a destination that answered in 3.2 seconds committed 3 of 3. So the rule the target state already names -- "a navigation that finds that answer waiting for it never commits" -- is exact: the navigation commits when the whole-page answer is **in hand**, and it does not when the answer is still arriving. In every failing run the reducer had already applied the destination (the canonical URL became the destination's), React rendered the destination tree, and the commit that moves the address bar never ran; the instrumented `pushState` never fired. **The Console now owns that navigation.** `console/src/components/navigation/whole-page-navigation.ts` asks for the destination's whole page, waits until that answer has arrived -- the browser's own record of the request is the signal -- and only then navigates in place, so the address bar and the page move together. The link's click no longer dispatches a navigation that has to answer for itself, and the write path's second round trip is gone: the destination the server renders after the write already carries the write's result, and a refresh behind it was a navigation racing the one already on its way. The ownership is guarded: `console/tests/navigation-performance.test.ts` asserts that a click navigates through the owner and that the owner waits before it leaves, and `console/tests/whole-page-navigation.test.ts` pins the owner's contract (the warm-up asks for the whole page, the navigation waits for the answer, a newer navigation replaces the one that is waiting, an answer is recognised by its destination and not by any request). Measured on the fixed build with a real browser: the provider detail link committed 6 times out of 6 (it had committed 1 time out of 8 on the same build before the fix), the Tools filter navigation committed 4 times out of 4 (0 to 7 times out of 20 before), and the skill-role revision rebuilt after the confirmed write 4 times out of 4, which is the acceptance's recurring failure. The acceptance on the runner remains the authority for a claim about in-place navigation; these are the measurements that pointed at the cause.
- **the three failures left on the runner were the three that hold the page's clock still, and the wait was a question asked on that clock.** The navigation-strand failures were gone once the owner landed: run `39704972308` on commit `bd048e9e` measured the Console project on the runner, and the two navigation-strand specs were no longer among the failures; the three that remained were all in `console/e2e/form-feedback-acceptance.spec.ts` -- the countdown dismissal, the keyboard close and the second write -- and all three hold the page's clock still on purpose, because a feedback that dismisses itself after five seconds has to be told apart from one the operator closed, and the way to tell them apart is to stop the clock. The owner's wait was a question asked on that clock: it polled the browser's record of the request on a `setTimeout` and compared it with `performance.now()`. A still clock stops both -- the timer never comes due and the clock does not move -- so the wait never ended, the navigation was never dispatched, and the page was never rebuilt around the write. **The wait is now an event rather than a question.** The owner installs a `PerformanceObserver` once and watches the requests that carry the answers: the browser's own record of a finished request is the signal, and it arrives as an event, so a clock held still cannot hold it back. The ordering the old poll approximated with timestamps is now an ordering of asks and answers -- the owner records the ask for a destination before it makes it, and an answer satisfies the wait only when it was seen at or after that ask, so an answer left over from an earlier visit is not mistaken for the answer the navigation is waiting for, while an answer that arrived while the operator was still on the link is. The ownership is guarded: `console/tests/navigation-performance.test.ts` asserts that the owner holds no timer and reads no clock, and `console/tests/whole-page-navigation.test.ts` holds the clock and the timers still in a test and asserts the answer still arrives and the navigation still leaves. The ownership is guarded from the other side too: `console/tests/navigation-ownership.test.ts` walks the Console's own source and asserts that no module but the whole-page owner, the form owner and the link obtains or drives the router, so the shape that strands -- a feature that navigates for itself -- cannot come back unnoticed. Measured on the fixed build in a real browser: the provider detail link committed in place -- the address bar moved to `/providers/claude` and the page moved with it -- and the skill-role write committed and rebuilt the page around itself -- the address bar moved to `/skills?save=pending` and the revision moved with it. **The runner says so as well:** run `39716271799` on commit `2e812b82` measured the whole acceptance and **115 tests passed in 3.7 minutes**, and the three that hold the page's clock still are among them -- the confirmed write that counts down and dismisses itself (861 ms), the keyboard close (854 ms) and the second write (925 ms). Those three had failed the same way, with the feedback owner stuck at `submitting` because the navigation never returned, in the four consecutive runs before it (`39705406093`, `39710323280`, `39710478531`, `39710814923`). The sandbox's own browser cannot hold a page's clock still to reproduce it, so that measurement belongs to the runner.
- **the boundary rules now read the Console's tests as well, and what they read is clean.** The `boundaries/*` rules reported zero violations over the Core, Data, Runtime and Console sources _and_ over the Console's own test tree: the config's `boundaries/include` already carries `tests/**` and `console/tests/**`, so the tests were inside the rules' scope and only the audit had left them out. The Playtesting sources another session owns stayed out of the audited set, which is what the row's claim says and is why the claim is scoped rather than absolute. What is left on that row is the manifest and import hygiene and the Console/Data integration, not a boundary violation.
- **the header rhythm broke a header's fit at 390px, and the fix belongs to the shared table rather than to one view.** The responsive sweep reported `/providers/claude at 390px clips th.px-4.py-2.5.text-xs.uppercase by 7px` and `clips span.flex.items-start.gap-1.5 by 23px`, identically in three consecutive runs: a deterministic regression rather than a flake. The cause is the header's new shape. The label and its help marker are one flex row now, and **a flex item's automatic minimum size is its min-content size, which `overflow-wrap: break-word` does not reduce** -- only `overflow-wrap: anywhere` does. So a header that is one long word ("AVAILABILITY") could not shrink at all, and a column too narrow for it clipped the word instead of breaking it; the provider detail's model table declared no weight for that column, so it had the default 100 and a 68px content box. **Two things are true now, and they are the same rule seen from two sides.** The floor is back: the label carries `min-w-0`, so it can shrink and the header's inherited `break-words` breaks the word -- which is what the header did before the flex row, and what the target state asks for ("a single-word header which cannot fit breaks rather than hiding which column it labels"). And the two model tables declare the weight their own header needs: 160, the weight the workspaces table already declares for the same header and the one the acceptance measures fitting at 390px there. The measurement the Console already had is what says a weight is too small: `console/tests/console.test.ts`'s "no column is narrower than its own header" reads each label by its own attribute and compares every column's share of its own table's floor against a measured minimum -- "Availability" measures 124px -- and it is what keeps a hand-tuned width from becoming fiction. `console/tests/table-header-fit.test.ts` pins the floor itself, and fails when the label's shrinkability is taken away.
- **the header's fit is confirmed on the runner, and the one failure left was a locator that named two things.** Run `39724013364` on commit `95a2b2c1` measured the whole acceptance on the runner: **114 passed, 1 failed in 4.0 minutes**, and the responsive sweep passed at all three widths -- "every canonical route fits 390px" (6.4s), at 768px (6.7s) and at 1280px (5.7s) -- so the header's floor and the declared weight hold on the runner's own font and not only in the local reasoning. The failure that was left was `console/e2e/providers-model-availability.spec.ts:78`, and it was not a behaviour change: the locator `getByRole("link", { name: "read_file" })` resolved to **three** links and Playwright's strict mode refused it. The cause is the row-scoped naming pass, which gave a row's chips the name of the row they filter -- "Filter tools exposed to orchestrator for read_file" -- so a tool's own name is a substring of names that point somewhere else, and a substring match reaches the chips as well as the row's own link. **A tool's own name has to address exactly one link, and now it does.** The locator asks for the exact name, which is the row's detail link, and `console/tests/tools-navigation.test.ts` pins the property it relies on: a tool's own name addresses exactly one link on the page, and that link is the row's detail link. The guard was run against a scratch violation -- a chip whose name is the tool's own name -- and it failed, as a guard that can fail has to. **The acceptance is green with both fixes in it:** run `39725269589` on commit `957c96de` measured the whole acceptance -- console project and playtesting project -- and **115 tests passed in 3.5 minutes**, with the two specs that had been failing now passing ("Tools source/role filters and resource/tab links navigate in place without remounting the document", 1.4s, and "every canonical route fits 390px", 4.5s).
- **the prompt's committed history is a page, and every committed revision of it opens.** The Console showed the newest twenty committed revisions and then said the rest was in Git, and it could not open a revision it had not just listed: the repository resolved a revision by finding it in the newest page of history, so an older commit was refused as unknown. **The history is one ordered list and a page of it is a window, so the repository reads a page and the Control API takes it as a query.** `loadCommandHistory(name, { offset, limit })` asks Git for one page (`--skip`, `--max-count`) and reports `hasMore` for that page; the version route takes `?offset=&limit=`, answers `autodev-control-prompt-versions-v2` with the page it carried, and **refuses a page it cannot answer** rather than clamping it, because a clamped page answers a question nobody asked. A revision is now resolved from Git itself: the repository asks whether the commit exists and whether that commit changed _this_ command, because a commit that never touched the command is not a version of it however well formed its hash is -- a commit that only touched another file produces a non-empty `git diff` against the working tree and would have been offered as a prompt revision. The Console walks the history a page at a time with the page in the URL, so the walk is addressable, and the revision a URL names is opened on the service's answer rather than on the page's own list. Measured: the Control API test walks 25 commits, reads the second page, opens a revision from it and refuses six malformed pages; the data tests pin the page model and the commit that never changed the command; 774 Console tests and 28 data tests pass, and the boundary audit reports **0 violations** over the Core, Data, Runtime and Console sources including the Console's tests. The whole acceptance ran green with the change in it -- run `39731619904` measured **115 tests passed in 2.8 minutes** -- but it does not reach this route, because the acceptance's Control API fixture does not serve it, so the evidence for the page itself is the contract and the unit tests.
- **the unsaved prompt source can be previewed, and the preview writes nothing.** The editor was the only place the unsaved source existed, and the only way to see how it would render was to save it -- and a save rewrites the canonical file, regenerates the projection and may need a restart. **The preview answers with Data's canonical RuleSync parser, the one the Runtime validates a write with, so the preview and the save cannot disagree about what the source says.** The parser is exported for that reader, because a preview that read the front matter itself would be a second reader of the canonical format; a source the parser refuses is reported with the reason the save would refuse it with. The renderer moved into its own module, since the saved body and the unsaved body are now rendered in two places and a renderer each of them carried would be two renderers. The island is registered as an approved interaction island, because it needs the editor's own text out of the document; every page read and the save stay server-owned. Measured: the route answers a same-origin request with the parsed body, refuses a cross-origin one and refuses a body it cannot read; the view carries the island beside the editor it reads; the Data test pins the parser's own answer. The browser acceptance reaches it as well: `console/e2e/canonical-source-acceptance.spec.ts` fills the editor with a body no saved canonical file carries, asks for the preview, and asserts both halves of the claim -- the preview shows the unsaved body rather than the saved one, and the canonical source the service holds is untouched, because asking is not saving. A source the canonical parser refuses is measured the same way: the refusal is the parser's own sentence, and the source is still untouched.
- **the Console's production build could not follow the Data barrel, and the acceptance died in its build step.** The Console's preview imported Data's barrel, and the barrel reaches the rule-sync repository, whose default repository root is resolved through the module's own URL -- a resolution a bundler cannot follow. The build failed with `Can't resolve '../../..'`, so runs `39734385884` and `39734470355`, on the preview and on the ledger entry that followed it, were both red in about eighty seconds with the webpack error and nothing else. **The fix is at the source of the coupling rather than at the bundler.** The canonical parser is a pure function of a command's text -- it reads the front matter and answers what the command says, and it never touches the working tree -- so it now lives in a module that resolves no path at all (`data/src/rulesync/command-parser.ts`), the Console imports it through a `./rulesync-parser` subpath export instead of through the barrel, and the barrel is no longer in the Console's graph. The parser is unchanged and is still the only reader of a command's front matter, so the preview and the save still ask the same function the same question. The production build is green again (`AUTODEV_CONSOLE_BUILD_DIST_DIR=.next-staging-preview pnpm build` exits 0, with `/api/prompts/preview` in the route table), and the acceptance run `39736356281` on commit `5f69296c` measured the whole suite green in 3.5 minutes.
- **the acceptance read the navigation's own state once, and the runner caught the read.** Run `39739142579` measured the acceptance with the preview's two new specs in it -- 116 passed, 1 failed -- and the failure was not the preview: "a narrow screen opens with the navigation as the compact rail" read the sidebar control's `aria-expanded` once, right after the page arrived, and read the server's copy of the state. **The server renders the navigation expanded, because it does not know the viewport, and the sidebar collapses it once it has measured the window** -- and the control's label agrees with the server's copy of the state, so the product is coherent and there was nothing to fix in the Console: the read was the thing that was wrong. So the read waits for the state instead of taking it once. **The wait is a stronger claim than the read was** -- it fails when the navigation never reaches the rail, rather than when it is read a moment too early -- the navigation's geometry is measured in the settled state, so the overlay and column measurements are of the state the operator is in, and the control that opens the rail waits for the default too, so a click taken before the client applied it cannot collapse the navigation instead of opening it. The other acceptance that reads the same state already waited for it: the providers spec asserts the "Expand sidebar" control is visible, which is the same wait. **Run `39741033694` on commit `bb419abe` measured the whole acceptance with the fix in it: 117 tests passed in 6.9 minutes, with the navigation's compact rail green (864ms) and both of the preview's new specs green (925ms and 1.0s).**
- **the manifest hygiene was measured, and it is clean, and now it is guarded.** `tests/platform/workspace-manifest-hygiene.test.ts` reads every workspace's imports out of the syntax tree rather than out of the text, because a `require` inside a template literal is not an import: the OpenLIT workspace sync _builds_ a script that requires `@prisma/client` inside the OpenLIT container, where that package is a dependency of the container and not of this workspace, and a text scan reports that generated script as a missing dependency of Data. Two properties are held: every import a workspace makes is a dependency its manifest declares, or is the workspace's own name -- the runtime's own modules reach each other through the exports map that states the contract -- and a cross-workspace import reaches only for an export the target declares, because a caller that reaches past it into `src/` is reading an implementation the target has not published. The measurement is clean for all four workspaces and for the root. **The guard was run against scratch violations and failed on both**: a Data source importing a package nobody declares, and a Console module reaching past Data's exports map into `src/rulesync/rulesync-repository.ts` -- each failure naming the file and the import. The root package declares no `main` and no `exports`, so there is no root implementation facade in place to restore.
- **the interaction contract is now measured in a browser, and the sandbox can measure it too.** Two properties cannot be read out of the markup: a control that is working keeps the operator's place, and a region that scrolls is reachable by a keyboard. `console/e2e/console-interaction-acceptance.spec.ts` measures both against the Console's own build: at 390px the agents table's region is focusable and the arrow keys scroll it, and the prompt preview's control keeps the focus from the click through the answer while it is working (`aria-disabled`, never disabled). Both were found by measuring rather than by reading: the preview disabled its control while the request was in flight, and the permission matrix scrolled sideways with nothing focusable inside it. **The browser can be started in the sandbox after all**, with one process: the multi-process launch dies on a Mach-port rendezvous the sandbox cannot register (`bootstrap_check_in ... Permission denied`), and `AUTODEV_ACCEPTANCE_SINGLE_PROCESS=1` starts the acceptance with `--single-process --no-sandbox` instead. A single-process browser does not survive a second page, so the specs are run one at a time locally; the runner, which starts a real browser, runs them together. **Run `39751634232` on commit `8a6b89d6` measured the whole acceptance with both specs in it: 119 tests passed in 3.6 minutes**, with the table's region green (1.3s) and the preview's focus green (2.5s).
- **the Console's own gates were red on main, and the two causes in the Console are fixed.** The `Gates` workflow's formatting step named two Console files, and one of them re-exported a symbol the episode presentation module does not own: `executionModeLabel`, passed through from the module that owns it, with no consumer of that path anywhere. `tests/console/nav-ownership.test.ts` exists to stop exactly that shape -- a module that re-exports a symbol owned by another module gives it a second documented home -- and it was failing on main. The pass-through is gone (and with it the missing newline it left behind), and the other file the formatting named is Prettier's own form again. **Run `39760152372` on commit `40646b5c` reports Check formatting: success and Typecheck: success**, and the ownership guard is no longer among the failures; the Console acceptance in the same push, run `39760152424`, measured **119 tests passed in 2.8 minutes**. The lint gate is still red, on 286 pre-existing errors in the playtesting strand's own files (`runtime/src/playtesting/*`, `data/src/playtesting/*`, `console/src/features/playtesting/*`); none of them is in a file this pass touched, and that debt belongs to the session that owns the strand.
- **the fixes are live in the console an operator uses.** The installed service on :3300 could not be restarted from inside the sandbox -- `launchctl` and `kill` are both denied -- so for a while it kept serving the build it was started with, and the new build was started a second time through the service's own launcher on **:3425** to be measured against it. The published build has since been installed: :3300 now answers with the same fixes, measured in Chromium on the user-facing port. The permission matrix is a named, focusable region ("Effective role capability matrix", `tabindex=0`) whose right-hand columns the arrow keys scroll at 390px -- 0 to 40 pixels, with a 2px focus ring -- and whose cells hold nothing focusable, which is the case that was unreachable before. The prompt preview's control says "working" without leaving the focus order: while the request is in flight it carries `aria-disabled="true"` and `data-submitting="true"`, it is never natively disabled, its label reads "Previewing…", and `document.activeElement` stays the control from the click through the answer. The failure notice carries its reason and no countdown of its own. `pnpm install:codex` is what publishes and restarts: it builds into a staging dir, publishes, and restarts, so the old build stays in place if the build fails.
- **the playtesting strand's working controls now say "working" the way the rest of the Console says it, and the rule lives in the vocabulary.** The shared button vocabulary said a busy control keeps its focus, and the Console's own surfaces used it -- but the playtesting surfaces still disabled their controls while they worked, which is the one thing a disabled control does that the operator feels: it drops them out of the page's focus order, and the request is one the operator just started. **So the rule moved into the vocabulary: a busy control does not act.** It is announced as unavailable, it keeps its place in the page, and the second press is swallowed by the shared button rather than reaching the caller's handler -- which is what makes the busy state a safe replacement for a control that was disabled while it worked. The comparison decision, the analyst dispatch, the visual target revocation and the overview's primary launch action say "working" now. What is genuinely unavailable stays disabled: a decision with no reason, a dispatch with no workspace, a launch with no approved target, and the revocations waiting for the one in flight. The playtesting acceptance is the guard: runs `39762727346` and `39763463753` on commits `37e39307` and `9d445775` measured **119 tests passed** each time, the playtesting project's twenty-eight specs among them. Measured in Chromium against the newest production build: the permission matrix is a named, focusable region whose right-hand columns the arrow keys scroll at 390px (0 to 40 pixels, a 2px focus ring), and the prompt preview keeps the focus on its control from the click through the answer.
- **the lint gate was red on main, and it is green now.** The `Gates` workflow's Lint step had been failing since the previous afternoon, on 286 errors in 38 files, all of them in the playtesting strand. Most of what it named was not a defect but the repository's own formatting: 162 were the rules a tool can settle without a judgement -- imports in the wrong order, imports nothing used, numeric literals without separators, switch cases without braces -- and those were settled by the gate's own fixer. The ten files that came out in eslint's shape rather than Prettier's were then put in Prettier's form, because the import order eslint wants and the line wrapping Prettier wants are not the same thing. The strand settled the rest in the playtesting layer, and the last of the gate was this: the lint gate gives the repository's tests a different bar from the rest of it -- bounded complexity, no line limits, no fixture strings hoisted into constants -- because a test states its fixtures, so a literal repeated across a fixture and a regex built inside an assertion are the shape of a test rather than a smell in it. **The acceptance specs are tests by every other measure** -- they drive the product in a browser and assert what it did -- but they were not covered by the glob that carries the rule, so the playtesting acceptance was the file that paid for it. The acceptance's _fixture_ is not a test: it stands in for the Control API, so it keeps the Runtime's bar. The lint gate reads the repository the way git sees it now as well, so a scratch directory or a build output can no longer decide whether it passes.
- **the acceptance's own failures are the environment, not the code.** The `Gates` workflow's Test step was red on the same runs, and the failures read like broken features: the openlit patch set, the statistics worker, the visual browser, the capability and human-study contracts. Run where the environment allows, they pass: the statistics file is 13/13 here, the control-api file that carries the capability, human-study and run-owner assertions is 33/33, and the adapter-mount file is 5/5. The two that cannot pass anywhere here are the ones that need something the machine will not give: the openlit patch set needs to clone a repository it cannot write into, and the visual loop needs a browser the sandbox will not start. The Console's own acceptance is the gate that measures the Console, and it is green.
- **the canonical skill is on the shared reconciliation contract, and the page that edits it shows the verdict.** A skill reaches the runtime as a link to the canonical source itself rather than as a projection, so the runtime's observation of a skill is a live fact: the installed link holds this source or it does not. That makes the observed generation the canonical revision whenever it does, and `null` when it does not -- the difference between "the runtime is running this" and "nothing has been observed", which the shared contract keeps apart. The Runtime answers the question through the platform layer that owns the installed-skill layout, so the Control API does not repeat the path, and the skill content read carries the view so the page can render the verdict, the generations behind it and the operation history. **Measured both ways**: the runtime test installs the link and reads `converged` with the observed generation equal to the canonical revision, then takes the link away and reads `not-observed` with no observed generation; the console test pins that the page renders the Runtime's own generations rather than deriving its own; and `console/e2e/skills-reconciliation-acceptance.spec.ts` drives `/skills/code-review` in a browser and reads the verdict, both generations and the empty operation history off the page ("the skill page reports the runtime's observation of the canonical source", 724ms, and "the skill page states that no operation has been recorded for the resource", 388ms). Run `39787706123` on commit `35e733a3` measured the whole acceptance green: **121 tests passed in 3.9 minutes**.
- **the provider's own convergence is on the shared reconciliation contract, and the page that edits a provider shows it.** The per-role convergence answered only the role's own assignment: a provider read told the operator that each role had or had not been observed, and nothing about the provider as a whole, so the page that edits a provider's roles and limits could not say whether the configuration the operator saved was the configuration the router was serving, and the operations recorded for the provider were not on the page at all. **A provider's routing configuration is Runtime-owned: the router consults the live routing policy for every request**, so there is no projection to refresh and nothing to restart between an apply and its effect. The provider's desired generation is therefore the identity of its configured routing state -- whether it is disabled, its agent limits and its role assignments together -- taken over a canonical serialization, so it changes exactly when the configuration changes and is the same for two providers in the same state. The observed generation is that same state read back from the policy the router serves, and it is reported only once the runtime has observed an apply for one of the provider's own resources: before any write the verdict is `not-observed` rather than a synthesized convergence, and a refused write is recorded in the history without counting as an apply, because a refusal changed nothing. The provider's resources are matched exactly rather than by prefix, because the operation history matches by prefix and the provider path `claude` would otherwise also match the history of a provider named `claude-code`. The read carries the view (Providers v3, the shared compatibility revision v11), the Console renders the Runtime's own view rather than deriving one, and the panel is the same shared panel the skill page uses. **Measured**: the runtime test reads the providers response before any write and finds `not-observed` with no observed generation and a digest-shaped desired generation; a viewer's refused write is recorded in the history and leaves the provider unobserved; and an applied limits write changes the provider's desired generation and is observed as `converged` with the observed generation equal to the desired one. `console/e2e/providers-reconciliation-acceptance.spec.ts` drives `/providers/claude` in a browser and reads the verdict, both generations and the empty operation history off the page ("the provider page reports the runtime's view of the provider", 1.1s, and "the provider page states that no operation has been recorded for the provider", 579ms). Run `39802018848` on commit `7478d2fb` measured the whole acceptance green: **125 tests passed in 4.1 minutes**, with the two provider specs green (712ms and 738ms). The gates on the same commit are unchanged by it -- the formatting, lint and test steps fail on the playtesting strand's own files exactly as they did on the commit before it (82 test failures in both runs, none of them a provider or a reconciliation), and the typecheck step is green.
- **the MCP page now shows what the Runtime has actually reached, and the catalog stays a configuration read.** The MCP catalog answered only "what is declared": it carried the canonical RuleSync declaration and the role projection, and every server read as unconnected no matter what the Runtime had done with it, so a declared server and a reached server looked identical on the page. **The two answers are separate questions, and the contract keeps them apart.** The Runtime's observations of the MCP servers it has reached are published on their own read path (`GET /control/mcp-runtime`, schema `autodev-control-mcp-runtime-v1`), not folded into the catalog, and the MCP page composes the two reads rather than the catalog carrying the other's claim -- which is what the target state's "composable on the same resource pages while remaining separate architectural data/control paths" asks for. The observation carries the Runtime's own verdict in the Runtime's own vocabulary (`configured`, `ready`, `error`, `observed`, `stale`), its initialization and tool-discovery attempts, its failures, the roles the server was seen from, and the tools it was seen calling; the Console renders that verdict and never derives one of its own. **A server the Runtime has not observed says so, and a server the Runtime could not be asked about says something different.** The observations arrive through a registered source, the way the live agent counts and the provider health do, so a Control API with no router attached reports the evidence as unavailable (`observedServers: null`) rather than reporting zero observed servers; and a Runtime that was asked and reached no MCP server reports `observedServers: 0` -- a finding, not a gap. The page carries the claim per row rather than once for the page, so a server the Runtime has reached and a server it has not are told apart on the same list. The observed tool calls are labelled as what was seen in use and kept apart from the configured allowlist, which is a different thing. **Measured**: `runtime/tests/control-api-mcp-evidence.test.ts` reads the catalog and finds no row carrying an observation, reads the runtime path with no source attached and finds the evidence unavailable, reads it with a source that observed nothing and finds a count of zero, and projects the Runtime's own telemetry into the record it publishes; `tests/router/control-api.test.ts` reads the path through the Control API and finds the Runtime's record published as it was reported, with the catalog beside it still configuration-only. `console/e2e/mcps-detail-acceptance.spec.ts` drives `/mcps` and `/mcps/{name}` in a browser against the synthetic `/control/mcps` and `/control/mcp-runtime` reads and asserts the per-row connection claim, the observed-server and runtime-health summary in the Runtime's own numbers, and the Runtime's evidence on the detail page ("MCPs keeps the declared default state, the missing declaration and the connection states apart", "the MCP detail reports the runtime's evidence for a server it has observed"). Run `39826557557` on commit `ceb66f7b` measured the whole acceptance green: **126 tests passed in 3.4 minutes**, with all eight MCP specs green (903ms, 329ms, 443ms, 1.3s, 337ms, 674ms, 511ms and 570ms). The gates on the same commit are unchanged by it -- the formatting, lint and typecheck steps are green, and the test step fails on the five playtesting-strand tests (a missing Docker socket and a symlinked approval root), exactly the five that failed on the commit before it (1079 tests with 1069 passing and 5 failing, against 1074/1064/5 before), so this slice adds none.
- **the MCP page can now say whether what the operator declared is what the Runtime applied.** The canonical RuleSync source is authoritative and the applied projection is generated from it, so the two are worth comparing: a server that is declared but not applied is a gap the operator can act on, and the MCP page could not see one at all. **The comparison is exact, and it is the Runtime's.** The Data layer publishes the canonical launch configuration one target would receive -- losslessly about the launch keys, because a comparison that cannot see a key cannot see it drift, and a target's own declaration winning over the base declaration for the same key -- and the Runtime reads the bridge catalogue the installer renders from that projection and compares the two through the shared reconciliation contract: the desired generation is the declaration's launch configuration and the observed generation is the applied projection's. Both sides are serialized through one function, so their digests are comparable and a difference in any launch key changes the digest. **A configuration that was never applied is not a converged empty one.** A machine that has never had the MCP configuration applied reports `not-observed`, and a catalogue that cannot be read reports `error`; neither is reported as an applied configuration with nothing in it. The applied configuration is published on its own read path (`GET /control/mcp-applied`, schema `autodev-control-mcp-applied-v1`, the shared compatibility revision v13), beside the declaration and the observation rather than folded into either, and the MCP detail page renders the Runtime's own launch configuration and the shared reconciliation panel beside the declaration. **Measured**: `runtime/tests/control-api-mcp-applied.test.ts` converges on a matching catalogue, reports a drifted catalogue as pending with two different generations, reports a missing catalogue as not-observed, and reports an unreadable catalogue as an error; against this repository's own installed catalogue the canonical declaration's codexcli target reproduces all eight applied servers key for key. `console/e2e/mcps-detail-acceptance.spec.ts` drives `/mcps/{name}?tab=configuration` in a browser and reads the applied launch configuration, the Runtime's verdict and both generations off the page, and the note on a server the Runtime did not publish ("the MCP detail shows the applied configuration and the runtime's verdict on it", 768ms).
- full retained-feature Console integration/parity remains open;

Patch-by-patch implementation history, superseded local image tags, and resolved intermediate failures belong in Git history/PR evidence rather than the active target or migration requirements. Keep this tracker focused on the current baseline and still-open gaps.

## Cutover rule

Do not remove an incumbent path until the replacement has end-to-end evidence. Once cutover is proven, remove the obsolete compatibility path instead of preserving permanent duplicate implementations.
